title: Online Learning of Heterogeneous Locomotion Dynamics under Reinforcement Learning Policies for Precise Loco-Manipulation
authors: Tianlin Zhang,Weipeng Xia,Lingwei Zhang,Yiyang Shao,Zhongyu Li,Yun-Hui Liu
comment: . Supplementary video:this https URL
abstract:
How to reuse a pretrained locomotion policy for precise loco-manipulation is still an open problem.
We propose an online method to learn the closed-loop dynamics under a frozen locomotion policy.
The learned model predicts floating-base motion and improves loco-manipulation accuracy.
However, unobserved latent conditions of the policy introduce heterogeneous responses,
meaning that the same observed state will lead to different motions.
Direct learning without accounting for this heterogeneity introduces bias and fluctuations
into dynamics estimates, degrading floating-base prediction and end-effector tracking.
To address this problem, a contaminated Gaussian model is proposed to approximate
the effects of latent conditions. The model uses two Gaussian components to approximate predictable
and unpredictable responses under the same observed state.
Then, the contaminated Gaussian model is combined with a Gaussian process to construct
an online learner using random Fourier features (RFFs).
The learner estimates each response’s probability of belonging to the predictable component
and uses it to weight online updates, capturing predictable responses
while reducing bias and fluctuations caused by heterogeneous observations.
With consistent and unbiased dynamics estimates, model predictive control (MPC) predicts
floating-base motion accurately and enables precise loco-manipulation.
A finite-sample error bound is established to ensure uniform convergence in online learning.
Simulation and hardware experiments demonstrate consistent end-effector
tracking across different manipulator configurations and tasks, with errors of 0.01 m.
introduction:
The heterogeneity of closed-loop dynamics under frozen
reinforcement learning (RL) locomotion policies has been largely overlooked,
degrading tracking accuracy when these policies are reused for loco-manipulation.
Although policy parameters remain frozen, unobserved latent states like
environmental conditions will produce different closed-loop responses under
the same observed state, as shown in Fig. 1.
Ignoring this heterogeneity leads to inaccurate locomotion prediction and
feedforward compensation.
The resulting errors propagate through whole-body kinematics to the end
effector, limiting manipulation precision. This motivates the central
question of this work: How can the heterogeneity of closed-loop dynamics
under a frozen RL locomotion policy be accounted for to achieve precise
loco-manipulation?

Legged loco-manipulation combines the mobility of legged robots with the
dexterity of manipulators, enabling whole-body interaction over workspaces
that cannot be reached from a fixed support [1] and
thereby attracting substantial research attention.
Recent advances in reinforcement learning (RL) have substantially advanced
legged locomotion, enabling robust controllers to operate across diverse
conditions [2, 3].
This progress, however, has not yet translated into equally mature
loco-manipulation.
Existing approaches still face challenges in achieving precise
loco-manipulation with sample efficiency while accommodating conflicting
task objectives [4, 5].
Sample-based policy optimization explores a high-dimensional state–action
space, whereas exact end-effector pose constraints, under regular kinematic
conditions, restrict feasible configurations to a lower-dimensional manifold
of zero measure in the full configuration space [6].
With finite tracking tolerances, admissible configurations occupy a
neighborhood that narrows as the required precision increases, making
successful samples difficult to obtain through unguided exploration.
Conflicts between locomotion and manipulation further complicate policy
optimization.
For example, efficient locomotion generally favors a nearly horizontal
floating-base, whereas end-effector tracking may require base tilting and
fine posture regulation.
Increasing the emphasis on one objective will therefore degrade the
other [7].
To mitigate this conflict, advantage mixing combines task-specific
advantage functions during training [8], cooperative policy
learning coordinates separately parameterized locomotion and manipulation
policies [9], and multi-critic learning separates reward
signals to reduce interference between objectives [7].
Despite these advances, consistently reconciling precise end-effector
tracking with robust locomotion across diverse task conditions remains an
open problem.

Reusing the locomotion policy through an explicit dynamics model offers a
promising way to retain its mobility capability while handling manipulation
objectives.
Offline approaches identify low-dimensional linear models of RL-controlled
robots [10] or learn motion models that map high-level
commands to the response of a black-box locomotion controller
[11].
Online dynamics learning further adapts predictions during deployment.
For example, representative methods use random Fourier features (RFFs) for recursive
identification [12] or dual Gaussian processes to
combine rapid adaptation with long-term memory [13].
However, these methods assume homogeneous system dynamics, where each
observed state corresponds to a single response.
They therefore pool observations from hidden operating conditions without
distinguishing their conditional responses.
This is restrictive when the same observed state and command correspond to
different response distributions.
Changes in the proportions of these conditions shift the pooled mean, while
differences among their conditional means introduce additional
between-condition covariance.
An offline model will consequently lose accuracy when the deployment
conditions differ from those represented in its identification data.
Online updates will follow transient mean shifts and alter the reference
response needed for subsequent compensation.
With limited online data, prediction errors also reflect epistemic
uncertainty in the learned mean, complicating the distinction between an
informative sample and a deviation associated with another operating
condition [14].
These effects reduce the reliability of learned predictions for precise
whole-body control.

To address this problem, an online learning method is proposed to account
for heterogeneous locomotion dynamics under a frozen reinforcement learning
policy and enable precise loco-manipulation.
The learner targets a reference residual mean associated with routine task
dynamics, including whole-body coupling and sustained task contact.
A contaminated Gaussian model anchors both components to the reference mean
and approximates additional deviations associated with other latent
conditions through covariance inflation.
A Gaussian process constructed with RFFs estimates the reference mean and
quantifies epistemic uncertainty.
Posterior probabilities from the contaminated Gaussian model account for
the epistemic uncertainty when weighting online updates, limiting the
influence of heterogeneous deviations while supporting learning in poorly
observed regions.
The learned residual model is then integrated into whole-body model
predictive control (MPC), where epistemic uncertainty regulates feedforward
compensation along the prediction horizon, limiting reliance on unreliable
predictions in regions insufficiently covered by online data.
As shown in Fig. 2,
the resulting method accounts for heterogeneous responses, enabling precise loco-manipulation without
retraining the locomotion policy.

The main contributions of this work are summarized as follows:

The statistical heterogeneity of locomotion dynamics under a frozen
RL policy is characterized through latent-conditioned response
distributions. The effects of pooled mean shifts and between-condition
covariance are analyzed, motivating a contaminated Gaussian approximation
centered on a task-relevant reference mean.

A posterior-weighted RFF online learner is proposed to account
jointly for heterogeneous response deviations and epistemic uncertainty
when learning locomotion dynamics under a frozen policy. A finite-sample
error bound is established to ensure uniform convergence in online
learning.

A residual-augmented MPC controller is developed to
regulate learned feedforward compensation using epistemic uncertainty
along the prediction horizon. Simulations across manipulator
configurations and hardware experiments involving trajectory tracking,
object grasping, door opening, disturbance recovery, and manipulation on
the move demonstrate precise loco-manipulation without retraining the
locomotion policy.

title: Movens-Zero: Scaling Humanoid Motion Foundation Models with Large-Scale Human Videos
authors: Wendong Bu,Tinghong Ye,Qizhou Wang,Jiacheng Li,Zhiqi Ge,Yuze Lin,Zhongqi Yue,Yi Su,Jingyu Wang,Kai Shen,Jingdong Liu,Chengyuan Deng,Xiaoxuan Chen,Xin Tan,Jiaming Ji,Wenqiao Zhang,Chenghong Jiang,Tuoyu Li,Siliang Tang,Jun Xiao,Tat-Seng Chua,Yueting Zhuang,Xingxing Wang,Juncheng Li
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
comment: Technical report. . Project page:this https URL
abstract:
Scaling humanoid motion foundation models is constrained by the scarcity of diverse, robot-executable data and by the difficulty of jointly learning from heterogeneous multimodal inputs while supporting real-time closed-loop control.
We present Movens-5M, constructed from raw Internet videos through clip generation, quality filtering, semantic annotation, motion recovery, and physical refinement with humanoid retargeting and execution verification.
It contains 15 million human-motion sequences and 5 million physically executable humanoid-motion sequences spanning over 10,000 hours, aligned with text, RGB video, speech, and music.
Building on this data, we introduce Movens-Zero, a scalable understanding–generation–execution architecture that supports joint learning across modalities and real-time closed-loop execution.
Task-mixed flow-matching training jointly optimizes a single action expert across seven generation tasks, enabling direct motion generation from text, speech, music, and video. Multimodal Real-Time Chunking connects overlapping chunks under continuously updated instructions and robot states for continuous closed-loop execution.
We further introduce Movens-Intent, a four-track benchmark with 8,192 expert-verified condition–motion pairs across text, speech, music, and video.
Experiments show consistent gains across all four modalities when scaling execution-verified data from 1% to 100% and action-expert capacity from 64M to 911M parameters, while demonstrating that data quality and cross-modal supervision improve generation and execution.
introduction:
Scaling training data and model capacity has substantially improved the capabilities and generalization of language and vision models (Brown et al., 2020; Gemini Team, 2023; OpenAI, 2024).
However, training data for humanoid robots are difficult to acquire directly from the Internet, unlike the vast web text corpora available for language modeling.
But the Internet contains countless human videos capturing actions and scenes, offering a potential data source (Mao et al., 2024; Wu et al., 2026).
This raises a natural question: can we scale learning through human videos from the Internet to build generalist humanoid robots?
Generalist humanoid robots would use vision and hearing to perceive their surroundings and understand human instructions in real time, then autonomously generate and execute humanoid motion in a closed loop, just like humans.
However, such robots have yet to be realized.
Based on experience in language and vision, we argue that this is because humanoid motion foundation models have not scaled up to the same extent as general-purpose foundation models in language and vision, limiting emergent capabilities such as multimodal instruction following.

Why haven’t humanoid motion foundation models scaled up?
Two closely related challenges constrain further scaling.
First, scaling data construction: how can human videos from the Internet be converted into supervision suitable for large-scale robot learning?
Internet videos vary widely in quality, and issues such as camera shake and occlusion can introduce errors into motion recovery (Shen et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2025b).
Even when human motion is accurately recovered, the human–robot embodiment gap can introduce further errors during motion retargeting (Xu et al., 2025b; Araujo et al., 2025).
Moreover, even if the resulting robot motion is accurate, it may not satisfy physical constraints, so its executability still needs to be verified.
Building generalist humanoid robots also requires multimodal human instructions accurately aligned with robot motion to support large-scale training for multimodal instruction following.
Second, scaling model training: how can large-scale training improve multimodal instruction following while supporting real-time closed-loop control?
Text, audio, and video differ in format and temporal structure.
A shared motion-prediction architecture is needed to handle these heterogeneous inputs.
Building on this architecture, a common learning objective and joint training strategy are needed to learn from data across modalities.
Scaling model capacity also increases inference costs, making real-time closed-loop control more challenging.

To construct supervision suitable for large-scale robot learning from human videos, we develop a multi-stage data engine that integrates fine-grained quality assessment, iterative motion refinement, and execution-based verification.
The pipeline shown in Figure 2 performs filtering, semantic annotation, motion recovery, physical refinement, cross-embodiment retargeting, and execution-based verification.
Through this pipeline, we construct Movens-5M entirely from raw videos collected across diverse Internet sources, rather than simply aggregating existing small-scale motion datasets.
The resulting dataset contains more than 10,000 hours and 5 million physically executable humanoid motion sequences, paired with corresponding human motions and aligned text, RGB video, speech, and music.
As summarized in Table 1, with 297 motion types, 16 coarse scenes, 6 physical-constraint families, and verification under 4 tracking policies, Movens-5M provides the volume, diversity, multimodal supervision, and executable quality needed to study data scaling for multimodal instruction following.
Details of data filtering, motion quality assessment, retargeting and execution verification are provided in Appendix A.
To support consistent evaluation of multimodal instruction following in humanoid robots, we further introduce Movens-Intent, a four-track benchmark comprising 8,192 expert-verified multimodal instructions across text, speech, music, and video (e.g., executing spoken commands, dancing to music, and video-based teleoperation).

Building on Movens-5M, we introduce Movens-Zero, an understanding–generation–execution architecture that unifies heterogeneous multimodal inputs for scalable instruction-following training while supporting real-time closed-loop control (Figure 7).
Its pretrained omni-modal backbone converts text, video, and audio into a shared token sequence that preserves temporal order and cross-modal context.
A shared flow-based action expert generates future motion conditioned jointly on this context, the latest observed robot state, and frame-wise motion progress.
At each generation step, Multimodal Real-Time Chunking (MM-RTC) receives the latest multimodal instruction and observed robot state and generates an overlapping motion chunk with the previous prediction’s unexecuted tail kept fixed, enabling continuous execution by a high-frequency tracking controller.
We jointly train the action expert in a task-mixed flow-matching stage across seven generation tasks.
During data and model scaling, the unified motion representation and training objective support joint learning from heterogeneous multimodal inputs, while MM-RTC translates multimodal instructions into motion chunks at a low generation frequency to support real-time closed-loop execution.
These designs enable multimodal instruction following to benefit from data and model scaling while remaining compatible with real-time closed-loop control.
The action expert scale configurations, task-mixture ratios, and complete training hyperparameters are provided in Appendices C and D.

Our experiments reveal three findings.
First, Movens-Zero jointly maintains condition alignment, motion fidelity, and robot executability across input modalities:
on the source-disjoint Movens-Intent benchmark, it achieves a text-conditioned R@3 of 62.57% (Table 3), reduces video-conditioned W-MPJPE100 to 49.1 mm, 16.2% lower than the strongest baseline (Table 4), reduces music-conditioned FID-k to 58.43, 1.7% lower than the strongest baseline (Table 5), and achieves a speech-conditioned R@3 of 74.30%, exceeding the strongest baseline by 11.90 percentage points (Table 6).
Second, increasing both data coverage and action-expert capacity yields consistent downstream gains:
with the model size fixed, scaling Movens-5M from 1% to 100% improves Text R@3 from 12.72% to 62.57% (Table 7). On the full dataset, scaling the action expert from 64.2M to 910.5M parameters improves Text R@3 from 10.30% to 62.57% (Table 8).
Third, data quality and cross-modal supervision improve generation and execution at matched scale:
with sample counts and training budgets matched, full data curation raises Text R@3 by 13.85 percentage points and Tracking Score from 0.41 to 0.72. Removing video–motion or audio–motion alignment lowers Text R@3 by 0.83 and 2.55 percentage points, respectively, while removing text–motion alignment increases Video MPJPE from 40.90 to 56.84 mm (Table 9).
Together, these findings establish a scalable path from web-scale multimodal human demonstrations to multimodal instruction following through humanoid motion generation and execution.

title: META-Robot: Self-Cognition and Capability Scaling in Agentic Robots
authors: Xuanzhi Feng,Zeyu Liu,Weiheng Gao,Xinchen Li,Jiankun Tang,Fangqi Zhu,Quanxin Shou,Hao Chen,Zhengyang Yan,Hualei Zhang,Junhao Li,Zhiyao Wu,Jie Zhang,Song Guo
abstract:
LLM-based robotic agent systems can generate programs for robot control, yet their generalization to new tasks often depends on elaborate scaffolding.
Expanding their skill repertoires alone offers limited guidance on how to assess new capabilities or identify what remains beyond their reach.
We introduce META-Robot, a framework that couples self cognition with capability scaling by expanding the criteria through which an agent evaluates and develops its skills.
At its core, action-level predicates express explicit conditions for assessing execution and provide a structured basis for LLM reasoning.
Using the resulting assessments, the agent identifies capability gaps, extends relevant evaluation criteria, and guides the structured expansion of its skills.
Proprioceptive feedback further grounds this self-scaling process in the robot’s physical state.
introduction:
Robotic agents have emerged as a promising paradigm for general-purpose robotic manipulation recently with generated code as control policy Liang et al. (2023); Xiao et al. (2026). While these systems Kumar (2026) can adapt to new tasks without training to some extent, their scalability remains limited. When tasks require evaluation criteria, feedback modalities, or skills beyond predefined scaffolds, agents cannot revise these system-level limitations, leading to repeated strategy switching and compounding ineffective modifications that make meta-level task generalization or reliable recovery nearly impossible.

Predicate scaling offers a natural solution by allowing agents to retain and reuse predicates acquired from previous tasks. This accumulation can improve transfer and reduce the need for additional predefined scaffolding. However, scaling predicates alone cannot overcome fixed system scaffolding, as systems cannot have explicit cognition of task and its own capability limits. Recent efforts to improve scalability follow a primary strategy: replacing accumulation of fixed predicates with validated, agent-discovered skills distilled from execution processes Zhang et al. (2026); Lu et al. (2026). This reduces manual engineering and allows past repairs to guide future tasks. However, these skills are accumulated without structured links to their expected effects and required evidence. Consequently, the skill library may continue to grow while the system’s understanding of the task and its own capabilities remains unchanged, limiting substantive capability scaling.

The emergence of Neuro-Symbolic Predicates (NSPs) Liang et al. (2025); Athalye et al. (2026) presents a compelling foundation for scaling robot agent system cognition beyond fixed mechanisms. By combining neural perceptual queries with programmatic logic, NSPs can construct abstractions for evaluation, offering a path toward adapting to new evaluation criteria. Nevertheless, extending predicate invention to self cognition and capability scaling in robotic agent systems remains challenging. Predicates must assess not only whether task goals are satisfied, but also whether the current system has sufficient observations, evaluation criteria, and executable skills. We argue that grounding predicates with physical evidence at the action level is crucial, as it allows the agent to exploit available proprioceptive signals when vision is insufficient, construct corresponding skills and evaluation criteria, and integrate them into control and verification, effectively coupling cognitive and capability scaling with evidence-grounded assessment.

To this end, we propose META-Robot, as illustrated in Fig. 1, a system for self cognition and capability scaling that grounds robotic meta-generalization in evidence-based, action-level predicates for both system self-assessment and task evaluation. By recording predicate transitions around skill executions, coupling validated predicates with reusable skills, and orchestrating proprioceptive feedback, META-Robot creates a scalable system for jointly scaling robotic cognition and capabilities.

META-Robot incorporates several key innovations. First, to mitigate the ambiguity between coarse execution logs and actual task-state changes, we introduce a closed-loop execution agent that evaluates each action execution through action-level predicate transitions. The agent records observations, inputs, outputs, and pre- and post-execution predicate states, associating program behavior with changes in robot action. When an error is detected, it performs targeted local repair and re-execution, followed by full-task validation of the revised program. Second, fixed evaluation criteria make failures beyond the coverage of the existing system difficult to diagnose and can lead to unstructured skill accumulation. To address this, META-Robot maintains coupled predicate and skill libraries that expand through validated execution experience. Although this design supports continual knowledge scaling, it also requires precise alignment between the two libraries. META-Robot establishes explicit predicate–skill associations to support grounded skill retrieval, composition, and expansion.

We conduct extensive experiments in both simulation environments [23] and real-world environments
to validate the effectiveness of META-Robot. (i) META-Robot achieves stronger overall performance than prior methods, reaching a success rate of 95.8% on the LIBERO-Pro Spatial-Task, compared with 60.0% for other baselines. Crucially, we observe (ii) emergent cognition and capabilities including the scaling of reusable skills and their corresponding evaluation criteria from validated execution experience. We further demonstrate (iii) robust generalization through zero-shot transfer to held-out long-horizon tasks without additional debugging and successful deployment across diverse real-robot tasks. Together with the ablation results, these findings establish META-Robot as a scalable framework for jointly expanding robotic cognition and capability. This paper makes the following contributions:

We introduce META-Robot, which scales its cognition and capability by jointly improving task policies and the supporting system itself through predicate-guided self-assessment.

We introduce META-Robot, which scales its cognition and capability by jointly improving task policies and the supporting system itself through predicate-guided self-assessment.

We develop coupled action-level predicate and skill libraries that support continual refinement of evaluation criteria and policies, as well as the generation of new structured criteria and skills beyond the existing repertoire.

We propose a proprioceptive signal orchestration mechanism that expands the system’s capacity for perception, evaluation, and control.

2. We develop coupled action-level predicate and skill libraries that support continual refinement of evaluation criteria and policies, as well as the generation of new structured criteria and skills beyond the existing repertoire.

3. We propose a proprioceptive signal orchestration mechanism that expands the system’s capacity for perception, evaluation, and control.

title: When the Simulator Fails, Not the Policy: Auditing Contact Artifacts in Simulated Robot Benchmarks
authors: Alex Zhou,Junhao Wu,Xueyang Zhou,Yixiao Huo,Hongcheng Gao,Di Zhu,Zhenghao Zhang,Yongchao Chen
comment: this https URL
abstract: Simulation benchmarks score robot policies by success rate, and every failed episode counts against the policy. Many of these failures are the simulator’s fault, not the policy’s; we find the cause and fix it. Testing a vision language action model and a world action model in simulation, we find that the policy often places the object and the simulator then ejects it, and that the benchmark’s own scripted demonstrations fail the same way. We present SimuGuard, an auditing plugin for LIBERO, RoboTwin, RoboCasa and RoboDojo. It leaves the evaluation unchanged. At every physics step, it records the state and flags an object that starts moving at a contact faster than the robot’s contact or gravity account for. It replays a recorded episode bit for bit, and it reruns the episode with one simulation parameter changed. With it we trace these episodes on RoboTwin step by step to the collision detection of the physics engine: for two pieces of collision geometry that are one to two centimeters apart, the engine reports a penetration of about two centimeters, and the contact solver removes that depth within the same physics step and throws the object out at several meters per second. The cause is one constant. The engine’s distance algorithm discards a triangle whose area falls below a fixed threshold, valid triangles fall below it once the collision geometry is at the centimeter scale, and a later version of the engine lowered the threshold by seven orders of magnitude. With that constant changed and nothing else, the false contacts disappear from the recorded pose sequences, from the benchmark’s scripted demonstrations, and from closed loop evaluation, where episodes with an artifact fall from 12 in 100 to none and the success rate on five container tasks rises from 89% to 98%. Success rates in simulation thus count failures that the simulator causes. Benchmarks on PhysX 5.3.1 or earlier should rerun in a repaired engine. Where the engine cannot change, they should report the success rate together with the range it spans when every flagged episode fails or passes: 75.8% to 98.5% around a reported 83.1% for LingBot-VA.
introduction:
Simulation benchmarks give a repeatable way to compare robot policies, from vision language action (VLA) models to world action models (Brohan et al., 2023a; Brohan et al., 2023b; Octo Model Team et al., 2024; Kim et al., 2024; Black et al., 2024; Björck et al., 2025; Gemini Robotics Team, 2025; Li et al., 2026). LIBERO (Liu et al., 2023), RoboCasa (Nasiriany et al., 2024) and RoboTwin (Mu et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2025) fix the tasks and the protocol and treat the simulator as faithful physics. Their success rates record which episodes failed, not why. A failure caused by the simulator’s treatment of contact enters the same count as a failure caused by the policy. Testing a world action model and a VLA in simulation, we find that such failures are frequent: the policy places the object, and the simulator throws it out.

In an episode of RoboTwin 2.0’s Place Can Basket, LingBot-VA (Li et al., 2026) places a can inside the basket, resting against its wall. The gripper releases it. After 0.28 s, within a single 4 ms physics step, PhysX reports a piece of the can 2.75 cm inside a piece of the basket wall, although the two pieces are 2.1 cm apart, and the can’s speed rises from 0.2 to 22 m/s while no robot link touches it and the robot is nearly still; the basket ejects it, the can lands 1.65 m away, and the benchmark records a failure (Figure 1). Nothing in the recording supplies the 2.4 J the can gains: no robot contact in that step and no drop. Replayed with the same recorded actions and the reported depth removed over several physics steps instead of one, the episode passes the benchmark’s own success check (Figure 3); in the engine with one constant of its distance algorithm corrected, the contact is never reported (Section 4.2). We call a contact response that sets an object moving faster than the robot’s contact or gravity account for a contact artifact. The impulse that starts one lasts a single physics step and falls between two camera frames; a video shows the can flying, not what launched it, and the success check cannot tell whether the policy or the simulator decided the episode.

SimuGuard is an auditing plugin that leaves the evaluation unchanged (Figure 2). An adapter attaches it to the benchmark’s own evaluation script; we provide adapters for LIBERO, RoboTwin, RoboCasa and RoboDojo. At every physics step it records the actuation, the object states and the contacts, and flags an object that starts moving at a contact faster than the robot’s contact or gravity account for. It replays a recorded episode bit for bit by rebuilding the seeded scene and applying the recorded actuation from the first step. A rerun is a replay with one simulation parameter changed, with the recorded actuation and the success check fixed. Prior work adds metrics to the success rate (Wang et al., 2025; Snyder et al., 2026; Jiang et al., 2026) or measures how solvers depart from physics (Erez et al., 2015; Le Lidec et al., 2023); neither connects an anomalous contact in a rollout to the outcome of that rollout.

In short, many failures in simulated robot benchmarks are the simulator’s fault, not the policy’s; we find the cause and fix it. Our contributions are:

A finding and its cause. Simulated benchmarks contain frequent episodes in which the policy has placed the object and the simulator then ejects it, so the benchmark scores a failure of the policy. On five RoboTwin tasks that place objects into containers with thin walls, 40 of LingBot-VA’s 44 failures and 6 of HyVLA’s 10 contain such an ejection, and the benchmark’s own scripted demonstrations, which act on ground truth object poses, fail the same way. We trace it to a fixed threshold in the distance algorithm of PhysX 5.3.1, which makes the engine report a penetration between pieces that do not touch; with that constant set to its value in PhysX 5.4.0, the ejections are gone.

A tool. SimuGuard monitors every physics step, replays a recorded episode bit for bit, and reruns it with one simulation parameter changed, so that a single contact report can be traced to the outcome of its episode and the trace verified by anyone. It attaches to the benchmark’s own evaluation script without changing it, on LIBERO, RoboTwin, RoboCasa and RoboDojo.

An evaluation practice. Where the cause of the artifacts can be removed, we measure the policy in the repaired engine: LingBot-VA succeeds in 98 of 100 closed loop episodes on the five tasks against 89 in the benchmark’s engine, with no artifact against 12 episodes. title: SketchMate: Agentic Geometric Reasoning for Zero-Shot Precision Insertion
authors: Jiaming Wang
abstract: Inserting an unseen part requires sub-millimetre precision and the correct orientation of keyed features. Current zero-shot agentic manipulation methods built on vision-language models (VLMs) produce spatial outputs that are far too coarse for this. We propose to let a VLM build a sketch model of the task, i.e., a few geometric primitives and two mate frames, which a VLM agent measures with geometric tools in multi-view depth and which a standard planner and compliant controller execute. Because a sketch describes the parts independently of their placement, the robot needs to build it only once per task. A sketch memory stores each agent run and transfers the stored sketch to later placements by point-cloud registration, so that the VLM is called only for unfamiliar parts. After grasping the part, the robot inspects both mating faces at close range and corrects the sketch by shape matching. On 69 simulated insertion episodes, our method inserts 88% of the parts at the assembled pose in a strict kinematic test, while ReKep and MOKA with the same VLM insert none. On new placements of eight tasks, reusing one stored run inserts as many parts as calling the agent in each episode, and it produces the sketch in 3.4 s3.4\text{\,}\mathrm{s} instead of about 90 s90\text{\,}\mathrm{s}.
introduction:
Insertion is at the heart of robotic assembly, whether a plug goes into a receptacle, a transceiver into a network card or a peg into a fixture. It is also the step that resists generalization. Typical parts mate with clearances of 0.1 mm to 0.3 mm0.1\text{\,}\mathrm{m}\mathrm{m}0.3\text{\,}\mathrm{m}\mathrm{m} and tolerate rotational errors of only one or two degrees. Many of them are also keyed, which means that they fit in a single orientation. For this reason, industrial practice engineers each new part individually with CAD models, fixtures and manually taught poses, and learning-based methods train a dedicated policy for each assembly or family of assemblies (Tang et al., 2023; Tang et al., 2024; Guo et al., 2025). In this paper, we investigate whether a robot can instead insert an unseen part, given only camera observations and a natural-language instruction such as “insert the USB plug into the task board”.

Vision-language models (VLMs) are a natural source of such generality, since they know what a USB plug is and which receptacle it belongs to. In agentic robotics, VLMs and other foundation models make at run time some of the decisions that engineers otherwise make before deployment (Wang et al., 2026). However, current zero-shot manipulation methods ground this knowledge in coarse spatial representations, such as marks and image tiles (Fang et al., 2024), keypoints on image patches with constraints written by the VLM (Huang et al., 2024b), or value maps on a voxel grid (Huang et al., 2023). The resolution of these representations is limited by patches and voxels of several millimetres. In addition, these methods ask the VLM to infer 3D correspondences from an image, for example which point of the plug has to meet which point of the receptacle.

We find that these representations are insufficient for insertion. When we port ReKep and MOKA to our tasks with our VLM, planner and controller, they insert none of the 69 parts at the assembled pose (Section 4.2).

Our approach assigns the semantic decisions to the VLM and the measurements to geometry. We let the VLM construct a sketch model of the task, which consists of a few geometric primitives covering the moving part and two mate frames. These frames locate the mating end of the moving part and specify which opening of the fixed part it enters, or which post it slides onto, and in which orientation (Figure 1). The VLM builds the sketch iteratively in an agent loop, using geometric tools that operate on multi-view depth data. In this division of labour, the VLM decides what to measure, and the tools provide the precision. For example, the VLM points at the rim of a hole, and a tool returns the circle fitted to the corresponding 3D points. A standard motion planner and a compliant controller then execute the sketch.

Running the agent takes roughly 90 s90\text{\,}\mathrm{s} and tens of thousands of tokens per episode, which is costly to repeat whenever the same parts reappear. However, a sketch describes the parts themselves independently of their placement, which means that the robot needs to construct it only once per task. We store each agent run in a sketch memory along with the point clouds of both parts. In a later episode, we register these point clouds to the new scene and transfer the stored sketch, so that the VLM is consulted only for parts that the memory fails to recognize.

Keyed parts reveal a second problem. The agent reliably identifies which part goes into which opening, but it frequently misreads the rotation of the moving part, for instance the side of a USB plug that carries the tongue (Section 4.3). More precise measurements cannot correct this correspondence error, because the VLM itself chooses the measurements.

However, the correspondence becomes a geometric problem as soon as both mating faces are visible. After grasping the part, our robot therefore holds its mating end over an upward-facing camera, views the fixed part at close range with a wrist camera, and searches for the pose in which the two shapes best complement each other. Because both views are close, the same search also corrects offsets below the resolution of the scene cameras, as well as the registration errors of reused sketches. The sketch still provides the opening, the axis and the depth, and it resolves ties between fits that are geometrically equivalent.

We evaluate our method in simulation on assemblies from AutoMate (Tang et al., 2024), connectors built to their published dimensions, a NIST-style task board (Kimble et al., 2020), the parts of the AI for Industry Challenge (Intrinsic, 2025) and six held-out connector types. Our method inserts 61 of the 69 development parts at the assembled pose in a strict kinematic test and 91% in physics simulation. In contrast, ReKep and MOKA insert none, because their keypoints and marks do not describe the mating features. The look-and-mate step corrects the rotations that the agent misreads as well as offsets below the resolution of the scene cameras, and on the held-out connectors, the complete method inserts all 18 parts in both tests. On new placements of eight tasks, reusing the sketch of a single agent run inserts 30 of 32 parts with registration alone, which matches the performance of calling the agent in each episode.

This paper makes three contributions. First, we introduce sketch models, a task representation that a VLM agent builds once per task with geometric tools, that a sketch memory transfers to new placements by registration and that a classical planner executes. Second, we propose a look-and-mate step that observes both mating faces at close range after the grasp and resolves their correspondence by shape complementarity under the semantic constraints of the sketch. Third, we evaluate our method against ported VLM baselines and report, besides success, the accuracy of each intermediate representation and the cause of each failure.

title: When Architectural Spaces Start to Act
authors: Alex Binh Vinh Duc Nguyen
abstract: Architectural spaces are increasingly gaining robotic capabilities. Architectural robots such as robotic partitions, ceilings, furniture, façades, and other spatial components can autonomously move and reconfigure in response to occupants’ needs and activities. Yet, when architectural robots start shaping the spatial conditions in which people continuously live, work, and interact, we may begin to experience the architectural space itself as robotic. What does this shift mean for how we inhabit such spaces? Drawing on our previous studies, I reflect on how architectural robots interact with people not only through their motions, but also through the spatial configurations that persist after those motions stop; how their actions may benefit some occupants while disadvantaging others; and how multiple robots may together make a whole architectural space appear to act. I argue that as computation gains the capacity to physically reconfigure our environments, interaction extends beyond the moment of computational action into the spatial conditions that people continue to inhabit. Understanding robotic architecture therefore requires us to look beyond short-term human-robot interaction and toward how people inhabit, negotiate, and maintain control over spaces that can autonomously reconfigure.
introduction:
Imagine an architectural space that is dear to you. Perhaps you would think of your childhood bedroom, a window that you always look out from, or a dining room where your family shares everyday meals. Perhaps you would remember the layout of the whole space, or only a corner of it: the shape of a piece of furniture, the surface of a wall, the smell of wood. Perhaps you are in that architectural space right now, and this paragraph makes you start looking around and notice everything that it has to offer. For much of our daily life, we rarely pay continuous attention to the architectural spaces we inhabit. Once a space becomes familiar, it recedes into the background while we work, eat, sleep, talk, and live within it.

Although architectural spaces mostly exist in the background of our attention, we continuously interact with them through adaptations. We consciously and subconsciously adapt our everyday activities, sometimes even our preferences, to fit ourselves into these architectural spaces. In turn, we also adapt these spaces to accommodate our needs, sometimes by physically reconfiguring them. We open a window when a room becomes stuffy, close a curtain when sunlight becomes uncomfortable, move a chair closer to a table, or rearrange furniture when our activities change. Spatial reconfigurations may differ greatly in scale: sometimes they take place through minor adjustments, and sometimes through major renovation projects. Yet, in our everyday lives, spatial reconfigurations usually remain within our control. We decide what should be reconfigured, we perform the reconfigurations ourselves, or at least we understand why a reconfiguration is happening.

Now, I ask you to remember again the same space that is dear to you. Imagine the window that you used to look out from; now it can automatically open or close to regulate the air quality of the room. Imagine the dinner table with your family, now with an additional capability to move and reconfigure its shape to act both as a kitchen island during cooking and a dining table during meals. Imagine the chair that you used to sit on; now it can move across the room to help your grandma when she has difficulties walking. Here, the architecture itself can initiate a physical spatial reconfiguration. Perhaps such robotic architecture sounds convenient, perhaps unsettling. Either way, it remains difficult to imagine how we would inhabit it in the same way that we currently inhabit our spaces.

I would like to emphasise that this idea is not new. Architects, designers, and roboticists have long envisioned how interactive technologies can become embedded within the physical fabric of everyday environments, ranging from responsive façades to robotic furniture and whole reconfigurable rooms (Green, 2016). The field of human-building interaction (HBI) is increasingly applying the principles of human-computer interaction (HCI) toward understanding buildings as networks of interactive systems (Alavi et al., 2019). The emerging interest in robotic furniture within the field of human-robot interaction (HRI) has shown how ordinary spatial components can perform movements with gestural qualities that people interpret as conveying cognition and intent (Hoffman and Ju, 2014). These developments connect robotic architecture to a longer trajectory of ubiquitous computing, which has long envisioned computation as receding into the fabric of everyday environments (Weiser, 1991), while everyday objects and architectural surfaces become interfaces between digital information and the physical world (Ishii and Ullmer, 1997). Robotic architecture extends this trajectory further: computation can now sense our activities and physically reorganise the environment itself. What remains unclear is how we would continuously inhabit such ever-changing architectural spaces.

In this article, I thus explore this problem through a thought exercise: How would ordinary lives unfold within a robotic architectural space that is sometimes the background and sometimes is not? How do we inhabit this shelter that should provide us with safety and security while also being capable of changing itself? What changes for HCI when the output of computation is a spatial condition that people must continue to inhabit? Throughout this article, I use architectural robots to describe individual robotic components that act as architectural elements, and robotic architecture to describe the larger inhabited environment that emerges through their actions.

title: Flexibility-Aware Robotic Manipulation: Deformation Estimation, Kinematics, and Control via Distributed Inertial Measurement
authors: Amir Hossein Barjini,Sadeq Yaqubi,Pauli Mustalahti,Jouni Mattila
abstract: Long-reach manipulators used in drilling, inspection, construction, and material handling can bend enough that joint measurements no longer predict the tool pose accurately. External tracking systems are often impractical in factories or work sites because they require line of sight and additional infrastructure. The proposed method uses compact inertial sensors mounted along the robot links. A practitioner specifies the link dimensions, material properties, payload, and expected motion bandwidth; the procedure then determines how many deformation components must be represented and checks whether the selected sensor locations provide sufficient information. The resulting measurements can be used in real time to estimate link bending, improve end-effector pose estimation, and provide deformation information to the controller. Experiments on hydraulic manipulators indicate that this approach can reduce the required instrumentation relative to a dense piecewise-rigid layout while supporting accurate pose estimation and closed-loop operation. The current implementation assumes planar motion and small deformation, and the modal analysis should be updated when the payload or operating bandwidth changes substantially.
introduction:
Robotic manipulators are increasingly required to perform dexterous and autonomous tasks in dynamic environments [1], where accurate state information underpins trajectory planning [2], task-space control [3, 4], and controlled physical interaction [5, 6].
However, as manipulator links become longer and payload demands increase, the conventional rigid-body assumption can become inadequate, since elastic deformation and vibration introduce discrepancies between rigid-model predictions and the actual robot motion, motivating the consideration of flexibility in heavy-duty manipulators [7, 8]. Advanced flexible robotic manipulation therefore requires not only joint measurements, but also real-time estimates of link deformation and their explicit incorporation into kinematics and control. The following subsection reviews the state of the art in these areas and identifies the remaining research gaps.

Deformation estimation in flexible robots has been investigated through a range of sensing technologies and estimation approaches.
Optical measurement systems, including camera-based methods and laser trackers, provide noncontact measurements for pose estimation, shape reconstruction, and deformation assessment in rigid, soft, continuum, and flexible manipulators [9, 10].
Embedded optical-fiber sensors infer local curvature from distributed strain measurements, enabling three-dimensional shape sensing [11, 12].
In parallel, model-based state estimators fuse pose or strain measurements with continuum models to reconstruct the configuration of continuum robots [13, 14], while partial differential equation (PDE) observers estimate distributed flexible-link states from boundary measurements [15, 16]. Collectively, these approaches establish a broad foundation for deformation perception, with different requirements for external infrastructure, sensor integration, and model knowledge.

Inertial measurement units (IMUs) offer a compact and cost-effective solution for robot perception, operating without external infrastructure, direct visual access, or specific lighting conditions, which makes them well suited to industrial applications [17].
In rigid robotic manipulators, accelerometer and gyroscope measurements have enabled reliable joint-angle estimation [18, 19], while IMU-assisted methods have also supported collision monitoring and fault-tolerant state estimation [20, 21].
Observability-based studies have further established how the number and placement of inertial sensors influence kinematic-state estimation [22].
Nevertheless, the use of distributed IMUs for continuous flexible-link deformation reconstruction, together with the relationship between the dominant modal content and the required sensor configuration, remains comparatively underexplored.

Flexible-link modeling consists of infinite-dimensional and finite-dimensional formulations.
Infinite-dimensional PDE models preserve the continuous distributed dynamics and provide a high-fidelity description of flexible robot motion [23, 24].
For real-time estimation and control, however, finite-dimensional representations are often preferred to reduce computational complexity [7]. Among these, finite-element methods discretize the link into elastic elements [25, 26], flexible-multibody formulations capture coupled rigid–flexible motion within complex mechanisms [27, 28], and assumed-mode methods (AMMs) approximate deformation using a finite set of spatial basis functions [29, 7].
The retained modal order is therefore crucial, requiring mode selection to balance model fidelity and computational efficiency while accounting for structural properties and payload variation [30, 31]. However, the relationship between the selected modes and the required sensor network remains largely unresolved.

Kinematics provides the bridge between deformation perception and task-space manipulation.
In continuum and soft robots, constant- and piecewise-constant-curvature models provide compact forward and inverse kinematic mappings [32, 33], while geometrically exact rod formulations and geometric-constraint-based models have been used to describe robot shape and deformation under external loading [34, 35, 36]. Learning-based methods have also been investigated for inverse kinematics under highly nonlinear deformation [37].
For flexible manipulators, measured or predicted deformation has been incorporated into kinematic transformations to correct end-effector position and orientation [38, 39]. More recently, distributed-IMU approaches have represented flexible links as piecewise-rigid chains for real-time pose estimation [40] and subsystem-based control [41]. These studies demonstrate the value of flexibility-aware kinematics; however, a sensor-efficient framework for serial flexible manipulators that reconstructs continuous link deformation using dominant mode shapes and explicitly incorporates it into the kinematics remains largely unexplored.

Accurate control of flexible manipulators requires accounting for elastic dynamics, since precise joint regulation alone cannot suppress link deformation and vibration or their resulting effect on the end-effector pose. Accordingly, existing strategies include visual servoing, neural-network and model-predictive control, reinforcement-learning-based control, and PDE-based control.
A vision-based method combines nonlinear state observers with visual servoing to regulate end-effector motion while suppressing structural vibration [42].
Neural-network and model-predictive controllers have also been experimentally investigated for motion regulation and vibration suppression [43, 44].
Actor–critic reinforcement learning has been employed for trajectory tracking and vibration suppression [45, 46, 47].
PDE-based controllers, in contrast, directly incorporate the distributed dynamics of flexible links into the control law [48, 49], thereby avoiding modal truncation and enabling rigorous stability analysis. More recently, a nonlinear PDE controller has been coupled with a learning-based planner that generates vibration-minimizing reference trajectories [10].
Despite these developments, deformation sensing and control have largely been treated as separate problems, although estimation latency and reconstruction errors can degrade closed-loop performance. In particular, the real-time integration of reconstructed link deformation into closed-loop control remains insufficiently investigated for heavy-duty serial flexible manipulators.

The literature reviewed above addresses individual elements of deformation sensing, flexibility-aware kinematics, and control, but does not provide the complete mode-informed sensing-to-control framework considered here. To the best of the authors’ knowledge, no existing framework links dominant-mode selection to a minimum observable IMU configuration, uses the resulting measurements to reconstruct continuous link deformation, and incorporates the reconstructed deformation into both flexibility-aware kinematics and PDE-based closed-loop control. The overall workflow of the proposed framework, from flexible-link characterization and dominant-mode selection to reduced-order IMU-based deformation reconstruction, flexibility-aware kinematics, and closed-loop control, is summarized in Fig. 1.

The main contribution of this paper is a unified flexibility-aware robotic manipulation framework that integrates sensor-efficient deformation estimation, flexibility-aware kinematics, and control. The specific contributions are summarized as follows:

A mode-selection procedure is developed to identify the dominant mode shapes of each flexible link based on response convergence and the system excitation bandwidth.

A sensor-efficient deformation estimation method is introduced, in which the retained modal coordinates are reconstructed using the identified dominant mode shapes. Under the modal observability condition, reconstructing mm dominant modes requires mm independent slope measurements and one reference IMU, defining the minimum observable IMU configuration.

The reconstructed link deformation is explicitly incorporated into flexibility-aware forward kinematics and a PDE-based joint-space controller, demonstrating its use in both end-effector pose estimation and real-time closed-loop control.

The proposed methods are validated on single-link flexible manipulator (SLFM) and double-link flexible manipulator (DLFM) using laser-tracker ground truth and are compared with conventional rigid and piecewise-rigid approaches.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section II presents the inertial measurement methods for joint-state estimation. Section III describes the flexible-link model, mode selection, and IMU-based deformation reconstruction. Sections IV and V develop the flexibility-aware kinematics and controller, respectively. Section VI reports the numerical and experimental results, and Section VII concludes the paper.

1. A mode-selection procedure is developed to identify the dominant mode shapes of each flexible link based on response convergence and the system excitation bandwidth.

2. A sensor-efficient deformation estimation method is introduced, in which the retained modal coordinates are reconstructed using the identified dominant mode shapes. Under the modal observability condition, reconstructing mm dominant modes requires mm independent slope measurements and one reference IMU, defining the minimum observable IMU configuration.

3. The reconstructed link deformation is explicitly incorporated into flexibility-aware forward kinematics and a PDE-based joint-space controller, demonstrating its use in both end-effector pose estimation and real-time closed-loop control.

4. The proposed methods are validated on single-link flexible manipulator (SLFM) and double-link flexible manipulator (DLFM) using laser-tracker ground truth and are compared with conventional rigid and piecewise-rigid approaches.

title: When the Past Shapes Action: Understanding Embodied Memory
authors: Siqi Li,Ziyi Bai,Xinrun Xu,Tinglei Huang,Börje F. Karlsson
abstract: Recent advances in generative foundation models have expanded the capabilities of embodied AI, enabling increasingly general navigation, manipulation, and long-horizon task execution. However, effective interaction with dynamic environments requires more than only strong perception and reasoning: agents must act with partial knowledge and retain, retrieve, and update information from past observations, actions, and experiences. This survey examines embodied memory as a mechanism for preserving decision-relevant information beyond the current observation. We organize existing approaches along two complementary dimensions: six fundamental memory requirements, spanning world-state persistence, task progress, belief maintenance, and experiential learning; and eight architectural categories, including recurrent states, fast weights, visual and symbolic representations, spatial memory, and experience-based systems. We analyze their capabilities and limitations, and examine how existing benchmarks evaluate memory-dependent behavior, distinguishing genuine use of historical information from general task performance. Finally, we identify open challenges in selecting relevant experiences, maintaining consistent beliefs in changing environments, and consolidating knowledge across episodes. Our analysis provides a framework for understanding memory as an essential component of reliable, adaptive, and lifelong-horizon embodied intelligence.
introduction:
“All those moments will be lost in time, like tears in rain.”
 — Roy Batty, replicant (Blade Runner, 1982)

Embodied intelligence depends on proper environment grounding and, critically, on information whose relevance outlasts its visibility. A robot may need to retrieve an object last seen inside a drawer, verify whether an earlier manipulation succeeded, or resume a procedure after an interruption. In each case, the current observation leaves decision-relevant variables unresolved, and successful action requires a state inferred from interaction history, zt=f(o1:t,a1:t−1)z_{t}=f(o_{1:t},a_{1:t-1}). This challenge extends beyond recalling what a camera once observed: actions affect the world, failures reveal hidden constraints, and previous experience may alter which strategy is appropriate. Memory must therefore maintain a usable relationship between past evidence and present decisions. This perspective connects embodied memory with state estimation under partial observability and with accounts of autonomous and spatial intelligence centered on constructing and revising internal world state [1, 2].

While recent advances in generative foundation models have expanded the perceptual, reasoning, and planning capabilities of embodied agents, the underlying challenges of maintaining and exploiting historical information are longstanding. Earlier research on belief-state planning, spatial mapping, and episodic control established complementary approaches to preserving and using past experience, providing useful foundations for understanding the requirements and limitations of modern embodied memory systems (e.g., [3, 4, 5]).

Recent work offers increasingly diverse mechanisms for carrying embodied history into action, but their diversity in approach and scope makes comparisons difficult. Recurrent policies compress observations into evolving latent states [6, 7]; event memories select sparse visual evidence [8, 9]; textual stores summarize task progress and constraints [10, 11, 12]; spatial representations preserve entities across viewpoints [13, 14, 15]; and experience libraries reuse trajectories or consolidate skills [16, 17, 18]. These designs preserve different information and introduce different failure modes. A compact state may retain a counter while losing an object’s appearance, whereas a detailed visual archive may preserve obsolete location information without recognizing that they may have been superseded. Consequently, architectural sophistication and storage capacity alone provide an incomplete explanation of when memory helps. The useful starting point is the historical variable that a future decision requires and the operations needed to keep that variable valid.

This survey organizes embodied memory through two complementary axes: six task requirements and eight architectural design categories. The requirements describe why historical information matters: hidden world state, action-induced state change, task state, delayed-relevance evidence, active belief maintenance, and cross-episode experience. The architectural categories describe how systems retain and use such history: recurrent states, fast weights, persistent visual tokens, event or keyframe stores, textual or symbolic stores, graph or 3D stores, experience or skill representations, and hybrid compositions. These are different analytical levels with a many-to-many relationship; they are not competing counts of memory types. The architectural grouping is a practical comparison framework rather than a partition into mutually exclusive substrates: event selection can operate over visual entries, experience can be stored in text, and hybrids combine several mechanisms, for example.

Moreover, evaluation of embodied memory approaches must establish which historical information actually matters in changing behaviour. Long episodes may remain locally solvable, while a brief episode can require memory when an early cue disappears before the decisive action. General embodied benchmarks measure valuable combinations of perception, planning, and control, yet their aggregate success rates do not identify the contribution of history. Dedicated suites such as RMBench [19], RoboMME [20], and MIKASA-Robo [21] create more explicit dependencies through counting, occlusion, and delayed recall. Even there, the observation interface, supplied demonstrations, and task-progress scaffolding determine what the agent itself must remember. We therefore examine concrete tasks, the historical variables they require, the outcomes they score, and the alternative explanations that remain. Our analysis distinguishes retaining evidence from revising stale state, and successful reuse of a specific past case from the formation of transferable knowledge.

For the purposed of this survey, We define embodied memory as a latent or explicit state that preserves task-relevant evidence from earlier embodied observations, actions, outcomes, or demonstrations and makes it usable after that evidence is absent from the current observation. The scope includes navigation, manipulation, task and action planning, and spatial or egocentric reasoning about previously encountered scenes and goals, with passive video evaluation distinguished from closed-loop execution. Retained context counts when it carries historical evidence into a later decision; a fixed window supplies bounded retention, while recurrent states, external stores, and fast weights offer other persistence mechanisms. Static instructions, generic pretraining knowledge, and parameter adaptation without demonstrated historical dependence do not by themselves establish embodied memory. Generic chatbot memory, document retrieval, computer-use agents, and hardware-memory optimization remain outside the core scope of this survey. Section 2 develops these boundaries, including the conditional roles of mapping, world models, and test-time learning.

Our literature selection supports a diagnostic narrative synthesis rather than an exhaustive systematic review. The collection prioritized relevant work from recent established conferences and journal issues, while inclusion remained conditional on a substantive memory mechanism or evaluation contribution. We combine broad searches for embodied or robot memory with terms for episodic experience, spatial maps, recurrent state, retrieval, skill consolidation, fast weights, and memory evaluation, then trace references, citations, and relevant conference records. Paper contents, official proceedings, code repositories, and project pages establish the mechanism and evaluation settings. Inclusion requires either an identifiable mechanism for retaining embodied history or an evaluation that explicitly tests historical dependence. The synthesis prioritizes coverage of distinct computational problems, and its claims about architectural suitability are analytical interpretations unless directly attributed to an experiment.

The survey contributes a requirement-centered taxonomy, an analysis of architectural trade-offs, and a task-level audit of evaluation evidence. Section 3 identifies the six requirements and explains their overlap; Section 4 relates them to the eight design categories and the bottlenecks of selection, compression, access, revision, and transfer. Section 5 distinguishes what representative benchmarks score from what their results establish about memory. Section 6 consolidates the resulting evaluation principles and research priorities, and Section 7 presents some final considerations. Across these analyses, the survey organizing question centers on which information must survive, remain valid, and become available at the decision that necessitates it. Answering that question connects memory design to observable behavioural consequences and provides a firmer basis for comparing methods than the presence of a memory module per se.

title: Interaction-Aware Sampling-Based Motion Planning for Autonomous Surface Vessels in Urban Waterways
authors: Elia Trevisan,Alejandro Gonzalez-Garcia,Jan Swevers,Javier Alonso-Mora
comment: This work has been submitted to the IEEE for possible publication
abstract: Autonomous surface vessels operating in urban waterways must coordinate with other vessels in confined spaces while complying with traffic regulations, often without knowing their intentions. We present a decentralized motion planner based on model predictive path integral control, a sampling-based model predictive control scheme. The planner jointly computes a trajectory for the ego vessel and a prediction of the trajectories of the other vessels, and therefore accounts for their interaction. Traffic regulations are encoded as discontinuous costs, which the sampling-based formulation admits without a smooth approximation. We evaluate the method in maps taken from real sections of Amsterdam’s canals, in encounters between two vessels and in scenarios with four interacting vessels. Across 780 randomized runs the method reaches every goal without collisions or deadlocks, and outperforms an optimization-based planner designed for the same domain, as well as a version of the proposed planner that does not account for the interaction. We further validate the planner on two scaled vessel prototypes in an outdoor environment, where planning and localization run onboard at 10 Hz, and head-on and crossing encounters are resolved without collisions or rule violations. Code and videos: https://autonomousrobots.nl/paper_websites/ia-mppi.
introduction:
As urban populations continue to grow, cities are compelled to improve their transportation and mobility infrastructure. In the case of the European continent, inland waterways provide an underutilized option for urban mobility and freight transport solutions. For instance, the City of Amsterdam has the opportunity to leverage its urban canals to transport goods, waste, and people, decreasing congestion and dependence on road infrastructure [1]. Autonomous Surface Vessels (ASVs) can be deployed on such urban waterways to enhance the safety and efficiency of operations, as was the objective of the Roboat project [2]. Furthermore, inland waterways also offer an underutilized, sustainable option for transporting goods and people across Europe, where ASVs could also help increase safety and reduce operational errors [3, 4].
Nevertheless, the nature of inland waterways poses a complex challenge to the development and deployment of ASVs. The confined spaces within narrow canals, complex vessel dynamics, floating and static obstacles, as well as other vessels, create a complex, unstructured environment. In the case of other waterway users, the ASVs must be able to safely interact with both human-piloted and autonomous agents, while obeying traffic regulations [5].

Sampling-based Model Predictive Control (MPC), and in particular Model Predictive Path Integral Control (MPPI) [6], solves motion planning problems with complex dynamics and non-smooth cost functions by rolling out and weighting a large number of sampled input sequences. In contrast to optimization-based methods, which often depend on convex approximations of free space and simplify collision avoidance by inflating the ego and obstacle agents into ellipsoids [7, 8], MPPI can handle the exact shapes of both static and moving obstacles, even when these shapes are non-convex, and it admits the discontinuous costs that encode traffic rules. These properties suit the narrow canals and close encounters of inland waterways. Safe navigation among other vessels also depends on cooperation [9]. A vessel that plans around a prediction of the other vessels resolves the encounter on its own, and the maneuver it chooses may not be consistent with the maneuvers that the other vessels choose. In contrast, a vessel that accounts for how the other vessels respond to its own motion can anticipate a joint maneuver. Therefore, we present Interaction-Aware MPPI (IA-MPPI), a decentralized version of MPPI in which each vessel plans jointly for itself and for the vessels around it, and so anticipates their maneuvers without exchanging plans. The contributions of this paper are:

We present a decentralized architecture for interaction-aware motion planning that requires minimal or no communication between agents.

We present a decentralized architecture for interaction-aware motion planning that requires minimal or no communication between agents.

We propose a cost function design that encodes navigation objectives, allowing the system to comply with traffic regulations during operation.

We validate the planner outdoors on two ASV prototypes, with planning and localization running onboard.

We release an open-source implementation of the method, which is portable across platforms and is intended to support its adoption on other autonomous systems.

We evaluate the method in maps taken from real sections of Amsterdam’s canals. In two-agent encounters we compare against a regulations-aware optimization-based MPC [7], and in scenarios with four interacting vessels we compare the decentralized variants against a centralized one. Across 780 randomized runs the method reaches every goal without collisions or deadlocks. In the field, two prototypes resolved twenty head-on and crossing encounters while sustaining a 10 Hz control frequency on their onboard computers. This paper builds on our previous work [10] in three aspects. The sampling distribution of the planner is informed by ancillary controllers, following the biased formulation of [11], so that distinct maneuvers are represented in the sample set. The simulation study is repeated with the resulting planner and extended with a comparison against the formulation that does not account for the interaction. The planner is further validated in field experiments with two ASV prototypes, and its implementation is released as open-source software.

The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. Section II reviews related work. Section III introduces the sampling-based control scheme and the vessel model on which the planner is built, and Section IV presents the planner, from its decentralized architecture to the sampling scheme and the cost formulation. The planner is evaluated in simulation in Section V and with real world experiments in Section VI. Section VII discusses what the two evaluations show, and Section VIII concludes the paper.

2. We propose a cost function design that encodes navigation objectives, allowing the system to comply with traffic regulations during operation.

3. We validate the planner outdoors on two ASV prototypes, with planning and localization running onboard.

4. We release an open-source implementation of the method, which is portable across platforms and is intended to support its adoption on other autonomous systems.

title: OpenVIO: A Versatile Open-Source Visual-Inertial Odometry System
authors: Seungwon Choi
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
abstract:
Visual-inertial odometry (VIO) is a fundamental topic in robotics research. Beyond research, VIO has been
adopted in a wide range of products. In this manuscript, we present OpenVIO, an open-source VIO system for research
and practical applications. It is released under the MIT license. OpenVIO supports pinhole and fisheye cameras and
extends this support to stitched 360° images. We describe each part of the system together with its design
considerations. We also report benchmark results with other open-source VIO systems on public datasets. OpenVIO is
available as open source at https://github.com/93won/openvio.
introduction:
Visual-inertial odometry (VIO) combines camera images with measurements from an inertial measurement unit (IMU)
to estimate ego-motion. This cost-effective sensor combination supports reliable motion estimation and has made VIO
useful in products such as mobile robots, drones, augmented reality (AR) devices and autonomous cars [4, 5, 6, 7].

In this manuscript, we present OpenVIO, an open-source VIO system with stable performance across diverse camera
models. It supports pinhole and fisheye cameras, as well as stitched 360° images with a full spherical
field of view (Fig. OpenVIO: A Versatile Open-Source Visual-Inertial Odometry System). Under the MIT license, it can be used in both research and products.
We compare OpenVIO with nine open-source VIO systems on EuRoC and TUM-VI in monocular and stereo
configurations. We also evaluate OpenVIO on the 17 flights of PanoAir.

The rest of this manuscript is organized as follows. Section II reviews related work.
Section III describes the OpenVIO pipeline, including the front end, initialization, filtering and
extensions for 360° cameras. Section IV reports
the benchmark results on EuRoC, TUM-VI and PanoAir. Section V concludes the manuscript.
