title: GPU-accelerated Incremental Euclidean Distance Transform for Online Motion Planning of Mobile Robots
authors: Yizhou Chen,Shupeng Lai,Jinqiang Cui,Biao Wang,Ben M. Chen
comment: Published in RA-L 2022. Author-accepted manuscript. Code:this https URL
abstract:
In this letter, we present a volumetric mapping system that effectively calculates Occupancy Grid Maps (OGMs) and Euclidean Distance Transforms (EDTs) with parallel computing.
Unlike these mappers for high-precision structural reconstruction, our system incrementally constructs global EDT and outputs high-frequency local distance information for online robot motion planning.
The proposed system constructs OGM with massive amount of data from multiple types of sensor inputs. Using GPU programming techniques, the system quickly computes EDT in parallel within local volume. The new observation is continuously integrated into the global EDT using the parallel wavefront algorithm while preserving the historical observations.
Experiments with datasets have shown that our proposed approach outperforms existing state-of-the-art robot mapping systems and is particularly suitable for mapping unexplored areas. In its actual implementations on aerial and ground vehicles, the proposed system achieves real-time performance with limited onboard computational resources.
introduction:
An accurate representation of the local environment is critical to the effectiveness of mobile robot navigation [1, 2, 3, 4]. Especially, the distance information to nearby obstacles is a must in many motion planning algorithms [5, 6, 7].
To that end, OGMs and EDTs are often used to bridge environment representation and planning. Both the OGM and EDT are voxel maps. In an OGM, each voxel records the probability of being occupied by an obstacle. An EDT records the distance information from each voxel to the nearest obstacle. Typically, a local EDT is required to be updated at high frequency for real-time performance of the local planner, while a global EDT is queried less frequently by the global planner.

Creating these maps is challenging due to limited onboard computational resources and real-time requirements of motion planning. To solve this problem, many researchers (see, e.g., [8, 9, 10, 11]) choose to sacrifice precision for increased runtime speed. However, their wavefront-based methods can incur large errors in real-world scenarios because the distance values only propagate on observed voxels. Besides, computational resources are highly stretched when updating global EDT with a lightweight onboard computing unit.
As the demand for a faster update procedure of global incremental EDT rises, it is natural to explore the possibility of computing OGM and EDT in a parallel fashion using GPU onboard. Unfortunately, most of the methods designed for CPUs reported in the literature have very limited parallelization capability.

We also note that various approaches to distance transformation have been studied in the pattern recognition society (see, e.g., [12, 13, 14]). These methods are mainly developed for fast distance transformation on a fully known binary map, usually a 2D image. However, in robotic applications, the environment map needs to be incremental as the robot moves, while the standard sensors of mobile robots have a limited sensing range. Moreover, the size of the map cannot be determined in advance for situations in unknown environments.

Motivated by the fast demand in real-time applications for small robots, such as small UAVs and UGVs, we propose in this letter an innovative and effective approach to increase the efficiency and accuracy of the mapping process through massive-scale parallelization. It is designed for the navigation purposes of a mobile robot and allows an incremental map to be constructed with dynamically adjustable map size.
The proposed mapping system is versatile enough to construct OGMs from commonly used onboard sensors such as depth cameras and 2D- or 3D-LiDAR. It computes a fast and exact batch EDT with the parallel Euclidean distance transform. The batch EDT is then integrated into the global EDT through a parallel wavefront mechanism. With the utilization of parallel computing techniques, both the local and global EDT can be updated in real-time. The proposed system can be deployed on miniature computing devices with GPU, such as Nvidia Xavier NX, commonly used for small robots or unmanned systems. We will make the source code of our system available as an open-source project.11

The contributions of this work are: i)
the development of an efficient approach that generates OGM and EDT through massive parallelization;
ii) the design of an EDT integration method that allows the incremental construction of global EDT with dynamically adjustable map size; and lastly iii)
the integration of the proposed algorithm in various ground/aerial mobile robots to demonstrate its effectiveness with onboard motion planning.

The rest of this letter is organized as follows:
In Section II, we recall some background materials in fast EDT algorithms and state-of-the-art mappers. In Section III, we present the overview and framework of our proposed mapping system. The technical details of the proposed system are given in Section IV. The experimental and simulation results that demonstrate the effectiveness of our system are presented in Section V, while the result conducted on robotic platforms is given in
Section VI. Finally, we draw some concluding remarks in Section VII.

title: ResMerge: Residual Policy Learning and Merging for Continual Adaptation of Pre-trained Robot Policies
authors: Kefei Zhu,Lingyun Xu,Yue Xin,Xiaoqi Li,Caixin Guo,Xincheng Du,Yuanpei Chen,Yaodong Yang,Hao Dong
comment: . Code:this https URL
abstract: Continual adaptation to new tasks is essential for robots deployed in the real world, but adapting pre-trained policies remains challenging due to parameter growth and the need for continual demonstration collection. Parameter-Efficient Continual Fine-Tuning (PECFT) isolates task-specific updates, but adapter-per-task designs require demonstrations and grow with the task set. We propose ResMerge, a two-stage framework that learns mergeable residual policies atop a frozen pre-trained policy: residual reinforcement learning (RL) acquires task-specific corrections without additional expert demonstrations during adaptation, and parameter-space merging consolidates compatible residuals to reduce stored parameters. We introduce Residual-Field Consistency (RFC), a simple, bounded, and interpretable metric that assesses compatibility in residual action-field space by comparing correction direction and magnitude. Experiments on LIBERO across two backbones and on a real-world Franka robot show improved continual learning performance over strong PECFT baselines, while selective merging reduces the residual-parameter footprint. Project website: https://resmerge.github.io/.
introduction:
For robots to remain useful in long-term deployment, they must continually adapt to new tasks while retaining previously acquired skills [12, 28, 14]. Pre-trained robot policies provide useful manipulation priors [6, 21]. Classical methods address forgetting through parameter isolation, expansion, or consolidation [17, 25, 26]. For large policies, Parameter-Efficient Continual Fine-Tuning (PECFT) reduces adaptation costs [20], but sequential updates can still interfere [29].

PECFT uses adapters [5, 9, 15] or expert architectures [11, 31, 22] to isolate updates. Demonstration-trained, adapter-per-task designs require new demonstrations and accumulate parameters (Fig. (a)). ResMerge (Fig. (b)) uses sparse-reward residual reinforcement learning [7] to adapt without additional expert demonstrations, and merges compatible residuals in parameter space [37] to reduce storage.

ResMerge has two stages (Fig. 2). Learn trains a residual policy atop the frozen base policy via residual RL. We design its LoRA architecture for subsequent merging during parameter-efficient continual adaptation, extending residual learning beyond controller refinement. Merge combines compatible residual experts in parameter space, followed by RL refinement on the associated tasks.

A key problem is identifying residuals that preserve their corrections when merged. Task-level similarity [30, 32] is insufficient: similar tasks can require opposing corrections, while different tasks can share compatible corrections (Fig. (c)). This identifies a gap in directly transplanting task-level merging criteria into residual RL. We therefore shift compatibility assessment from task space to residual action-field space. Our Residual-Field Consistency (RFC) metric compares correction direction and magnitude on shared observations to select compatible experts for low-rank merging.

Our contributions are:

We propose ResMerge for continual adaptation without additional expert demonstrations. Its LoRA-parameterized residual architecture improves merging in our architecture comparison, reducing the parameters needed to retain learned skills.

We introduce Residual-Field Consistency (RFC), a simple, bounded, and interpretable metric that shifts compatibility assessment from task-level similarity to agreement between residual action-correction fields.

ResMerge consistently improves continual learning performance over strong PECFT baselines across two backbones on LIBERO and a real-world Franka robot, while selective merging reduces stored residual parameters.

1. We propose ResMerge for continual adaptation without additional expert demonstrations. Its LoRA-parameterized residual architecture improves merging in our architecture comparison, reducing the parameters needed to retain learned skills.

2. We introduce Residual-Field Consistency (RFC), a simple, bounded, and interpretable metric that shifts compatibility assessment from task-level similarity to agreement between residual action-correction fields.

3. ResMerge consistently improves continual learning performance over strong PECFT baselines across two backbones on LIBERO and a real-world Franka robot, while selective merging reduces stored residual parameters.

title: $\nabla$Mimic: Ultra-Efficient Humanoid Control with Differentiable Simulation
authors: Weyl Lu,Yubei Chen
abstract:
Robot policy learning is dominated by zeroth-order methods such as PPO, which treat the simulator as a black box and
pay for it with enormous sample counts. First-order policy learning differentiates through the dynamics, but on
contact-rich whole-body control it has rarely worked: its gradients explode. A recent world-model method showed that
derivative information can make humanoid motion tracking far more efficient, using surrogate gradients of a learned
model. We show that exact gradients of the simulator itself do better, once two obstacles are removed. Exact gradients
contain rare unbounded samples, because contact dynamics is not differentiable everywhere and its derivative diverges
near some events; and they are expensive, because the simulator’s adjoint has to replay the contact solve.
introduction:
Motion tracking has become a central task in humanoid learning. A tracking policy imitates reference motions in
physics, so any human motion that can be retargeted to a robot becomes a behavior it can execute. The idea goes back to
DeepMimic and its successors in character animation [58, 41, 71],
and has moved to real humanoids [24, 30, 87, 26, 78]. Two
developments made it a foundation rather than a single skill. Large motion datasets of better quality, from AMASS and
LAFAN1 to BONES-SEED, together with robot retargets of them, now cover hours of diverse motion
[46, 23, 43, 7]. And a single general tracker trained on
such data can serve as the low-level policy of larger systems: its encoder–decoder structure provides a motion
interface for teleoperation, generation and downstream tasks [9, 40, 42].

Almost all of these trackers are trained with zeroth-order policy gradient methods, chiefly PPO
[63], which need only rewards from a black-box simulator and pay for it with enormous sample
counts. Massively parallel GPU simulation [47, 20, 21] made the samples cheap,
yet a whole-body tracking policy still takes hours to days of GPU time, and this cost bounds how far the approach can
scale.

First-order policy learning differentiates the return through the dynamics, so every simulated step contributes an
update direction instead of a scalar reward [14, 11, 81, 70]. On
contact-rich whole-body control this promise has rarely held: gradients through stiff contact dynamics explode
[49, 70]. SHAC [81], the standard first-order method, is no exception. On
whole-body tracking with the Unitree G1, every SHAC run hits exploding gradients and stops within minutes
(Section 4.1).

Policy learning through the derivatives of a learned dynamics model has a long history, from stochastic value
gradients and model-augmented actor-critic to Dreamer and to tracking controllers for physics-based characters
[27, 10, 22, 15, 82, 37].
SuperMimic [39] recently brought this approach to humanoid whole-body tracking at scale: it
differentiates through a learned world model instead of a simulator and trains a tracking policy far faster than PPO.
We read SuperMimic’s result differently: not as evidence for world models, but as evidence for derivatives. The gain
comes from using the dynamics’ derivatives at all; the world model is the price SuperMimic pays to make those
derivatives bounded and cheap. This raises the question of what that price buys, and whether it has to be paid. A world model supplies surrogate gradients: smooth, bounded and cheap, but derivatives of a
different system. A simulator supplies exact gradients: derivatives of the simulated system itself, but with
rare unbounded samples, because contact dynamics is not differentiable everywhere and its derivative diverges near some
events, and expensive, because the simulator’s adjoint has to replay the contact solve (Section 4).

This paper removes both obstacles. ∇\nablaMimic handles the samples: it bounds the rare extreme gradients per
sample and turns the rest into action targets whose step size is fixed in physical units, so that no single sample can
take over an update (Section 5). NablaEngine handles the cost: a differentiable GPU engine specialized to the
G1, with the adjoint of a whole control step as a single megakernel, whose exact gradient costs less than an extra
forward step (Section 6).

On all 40 LAFAN1 clips, with one policy and one GPU, ∇\nablaMimic reaches SuperMimic’s score of 0.82 in 20 minutes, where
SuperMimic reports 1.2 h, and 0.874 in 1.8 h, with no seed falling on any clip from 1.5 h on (Fig. 1).
PPO on the same engine stays below 0.82 for 6 h. The engine behind this simulates 18.8 h of robot motion per
second of wall clock (Fig. 1b). Motion tracking suits exact gradients, since its reward is dense and
points toward the reference almost everywhere; for sparse rewards, a longer gradient window trades reliance on the
critic against accumulated extreme gradients (Section 4.2).

An analysis of exact and surrogate gradients for policy learning. Unbounded exact derivatives near
non-differentiable contact events, accumulating along long windows, are consistent with the failure of prior
first-order methods on whole-body control; the low cost of a world model, with the success of surrogate gradients.

An analysis of exact and surrogate gradients for policy learning. Unbounded exact derivatives near
non-differentiable contact events, accumulating along long windows, are consistent with the failure of prior
first-order methods on whole-body control; the low cost of a world model, with the success of surrogate gradients.

∇\nablaMimic, a first-order policy learning method that is stable on exact contact gradients at the scale
of thousands of parallel environments, with each component ablated.

NablaEngine, an open-source differentiable simulation engine for the Unitree G1 whose analytic gradients
match float64 finite differences.

Humanoid motion tracking at the level of the world-model state of the art without a world model, on one GPU:
the LAFAN1 score of 0.82 in 20 minutes instead of 1.2 h.

title: Direct Action-Manifold Modeling for Efficient and Robust Bimanual Manipulation
authors: Hongren Wang,Mingyu You,Zihan Li,Zhipeng Wang,Shuo Jiang,Bin He
abstract: Diffusion and flow matching visuomotor policies require iterative denoising or numerical integration for multimodal action generation, introducing latency and execution mismatch. We instead consider a different formulation: conditioned on vision and proprioception, demonstrated bimanual action chunks concentrate in a structured observation-dependent region of joint-action space, making the action target more direct to model than the generative process. Based on this view, we propose the Direct Manifold Action Transformer (DMAT), which reformulates action generation as the direct modeling of clean, observation-conditioned joint-space action chunks from stochastic interpolants, thereby enabling single-step inference without relying on iterative generative inference or auxiliary trajectory-straightening procedures. Within DMAT, local 3D geometry anchors predictions to spatial structure, while State-Consistent Spectral-Time Refinement (STR) reconciles predicted chunks with proprioception and suppresses high-frequency residuals. Across 567 standard and out-of-distribution (OOD) trials per method, DMAT outperformed Improved 3D Diffusion Policy (IDP3) and DiTFlow3D in aggregate success rate, achieving relative improvements of 129.1% and 95.7%, respectively, while generating action chunks 2.06×\times and 1.34×\times faster and remaining robust under repeated 50 N interventions. These results pave the way for a novel generative paradigm for efficient and robust bimanual manipulation.
introduction:
Generative visuomotor policies support flexible robotic automation by connecting visual and proprioceptive information to coordinated actions. Bimanual coordination, sustained contact, and material transfer require actions that remain coherent as visual and proprioceptive states evolve [1], [2]. The information-processing challenge spans both prediction and delivery: spatial observations must inform temporally coordinated action chunks, and those chunks must remain compatible with the reached robot state.

Diffusion and flow matching policies construct expressive actions through a learned generative process. Diffusion policies iteratively denoise action sequences [3], whereas flow matching policies integrate learned velocity fields [4], [5]. Consistency, distillation, and few-step methods reduce this cost [6], [7], while the remaining policy computation can delay the next command chunk [8].

The central question is therefore whether a generative path should remain the primary modeling target for a robot action chunk. Joint commands are lower-dimensional than images and constrained by configuration, coordination, local geometry, and task phase; under a fixed observation, demonstrations can occupy a structured region of joint-action space. We use this property to define direct clean action prediction from a stochastic interpolant, rather than incrementally shortening an existing denoising or integration procedure. This is a change in modeling viewpoint, not merely in inference step count (Fig. 1).

Direct chunk prediction must retain spatial information for grasping, contact, and coordinated transport. Pooled pointcloud representations supply a shared scene summary [9], [10], whereas DMAT gives each temporal action token access to unpooled 3D features.

Geometrically grounded prediction alone does not ensure robust action chunk execution. Servo error, contact, or intervention can move the robot away from the state assumed by queued references. Real-Time Chunking (RTC) corrects latency-induced observation–action misalignment [8], but does not explicitly reconcile a new action chunk with physical state deviations. Robust execution therefore requires state consistency at regeneration boundaries.

These requirements motivate the conditional action-manifold hypothesis: observation-conditioned demonstrations concentrate around structured bimanual action patterns shaped by configuration, local geometry, coordination, and task phase. DMAT operationalizes this hypothesis with clean action targets, local geometric conditioning, and state-consistent delivery.

We introduce direct action-manifold modeling and instantiate it with the DMAT. Under the conditional action-manifold hypothesis, DMAT couples single-step clean action prediction with local geometric conditioning and STR for physical execution (Fig. 2). The contributions are:

We formulate bimanual action generation around the conditional action-manifold hypothesis and make clean observation-conditioned action chunks the primary modeling target. By construction, DMAT maps stochastic interpolants directly to these action chunks without solving an iterative denoising chain or numerically integrating a learned generative velocity field.

We develop a local geometry-anchored action space decoder that preserves position-specific 3D conditioning. Temporal action tokens query unpooled spatial tokens through cross-attention, retaining the coupling between action sequences and scene structure.

We introduce STR to carry directly generated chunks into state-consistent action chunk execution. It reconnects pending actions to the measured joint state and attenuates high-frequency residuals at regeneration boundaries.

We validate the complete chain on a Fourier GR2 robot through standard, OOD, and prescribed 50 N lateral-pull tests. Progressive ablations evaluate successive additions of geometric conditioning and STR to the direct predictor.

title: RTPolicy: Real-Time (32.9 Hz) Multi-View Visuomotor Policy for Robotic Manipulation on Edge Devices
authors: Xianbao Hou,Zehao Ni,Yonghao He,Lingfeng Qian,Xin Shi,Hu Su,Wei Sui,Cong Yang
abstract:
Low inference latency is critical for closed-loop robotic manipulation, especially under asynchronous inference, where action chunks must be updated promptly to correct accumulated deviations.
However, existing visuomotor policies rely on computationally expensive visual backbones, resulting in high inference latency and deployment overhead.
In this paper, we propose RTPolicy, a multi-view visuomotor policy that attains accurate manipulation with high inference efficiency.
Its core design combines view-aware feature fusion with visual compression to aggregate complementary information across camera views into a compact token representation.
The representation conditions a flow-matching action generator with the robot state and flow time, reducing the cost of action generation.
Extensive experiments demonstrate that this design reduces the computational cost of visual representation and action generation while preserving visual information required for manipulation.
On the RoboTwin 2.0 single-task clean evaluation across 50 tasks, RTPolicy attains a mean success rate of 52.26%, outperforming the strongest leaderboard baseline π0\pi_{0} (46.4%).
We further evaluate RTPolicy under asynchronous streaming inference on a real bimanual platform, where RTPolicy attains a mean success rate of 72.0% and sustains real-time inference at 30.35 ms (32.9 Hz) on the RDK S600 and 149.72 ms (6.7 Hz) on the RDK S100, both in INT16. Project Page: https://d-robotics-ai-lab.github.io/RTPolicy.project.
introduction:
Precise manipulation requires policies that learn from demonstrations while maintaining temporal coherence and responding to new visual observations, especially under asynchronous inference.
Visuomotor policies therefore predict short action trajectories and execute them in a receding horizon, as in action chunking [1].
Closed-loop correction [2, 3] keeps the executed plan consistent with the current observation.
Inference latency therefore directly determines how quickly fresh observations can affect the executed trajectory.

Current visuomotor policies face crucial and coupled sources of inference cost (Fig. 1).
Large visual backbones [4] can make visual encoding a substantial part of latency.
Multi-view image conditioning in π0.5\pi_{0.5} [5] increases the number of visual features that the action model must process.
Iterative denoising and flow sampling [6, 7, 8] add further computation before an action chunk can be executed.

Existing methods address individual sources of inference cost.
Consistency and flow-based policies [6, 7, 8] reduce the number of action generation steps, but generally leave the visual encoder and multi-view conditioning path unchanged.
Diffusion Policy (DP) [9] offers low latency, but its mean success rate is 29.3% and its single-view setup does not address the cost of multi-view conditioning (Fig. 1).
Achieving low latency and high manipulation accuracy with multi-view inputs remains a challenge for deployment on edge devices.

Hence, we propose RTPolicy, a visuomotor framework that jointly reduces the costs of visual encoding, multi-view conditioning, and iterative action generation.
It uses a frozen DINOv3 ConvNeXt encoder [10] to obtain visual features from multi-view images.
VGGT [11] and VO-DP [4] have demonstrated the value of geometric
visual representations for perception and manipulation.
To preserve spatial information across views, our view-aware feature fusion module assigns a
learnable embedding to each view and exchanges information within and across views.
A visual compression module then compresses the fused representation into a compact visual condition before it feeds a flow-based Diffusion Transformer.
This framework reduces visual conditioning cost while retaining spatial information for precise manipulation (Fig. 1).
In simulation and on a real bimanual platform, RTPolicy attains the highest mean success rate among the compared methods while supporting real-time deployment across the tested devices (Fig. 1).
In summary, our contributions are as follows:

We develop RTPolicy, an efficient end-to-end visuomotor policy that jointly reduces visual encoding, multi-view conditioning, and action-generation costs for precise manipulation.

We introduce view-aware feature fusion and visual compression, where learnable view embeddings guide cross-view information exchange, and the fused representation is compressed before action generation.

RTPolicy is evaluated in simulation and on a real bimanual platform, achieving the highest mean success rate among the compared methods while running in real time on the RTX 4090 and three edge devices.

1. We develop RTPolicy, an efficient end-to-end visuomotor policy that jointly reduces visual encoding, multi-view conditioning, and action-generation costs for precise manipulation.

2. We introduce view-aware feature fusion and visual compression, where learnable view embeddings guide cross-view information exchange, and the fused representation is compressed before action generation.

3. RTPolicy is evaluated in simulation and on a real bimanual platform, achieving the highest mean success rate among the compared methods while running in real time on the RTX 4090 and three edge devices.

title: VLA Policies Do Not Know When Not to Act: Unintended Task Execution and Start Suppression
authors: Minsu Jang,Jae-Woo Choi,Youngwoo Yoon,Dohyung Kim
comment: . Code:this https URL
abstract: A robot should act only on an instruction from a person or on an intent that the robot explicitly represents and generates. Unintended actions taken without such an instruction can cause risk or inconvenience to people and the environment. We examine how recent vision-language-action (VLA) policies respond when the instruction is missing or meaningless. We apply a paired protocol with empty, neutral, nonsense, infeasible, and wrong-task instructions to six model checkpoints in LIBERO-Goal simulation. Holding the initial state fixed and varying only the instruction, we ask three questions: whether the robot starts to move, which task it completes, and what the instruction determines. Even when the instruction was empty, the robot started moving in every episode with all six checkpoints, and with five of them it often completed a task that the instruction had not specified. On two GR00T checkpoints, the instruction determined which task was executed but not whether the robot started moving; the robot moved even on infeasible instructions. We then tested three methods for suppressing the start: prepending “if no task is given do not move” to the instruction; a gate that holds the robot when the first action chunk for the given instruction nearly equals that for an empty instruction; and fine-tuning the policy to hold still on non-task inputs. The prefix stopped the robot in none of the six checkpoints, and the gate held it on non-task inputs in five of the six checkpoints. The fine-tuned policy never completed a task on non-task inputs, but it did not reliably keep the robot still, and it failed to suppress the start on infeasible instructions.
introduction:
We expect a robot to begin a task only after a person has given it an explicit instruction. A robot that starts without such an instruction may perform actions that its user did not intend, such as handing over an object before the person is ready [27] or picking up an object after an observed event that calls for no action [19]. Acting without an instruction is appropriate only when the context explicitly permits it, and that context should not be left implicit in the policy’s weights. The robot should explicitly represent and generate the intent on which it acts, namely what it is about to do and whether to start now, and the action should follow from that representation rather than from the arrival of an input. Proactive Robot Assistance [19] is an example in which the judgment is generated explicitly, by a vision-language model reasoning over a state change, before any instruction-free action. The vision-language-action (VLA) policies studied here have no such representation. They map camera images, proprioception, and a language instruction to robot actions, and the recipe that trains them does not address the requirement. Language-conditioned behavior cloning pairs every training input with a demonstrated action [2, 12]. Each demonstration begins with a task instruction and ends when that task is completed, and some data pipelines also remove the stationary (“no-op”) steps in which the robot does not move [16]. As a result, the training data contain no sample in which the policy is asked to hold. A policy trained this way emits an action chunk for every input, including the inputs that a deployed robot meets when the instruction channel is empty, corrupted, or names something on which the robot cannot act. Examples are a speech-recognition result that was dropped, an unrelated sentence picked up from a nearby conversation, and a request that refers to an object that is not present. What the policy does in these states is specified neither by the recipe nor by the standard evaluation, which measures whether the robot does what it is asked to do by reporting the fraction of episodes in which the instructed task is completed. This evaluation does not measure whether the robot performs tasks that it was not asked to perform. When the designated task is not completed, the policy may have held still, may have attempted the designated task and failed, or may have completed a different task. A robot that, given no executable instruction, selects and completes one of the tasks available in the scene performs an unintended action; a robot that holds still does not. The two outcomes carry different consequences for the people and objects around the robot.

Several studies have removed or corrupted the instruction and reported either a drop in success or little change in behavior. Grant et al. [7] report LIBERO-Goal designated-task success of 12.0% or lower under an empty string for OpenVLA-OFT [15], X-VLA [32], and π0.5\pi_{0.5} [1]. LIBERO-PRO [33] reports that policy outputs remain nearly unchanged under corrupted instructions, and LIBERO-Plus [6] reports that language perturbations cause the second-smallest average drop in success among its seven perturbation types. In a scene where several tasks are feasible, both results are consistent with a third outcome: the policy completes a default task that the instruction never specified. Two studies have observed this outcome. In LIBERO-CF [5], the grasp positions of π0.5\pi_{0.5} under an empty instruction stay centered on the object of the scene’s well-learned training task. Xie and Alanwar [26] evaluate the goal predicates of every LIBERO-Goal task and report that OpenVLA-OFT and π0.5\pi_{0.5}, given gibberish or an empty string, execute one default task. OpenVLA-OFT, for example, turns on the stove or puts the bowl on the stove. Neither study measured whether the policy starts at all, which is the quantity to which the requirement above refers. title: A complete analytical characterization of optimal collision-free motion for two robots
authors: Jan Kamm,Antonio Terpin,Raffaello D'Andrea
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Systems and Control (eess.SY); Optimization and Control (math.OC)
abstract:
Collision-free motion planning for multi-agent robotic
systems remains an active research area because of the complexity of coordinating
robot trajectories, with applications ranging from coordinated drone shows
to autonomous operations on land, in the air, and on water.
Importantly, the analytical
difficulty of nonconvex collision-avoidance constraints has so far driven the development
of exclusively numerical methods.
We derive a complete analytical characterization of the optimal
trajectories for two robots that start and end at rest,
under double-integrator dynamics and a squared-acceleration objective.
We prove that these trajectories belong to eight distinct contact
families and determine which family applies for each configuration of initial
and final positions. We analyze the geometrical properties of the optimal trajectories, provide a numerical algorithm for computing them, and discuss how these insights may improve the performance of existing numerical trajectory optimizers.
introduction:
Collision-free motion planning for multi-agent robotic systems remains an active
research area because of the complexity of coordinating robot trajectories,
with applications ranging from coordinated drone shows to autonomous operations
on land [40], in the air
[2], and on water [21].
A variety of numerical methods exist to solve this problem, from sampling and
graph search
[22, 31, 30, 38]
to joint assignment and planning [35] and hybrid search and
trajectory optimization [18].
Trajectory optimizers use mixed-integer formulations [13],
spline parameterizations [36, 39],
sequential convex programming (SCP) [2, 29, 7, 15], learning-based methods
[9, 17], distributed optimization
[37, 32], and separation principles [33, 27].

We consider collision-free motion planning under double-integrator dynamics,
with fixed duration and endpoint data.
The squared-acceleration objective measures control effort and is equivalent to
squared-thrust minimization [2].
This objective is used for multi-agent assignment and collision avoidance
[5, 4], navigation among polygonal
obstacles [6], and, alongside other cost terms,
distributed quadrotor planning
[25].
In drone and floating-robot experiments, simplified planning models generate
reference trajectories while low-level controllers handle the physical dynamics
during execution
[2, 25, 21].
However, these approaches compute trajectories numerically because nonconvex
collision-avoidance constraints make an analytical solution difficult. Even for
two robots, existing theory provides no complete analytical characterization of minimum-effort
transitions between prescribed endpoint states over a fixed time horizon under
double-integrator dynamics.

Importantly, the two-robot case isolates the pairwise interaction that underlies
fleet planning, and an analytical characterization would identify the fundamental
properties of optimal collision-free motion, opening up new possibilities for
efficient planning.
Analytical characterizations exist in other settings.
Hu et al. [19] construct exact optimal motions for two planar
agents through a geometric analysis of the separation constraint.
They minimize squared velocity and leave endpoint velocities free.
Kirkpatrick and Liu [23] give a complete
geometric characterization for two discs minimizing total path length, with
paths consisting of straight segments and circular arcs. They extend this
characterization to convex centrally symmetric robots
[24].
The path-length objective does not distinguish different time parameterizations,
whereas acceleration cost depends on them.
For the squared-acceleration objective, Beaver and Malikopoulos [5]
construct trajectories by successively inserting constrained arcs and solving
for their joining times. Their method optimizes each agent against prescribed
higher-priority trajectories and restricts sustained contact to constant relative
speed. A complete characterization of the jointly optimal two-robot motion
requires accounting for variable relative speed and determining which combinations
of isolated contacts and sustained contact are globally optimal.

Contributions.
In this paper, we provide a complete analytical characterization for the
optimal trajectories of two robots starting and ending at rest under double-integrator dynamics and a squared-acceleration objective.
We prove that the contact
set consists of finitely many isolated points and boundary arcs,
with cubic motion between contacts. We derive an exact cost identity that gives
a sufficient condition for global optimality
(Sections 2.2.1 and 2.2.2).
We prove planarity, classify selected minimizers into
eight contact families, and show that their admissible construction
images partition endpoint space
(Section 2.2.3).
We give a certified numerical procedure that recovers the selected
trajectory and its cost to any prescribed positive accuracy for
algebraic endpoint data (Section 2.2.4).
Our two-robot characterization underlies the contact-based fleet planner
in [20], which incorporates acceleration
constraints and computes collision-free trajectories for one million
robots in minutes.

title: Contact-based optimization for collision-free motion planning for a million robots
authors: Jan Kamm,Antonio Terpin,Raffaello D'Andrea
abstract:
Multi-agent robotic systems have attracted growing
interest in recent years, with applications ranging from coordinated drone shows
to autonomous operations on land, in the air, and on water. At the planning
level, robot motion is often modeled using double-integrator dynamics
(with low-level controllers handling the physical dynamics during execution)
with a
minimum-energy objective subject to collision-avoidance constraints and
limits on position, velocity, and acceleration.
The complexity of the problem resides in the constraints, which couple the
trajectories and make the optimization problem nonconvex.
Existing numerical approaches typically discretize and optimize entire trajectories, which becomes expensive for large fleets. We exploit the structure of optimal trajectories by organizing optimization around contacts, at which robots reach the minimum allowed separation. We formulate a coupled algebraic system in contact variables and reconstruct trajectories analytically between contacts. Our algorithm, sequential contact insertion (SCI), starts from unconstrained trajectories, inserts contacts at separation violations, and jointly adjusts their times and states. Numerical experiments demonstrate planning for one million robots in minutes and thousands of robots in fractions of a second. On problems feasible for a fixed-grid sequential convex programming (SCP) baseline, SCI achieves median speedups of several orders of magnitude at matching solution accuracy.
introduction:
Multi-agent robotic systems have attracted growing interest in recent
years, with applications ranging from coordinated drone shows to autonomous
operations on land [26], in the air
[1], and on water [17].
Planning collision-free motion for a robot fleet is difficult because each
robot’s trajectory constrains the motion of the others. We consider transitions
between prescribed initial and final states over a fixed time horizon with
double-integrator dynamics, a squared-acceleration objective,
collision-avoidance and box constraints on position, velocity, and acceleration. This model is
commonly used in the literature for fleet motion planning
[1, 18, 17, 3, 4], typically paired with
low-level controllers that handle the physical dynamics during
execution.
The complexity of the problem resides in the pairwise separation constraints that make the
joint optimization problem nonconvex. The problem is therefore often solved
numerically [21, 15, 25, 12, 24, 23], with
sequential convex programming (SCP) as a popular choice [1, 20, 14, 27, 9].

A different route to efficient planning, and the one explored in this paper,
is to exploit the structure of optimal
trajectories. State-constrained optimal control supplies conditions
for unconstrained and constrained trajectory pieces and for matching them
[13, 6].
Shooting methods use these conditions to construct a finite system of
equations for these pieces and the times at which they meet
[6].
For collision avoidance, Beaver et al. [4] derive such matching
conditions for one agent relative to a prescribed reference trajectory.
For single-robot planning around fixed obstacles,
Beaver, Tron, and Cassandras [5] solve trajectory equations within a search over
obstacle-vertex sequences.
For fleets, Beaver and Malikopoulos [3] solve a square algebraic system
for each robot’s trajectory while holding higher-priority trajectories fixed.
Finally, Kamm et al. [16] completely characterize optimal two-robot motion with resting endpoints
for the squared-acceleration objective considered here.
We exploit this characterization within our numerical algorithm to construct solutions for larger fleets.

In this work.
We formulate fleet planning in terms of pairwise contacts, at which robots
reach the prescribed minimum separation. The stationarity conditions yield
a coupled algebraic system for the contact times and states, from which
the trajectories between contacts are reconstructed analytically.
The contact graph decomposes this system into independent groups of
interacting robots.
Our approach accounts for position, velocity,
and acceleration box constraints.
Sequential contact insertion (SCI) starts from independent robot trajectories, inserts contacts
at separation violations, and jointly adjusts their times and states.
 illustrates the algorithm and a grid-to-double-helix
transfer for N=1000N=1000 robots. We scale SCI to N=106N=10^{6} robots,
which is, to our knowledge, a scale unprecedented in the literature.
For fleet sizes amenable to existing methods, SCI obtains median speedups of several orders
of magnitude over an SCP baseline at matching accuracy.

title: AC-SMPC: Differentiable Actor--Critic MPC with State Constraints for Safe and Fast Robot Navigation
authors: Chaoran Wu,Jiayu Fan,Qichen Tan,Yuyi Liu,Jin Wang
abstract: Achieving safe navigation in confined dynamic environments remains a challenging problem, as robots must balance navigation efficiency with safety. Existing actor–critic MPC architectures typically employ differentiable MPC layers, but this way cannot readily accommodate explicit state constraints, making it intractable to involve collision avoidance within learning-based planning. To address this issue, we propose an actor–critic model predictive control framework with state constraints. We first use vertices to represent the robot and obstacles, and half-spaces to represent the workspace. Based on these, the nonlinear robot dynamics is locally linearized and the hyperplane-based collision avoidance constraints are convexified into the differentiable MPC layer, and then the actor exploits closed-loop feedback to adjust the MPC objective parameters that shape local motion behavior, while the critic evaluates long-term task performance. We further relax the convexified constraints with bounded and penalized slack variables to form an elastic quadratic program, accommodating cases where the local constraint approximations cannot be satisfied simultaneously. Simulation tests and experiments, involving dynamic collision avoidance for multi-robot in narrow cases, illustrate the advantages of the proposed framework in adaptively adjusting the learned policy and improving navigation efficiency over existing approaches while maintaining the motion safety.
introduction:
Fast and safe navigation for robots in confined dynamic environments depends on both interaction timing and geometric clearance. As openings created by moving obstacles change over time, a fixed tracking objective may produce persistent waiting or poorly timed motion. Learning-based MPC combines closed-loop adaptation with model-based prediction [1, 2]. Reinforcement learning can adapt the tracking objective according to observed interactions [3, 4, 5, 6], while MPC retains the system dynamics, actuator limits, and receding-horizon optimization [7]. Objective adaptation alone, however, does not ensure footprint-level geometric admissibility. A finite collision penalty can discourage proximity but does not impose the corresponding state constraint. Moreover, an inner footprint approximation cannot guarantee that the actual robot body remains collision-free, whereas an outer approximation may introduce conservatism. Explicit geometric constraints can represent collision avoidance and workspace containment directly over the embodied footprint [8, 9, 10], but their nonlinear dependence on robot position and orientation complicates their integration into differentiable actor–critic MPC. We address this problem by locally linearizing the robot dynamics and polygonal geometry and incorporating the resulting separation and containment constraints into a differentiable MPC layer. The actor adapts the tracking objective from closed-loop observations, the critic evaluates long-term performance, and bounded elastic relaxation handles locally incompatible constraint approximations.

Model predictive control is widely used in robotics because it combines prediction, receding-horizon replanning, and explicit input or state constraints in a single online optimization problem [2]. Reinforcement learning can complement this structure by adapting local motion behavior from task returns rather than relying solely on a hand-designed tracking objective [3, 4, 5, 6]. A central design choice is which part of the predictive controller is learned. Existing approaches learn dynamics, uncertainty descriptions, terminal ingredients, controller approximations, or objective parameters [11, 12, 13, 14, 15]. When the model is available, adapting the tracking objective or controller parameters allows MPC to remain the action-generating layer. Differentiable optimization layers and predictive controllers provide the corresponding gradient path through the optimizer [16, 17, 18, 19, 20, 21, 22]. In particular, AC-MPC embeds a differentiable MPC layer in an actor–critic policy [23], but its action-generating formulation does not include the footprint-dependent separation and containment constraints considered here [6]. Objective adaptation can therefore reshape local motion behavior, while footprint-level admissibility requires the corresponding state constraints to be explicitly represented in the action-generating optimization.

State constraints can enter learning-based control at different levels. Constrained and state-wise safe RL incorporate admissibility into policy updates [24, 25, 26], whereas control barrier functions and predictive safety filters impose model-based conditions on candidate or applied actions [27, 28, 29, 30, 31, 32]. These approaches determine how a prescribed admissible set influences learning or control, but its geometric fidelity remains a separate issue. A constraint defined only for a reference point or simplified body may be satisfied even when part of a noncircular robot footprint intersects an obstacle or crosses the workspace boundary.

Optimization-based planners represent collision geometry through signed distances, convex regions, dual formulations, separating planes, and local convex approximations [33, 34, 35, 8, 36, 37, 9, 38]. Such representations enable the occupied region to be modeled directly rather than inferred from a reference-point trajectory [10]. These works primarily address geometric feasibility under prescribed control objectives. AC-SMPC incorporates this geometric structure into a differentiable actor–critic MPC framework, allowing the tracking objective to be adapted online while the separating and containing constraints remain explicitly represented.

To achieve safe and efficient navigation in confined dynamic environments, we first use geometric representations to model the robot, obstacles, and workspace. A nonconvex obstacle region is constructed as a union of multiple convex polygons, and the workspace is represented as an intersection of half-spaces. The robot footprint and each convex obstacle component are represented as convex polygons. Based on these representations, we introduce two forms of state constraints: separating constraints that prevent collisions between the robot and obstacles, and containing constraints that keep the robot within the workspace. We locally convexify these constraints and embed them into a differentiable MPC layer, thereby explicitly constraining the control action while retaining a local gradient path from the control action to the learned objective parameters. These parameters are adapted online by an actor–critic architecture, in which the actor adjusts the MPC tracking objective from closed-loop feedback and the critic evaluates long-term task performance. The main contributions are as follows.

We propose an AC-SMPC framework which allows involving state constraints in the differentiable MPC layer. Compared to existing penalty-based collision avoidance in the objective function, the proposed framework can improve motion safety for robots.

We propose a parameter-adaptive MPC framework by introducing the actor–critic module, which adapts to modify tracking behavior in confined environments. Compared with fixed-cost MPC, AC-SMPC reduces the mean navigation time by 23.1% (from 12.28 s to 9.44 s), while the mean low-speed ratio decreases from 50.99% to 18.01%.

We validate the sim-to-real transfer of AC-SMPC for robot navigation in narrow dynamic corridors. The results illustrate the intelligent and fast navigation of AC-SMPC as well as its real-world applicability.

title: SAFARI: Semantic- And Frontier-driven Autonomous Risk Inspection
authors: Ugur Kafkasyali,Mihnea Toader,Julia Richter,Turcan Tuna,Cesar Cadena,Marco Hutter
comment: First two listed authors have equal contribution. Submitted to IEEE Transactions on Field Robotics
abstract:
Robotic exploration can reduce human exposure to hazardous environments by autonomously searching unknown areas for objects of interest while constructing a complete, risk-aware map.
However, existing autonomous exploration approaches typically prioritize geometric coverage or information gain, without explicitly coupling semantic object detection and the risk associated with operating near potentially hazardous objects.
Moreover, many systems have been demonstrated primarily in simulation or controlled environments, leaving limited validation of risk-aware semantic exploration in complex, unstructured field settings.
To address this gap, we propose SAFARI, a framework that treats object detection as a native channel of a unified probabilistic map, thereby jointly informing exploration and planning with both geometric and semantic evidence.
We evaluated SAFARI in 11 missions across three field sites on a quadruped platform. The framework achieved an average coverage of 98.7 %98.7\text{\,}\mathrm{\%} of the accessible mission area, without operator intervention for 97.6 %97.6\text{\,}\mathrm{\%} of mission time, and detected objects with characteristic dimensions as small as 15 cm15\text{\,}\mathrm{cm}.
Lastly, through ablation studies and a detailed analysis of system behavior, we show that object-size awareness and safety-aware path planning are crucial for effective hazardous-object search.
introduction:
Autonomous exploration is fundamental for many robotic applications involving reconnaissance, such as disaster response, search and rescue, and forest inventory. A key challenge in these tasks is that the environments may contain unknown hazards.
Such hazards can pose a threat not only to the robot but also to the environment or the robot operators. To make such tasks as safe as possible, reduction of human interaction through increased robot autonomy is a must [1].

Conducting reconnaissance autonomously can reduce human exposure to hazardous environments, while some tasks still require fine motor skills, precise judgment, and other capabilities that are not yet reliably reproducible by robots.
Hence, a robot-led reconnaissance mission prior to human involvement directly addresses this problem: given an area to explore, the robot should detect objects of potential interest (OPIs) – hazardous items or any other mission-relevant class – and create a map that marks areas as dangerous, observed to be safe, or unobserved.

Autonomous exploration around OPIs is challenging.
To achieve complete coverage efficiently, the robot must continuously assess traversability, determine which regions are safe with sufficient confidence, and minimize mission duration while accounting for uncertainty in its observations.
Depending on the task, a missed detection can range from inconvenient to catastrophic.
Additionally, the range at which it is possible to detect visible OPIs decreases with object size: the robot must get closer to small objects to reliably detect them, whereas larger objects are discernible from farther away.
Finally, traversability and OPI placement must be jointly reasoned over when deciding which region to explore next, since considering either in isolation omits critical information.

In this work, we present SAFARI, a detection, mapping, and path planning pipeline for autonomous exploration and reporting of OPIs in unstructured outdoor environments.
SAFARI accumulates depth-supported positive detections and object-size-dependent negative evidence in a persistent risk field. The resulting observation demand guides frontier and viewpoint selection together with geometric traversability and risk.

title: Physically Constrained Kinematic Calibration for High-Precision Robotic Needle Guidance
authors: Prabhu Nithin Gollapudi,Andreas Maier,Franziska Mathis-Ullrich,Water Zhao,Jia Wang,Siming Bayer
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Systems and Control (eess.SY); Optimization and Control (math.OC)
abstract: Percutaneous needle insertion is a common practice in minimally invasive procedures whose clinical success depends on accurate needle placement. However, achieving the necessary precision is a challenge for manual operators. Robotic assistance can improve targeting accuracy and reduce operator dependence, but residual millimeter-scale errors persist because nominal kinematic models do not fully represent the physical manipulator. This paper presents a robust bound-constrained kinematic calibration method designed to improve positional accuracy for a 6-Degree-of-Freedom (6-DoF) robotic needle-guidance manipulator. The approach uses physically plausible parameter ranges to regularize a compact 19-parameter geometric identification model. By treating these bounds as active optimization constraints rather than mere numerical safeguards, the framework effectively mitigates parameter coupling and overfitting, ensuring highly stable parameter identification. In simulation, the proposed method reduced end-effector Root Mean Square Error (RMSE) from 3.422 mm to 0.690 mm (a 79.8% improvement). In benchtop hardware experiments, the calibrated model achieved sub-millimeter validation accuracy, including 0.865 mm RMSE in experimental trajectory validation and 0.610 mm RMSE in a coordinate-lattice verification task. These results demonstrate that physically constrained kinematic calibration can enhance robotic needle-targeting accuracy, establishing a high-precision foundation for future clinical applications.
introduction:
Accurate percutaneous needle insertion is a critical component of various minimally invasive interventions, including biopsies, localized drug delivery, and thermal ablation. Among these, percutaneous thermal ablation for liver tumors represents a particularly demanding application. While ablation serves as a primary therapeutic alternative for patients ineligible for surgical resection [1, 2, 3], its clinical efficacy relies heavily on precise targeting. Achieving complete tumor necrosis requires a strict 5–10 mm safety margin while carefully avoiding collateral damage to adjacent vasculature and bile ducts [4, 5, 6, 7]. Even small targeting deviations can lead to incomplete ablation or severe complications. Consequently, robotic assistance has emerged as a promising solution for reducing operator variability and enabling consistent, high-precision workflows [3, 7, 8].

Despite these advantages, the absolute positioning accuracy of current robotic systems is still limited by discrepancies between the nominal kinematic model provided by the manufacturer and the actual physical manipulator. These discrepancies, caused by manufacturing tolerances, assembly errors, joint compliance, and encoder offsets, typically result in millimeter-scale Cartesian positioning errors at the end-effector [9, 10].

Kinematic calibration is the established method for compensating for such geometric inaccuracies in serial manipulators. However, existing approaches often face a fundamental trade-off between model fidelity and robustness. High-dimensional models suffer from parameter coupling and overfitting, while simplified models may miss critical error sources. Moreover, most studies emphasize in-sample fitting accuracy with limited attention to parameter stability, generalization performance, or the incorporation of physical constraints [11, 9, 12].

To address these limitations, this paper proposes a robust kinematic calibration framework for a 6-DoF serial manipulator tailored for percutaneous needle guidance. Rather than treating parameter bounds merely as numerical safeguards, our approach utilizes physically motivated bounds as an explicit regularization mechanism to ensure parameter stability and predictive accuracy.

The specific contributions of this work are:

A 19-parameter geometric identification model that captures the dominant error sources of the manipulator.

A calibration pipeline combining observability-optimized configuration sampling, Kabsch-based tracker-to-base initialization, and bound-constrained Trust-Region Reflective (TRF) optimization.

Comprehensive benchtop validation utilizing a 10-fold cross-validation methodology, simulation, and physical hardware experiments that demonstrates robust sub-millimeter positioning accuracy. This establishes the fundamental kinematic precision required prior to future phantom and ex vivo studies.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows: Section II reviews related work. Section III details the kinematic modeling and the proposed calibration methodology. Section IV describes the experiments and results, and Section V concludes the paper.

1. A 19-parameter geometric identification model that captures the dominant error sources of the manipulator.

2. A calibration pipeline combining observability-optimized configuration sampling, Kabsch-based tracker-to-base initialization, and bound-constrained Trust-Region Reflective (TRF) optimization.

3. Comprehensive benchtop validation utilizing a 10-fold cross-validation methodology, simulation, and physical hardware experiments that demonstrates robust sub-millimeter positioning accuracy. This establishes the fundamental kinematic precision required prior to future phantom and ex vivo studies.

title: BioAgent: Self-Directed Skill Acquisition and Capability Growth for Long-Horizon Laboratory Protocols
authors: Gaojing Zhang,Changwen Chen,Zichen Luo,Jialiang Li,Yuhan Wang,Yifei Xie,Wenzhao Lian
abstract:
Executing an unfamiliar laboratory protocol requires a robot to identify missing capabilities and determine whether each operation remains valid as the experiment progresses. This letter presents BioAgent, an embodied agent that addresses these coupled challenges of capability sufficiency and experimental validity. It matches human-reviewed requirements to validated skills and task packages, selects tool-based implementations for missing behaviors, and requests human teaching when needed during learning. Learned skills undergo sequential task-package validation to check outcomes and compatibility between successive operations. During execution, precondition, outcome, and experimental-state checks govern progression, autonomous recovery, or termination. Execution evidence guides tool selection, while accepted experience supports offline policy updates and task packaging. On the second task, BioAgent reuses 17 skill types unchanged,
revises two existing implementations, and acquires five new types. On two dual-arm laboratory tasks with 20 and 31 ordered skill invocations, BioAgent achieves complete-task success rates of 66% and 58% with autonomous recovery over 50 runs per task. Across 25 atomic skills evaluated over 50 autonomous trials each with recovery disabled, success rates range from 84% to 100%, with 17 skills achieving 50/50. Project page:https://suiuko.github.io/bioagentweb/.
introduction:
A robot prepared for one laboratory protocol is not necessarily ready for the next. New protocols can require operations or skill combinations beyond its finite repertoire. Even when the required skills are available, earlier steps or failures can change the conditions under which they can be used. Executing an unfamiliar protocol therefore poses two coupled challenges: capability sufficiency, whether the robot has the capabilities required by the task, and experimental validity, whether the current state permits execution under the specified constraints.

Automated laboratory systems carry out routine handling operations as part of multi-step experimental workflows [1, 2, 3]. More recent systems use protocol instructions to guide robotic planning [4] and vision–language–action (VLA) models to execute laboratory manipulations [5, 6]. However, translating a protocol into a plan does not ensure that the robot can perform every required operation. Even when most of the workflow is supported by existing skills or their compositions, a single missing behavior can prevent its completion. Guided demonstration and continual skill learning provide ways to acquire additional capabilities [7, 8]. The challenge is therefore to identify which protocol requirements remain unsupported and direct learning toward those gaps while retaining validated skills for reuse.

Capability sufficiency alone does not establish experimental validity. Each operation acts on the state produced by preceding steps. After a partially completed liquid transfer, for example, the robot may still be able to repeat the motion, but doing so may no longer satisfy the experimental requirements. The decision to continue depends on the current sample, container, and liquid states and the protocol’s timing constraints. A missing capability calls for acquisition; an unmet but restorable precondition calls for preparation or recovery; a confirmed validity violation requires termination.

This letter presents BioAgent, an embodied agent system that enables robots to execute unfamiliar laboratory protocols by closing only the capability gaps that prevent valid execution, while retaining validated capabilities for future reuse (Fig. ). BioAgent matches human-reviewed requirements to validated skills and task packages, then refines unsupported requirements to distinguish reusable compositions from missing atomic behaviors. For each missing behavior, it selects or combines tools and requests human demonstrations or corrections only when needed during learning. Newly learned skills then undergo sequential task-package validation, which checks both their outcomes and the conditions linking successive operations.

During execution, precondition, outcome, and experimental-state checks determine whether to proceed, retry, restore preconditions, or terminate. A missing recovery skill identified during development returns the affected requirement to learning. Execution evidence guides subsequent tool choices, while accepted demonstrations, execution traces, and corrections support offline policy updates and task packaging. Validated candidates enter the reusable repertoire, linking task execution to capability growth in subsequent experiments.

Our contributions are threefold:

We develop a targeted capability-acquisition procedure that matches task requirements to validated skills and compositions, identifies missing behaviors, and directs tool-based skill construction and, when needed, human teaching toward those gaps.

We develop a recovery mechanism that couples experimental validity with capability acquisition. BioAgent uses observed partial effects to identify admissible recovery, composes validated skills or requests targeted teaching for missing recovery behaviors during learning, and reassesses sample, container, liquid-state, and timing constraints before resumption.

We present an acquisition–execution–reuse mechanism that separates skill learning from sequential task-package validation, uses execution evidence to guide tool selection, and converts accepted experience into candidate policies and task packages for validation and reuse.

Experiments on two dual-arm laboratory tasks demonstrate BioAgent’s ability to close capability gaps selectively while retaining validated skills for reuse. On the second task, BioAgent reuses 17 skill types unchanged, revises two implementations, and acquires five new skill types, expanding the validated repertoire from 20 to 25 types. Validity-aware recovery improves complete-task success by 12 and 18 percentage points on the two tasks, respectively.

title: MolmoSpaces-CommonSense: Evaluating Commonsense in Robotic Manipulation Policies
authors: Arjun Guru,Max Argus,Jae Sung Park,Jiafei Duan,Ali Farhadi,Ranjay Krishna
comment: Project page:this https URL
abstract:
Real-world robotic manipulation requires reasoning about cluttered scenes, partially observable or hidden objects, and semantically appropriate actions, in addition to low-level execution within those scenes. However, existing simulation benchmarks primarily test the latter and remain dominated by comparatively clean environments with limited clutter and narrowly scoped task structure, leaving many forms of commonsense reasoning untested. We address this by introducing a taxonomy of reasoning processes for robotic manipulation grounded in developmental cognitive science. We operationalize this taxonomy through a new benchmark of robot tasks, MolmoSpaces-CommonSense, that requires reasoning about occlusion, containment, support relations, semantically correct grasp points, spatial affordances, and hidden objects. These evaluations require policies not only to recognize relevant scene structure but also to execute correct actions in them. We evaluate several zero-shot generalist manipulation policies. Across model types and architectures, we observe consistent failures in commonsense reasoning: success rates in cluttered scenes drop by over 50% as distractors increase, policies act on incorrect objects in cluttered settings 30% of the time, and affordance-sensitive grasping remains unreliable even with highly specific language prompts, with correct object part selection happening only about 50% of the time.
Further, VLM-based success estimation struggles to reliably evaluate rollouts in these settings, suggesting that the challenge extends beyond control to the broader perception-reasoning-action stack.
Our results suggest that existing benchmarks may substantially overestimate zero-shot real-world readiness. Code and policy leaderboard link at https://github.com/allenai/molmospaces.
introduction:
Manipulation in the real world is a reasoning problem before it is a control problem. A robot must decide which object an instruction refers to in clutter, infer what remains true when objects become partially hidden, determine what actions the scene affords, and choose behaviors that are physically and semantically appropriate for the goal. Cognitive science has long treated these capabilities not as a single faculty but as interacting forms of physical reasoning, affordance perception, and object permanence [1, 2, 3]. Yet the benchmarks that currently anchor progress in robot learning [4, 5, 6, 7, 8] are still built primarily around executing predefined task suites in comparatively controlled scenes with a small set of task-relevant objects, rather than systematically requiring reasoning under clutter, occlusion, or hidden state.

This gap is ubiquitous in homes, labs, and workspaces, which are cluttered and where targets are often occluded, covered, contained, or displaced out of view. Yet current robot policies are largely neither trained nor evaluated in environments that make these capabilities necessary [9]: a policy that succeeds only when the target is cleanly visible and the correct action is obvious is not one that can be deployed in the real world.

In this work, we introduce a taxonomy of commonsense reasoning processes for robotic manipulation, grounded in decades of cognitive science. The taxonomy (see Fig. 1) organizes a practically important subset of embodied commonsense into three categories: physical reasoning (object presence and relations under occlusion, covering, and containment), affordances (grasping affordances at the object-part level and spatial affordances at the surface level), and object permanence (acting on objects seen but no longer visible). Our goal is not to claim completeness but to provide a concrete framework for asking which reasoning processes current manipulation policies actually utilize.

We operationalize this taxonomy by extending MolmoSpaces [9] with environments that force these reasoning processes to matter at action time. MolmoSpaces provides a scalable ecosystem of diverse indoor scenes, richly annotated objects, and infrastructure with strong sim-to-real alignment, making it a natural substrate for this evaluation. On top of it, we construct tasks and conditions that demand reasoning at action time, such as dense distractor clutter, targets hidden beneath covers or inside containers, and prompts requiring semantically correct grasp points. Because these evaluations are closed-loop, success requires more than recognizing the right relation in an image; the policy must use that relation to produce the right action sequence.

We use MolmoSpaces-CommonSense to evaluate representative zero-shot generalist policies spanning both VLA and WAM paradigms, including π0.5\pi_{0.5} [6], MolmoAct2 [10], and DreamZero [11]. The main pattern is strikingly consistent across architectures. In cluttered physical-reasoning tasks, success drops by more than 50% as the number of nearby distractors increases, and the dominant failure mode is not generic instability but selecting or moving toward the wrong object. In affordance-sensitive grasping tasks, overall success remains low, around 25%, and increasing prompt specificity does little to improve whether the object is grasped the correct part. Together, these results suggest that current policies can often execute atomic motions once the scene is easy, but they do not yet reliably reason through the scene conditions that make real manipulation hard. We further find that VLM judges struggle to reliably classify success and failure from rollout videos in these scenes, suggesting that the difficulty extends across the broader perception-reasoning-action stack.

More broadly, this study is about what we choose to measure. If benchmarks do not test hidden-object reasoning, affordance-sensitive action selection, or behavior under partial observability, then high success rates can tell an overly optimistic story about readiness for deployment. By grounding benchmark design in cognitive science and instantiating that design in scalable embodied environments, we hope to make commonsense reasoning a first-class target for robot policy evaluation and improvement.

title: DiffWBC: Unlocking Steerable General Humanoid Motion Tracking via One-Step Diffusion Whole-Body Control
authors: Yifei Huang,Yazhao Yang,Weijia Li,Zhiheng Ma,Dian Shen
abstract:
General humanoid motion trackers typically rely on deterministic policies that cannot adapt online without brittle reference editing or costly retraining.
We present DiffWBC, shifting whole-body control to a generative paradigm via a one-step diffusion model.
By modeling distributions over future trajectories, DiffWBC unifies general tracking, test-time steering, and simulation-free failure discovery within a single controller:
(1) Generative general tracking: DiffWBC requires a single forward pass per 50 Hz control step and can be distilled from an RL teacher or trained from scratch via model-based RL, achieving the lowest local tracking error among six general trackers on held-out benchmarks (20.120.1 mm on BONES) and deploying on a physical Unitree G1.
(2) Zero-shot test-time steering: differentiable cost gradients and body-group masks modulate the frozen controller online, substantially outperforming kinematic reference editing (0.84 clean pass at 1.25 m ceiling vs. 0.10) and zero-shot generalizing across hurdles, spatial reaching, actuator faults, and tray balancing.
(3) Simulation-free failure discovery: plan dispersion across generation noise effectively identifies physical tracking failures (91% precision in top 2%) without physics simulations; targeted fine-tuning on flagged clips resolves 50% of failure cases. Videos and interactive demonstrations are available at https://diffwbc.github.io/#selfassess.
introduction:
Motion tracking serves as the foundational paradigm for humanoid whole-body control, enabling robots to realize diverse kinematic reference trajectories on physical hardware through computed joint-level actuation commands [26, 34, 5, 10, 9, 50, 28, 20, 36].
Yet, contemporary general-purpose trackers almost universally employ deterministic feed-forward policies; once trained, their learned mappings are rigid and invariant.
Consequently, when unforeseen environmental constraints or auxiliary operational objectives arise during deployment—such as crouching beneath low-clearance obstacles, clearing hurdles, or reaching towards spatial targets—these deterministic controllers lack the latent flexibility necessary for real-time behavioral modulation.

To address task flexibility, prior literature has explored three predominant avenues, each presenting fundamental limitations in training-free general control:

Perceptive tracker adaptation (e.g., Perceptive BFM [43], ViBe [16]): integrating vision into tracking policies. However, they rely on specialized terrain-conformal reference synthesis or skill-specific RL fine-tuning; altering obstacle geometries or behavioral objectives necessitates costly data re-generation and policy retraining.

Hierarchical planner-tracker pipelines (e.g., CLoSD [38], TextOp [47], Heracles [46], OMG [12]): deploying generative models as upstream planners to modify kinematic references for an independent tracker. This decoupled hierarchy inherently suffers from planner-controller mismatch [48]: kinematically edited trajectories routinely violate actuator limits, while tracking lag precipitates collision under dynamic obstacle constraints.

Task-conditioned action diffusion (e.g., PredActor [48], BeyondMimic [22], Diffuse-CLoC [14]): jointly modeling state-action dynamics within a single policy. However, conditioned solely on semantic prompts or sparse spatial targets rather than full-body reference horizons, their behavioral repertoires remain confined to narrow task-training distributions.

In this work, we propose DiffWBC, bridging this dichotomy by unifying general-purpose reference tracking and generative trajectory modeling within a single, high-frequency whole-body controller.
Rather than decoupling planning from execution, the 50 Hz controller itself is formulated as a one-step diffusion model.
At each control step, conditioned on current proprioceptive feedback and a sliding multi-group reference window, DiffWBC generates a distributionally coherent horizon of future states and joint actions in a single forward pass, mapped to low-level actuation via an inverse-dynamics head.
By formalizing whole-body control as learning a distribution over physically grounded future trajectories, DiffWBC confers three key capabilities unattainable by conventional feed-forward or decoupled pipelines (Fig. 1):

1. Generative general tracking with dual training paradigms.
DiffWBC represents, to our knowledge, the first one-step diffusion whole-body controller capable of general humanoid motion tracking.
It can be distilled online from an RL teacher (32 GPU-hours) or trained from scratch via model-based RL through a learned neural world model (20 GPU-hours) without teacher supervision.
Across six general trackers on held-out motions, from-scratch DiffWBC establishes the lowest local tracking error (20.120.1 mm on BONES), and its physical viability is verified on a real Unitree G1 humanoid robot.

2. Training-free test-time steering and body-group yielding.
By modeling future trajectory distributions, DiffWBC permits real-time behavioral steering without policy fine-tuning.
Differentiable costs (whole-body signed-distance fields, spatial reach hinge losses, joint torque limits) directly guide the generator’s input noise through analytic gradients.
Operating within the closed-loop controller, this resolves planner-controller mismatch, boosting collision-free passage under a 1.25 m ceiling from 0.10 to 0.84.
Furthermore, body-group reference masking enables designated limbs to yield control authority entirely to task objectives while unmasked groups maintain stable tracking.
The identical frozen model zero-shot resolves hurdle clearing, target reaching, actuator fault compensation, tray balancing, and velocity command following.

3. Low-cost failure discovery and targeted self-repair.
DiffWBC utilizes the dispersion of predicted plans across input noise as an intrinsic measure of predictive uncertainty.

Hierarchical planner-tracker pipelines (e.g., CLoSD [38], TextOp [47], Heracles [46], OMG [12]): deploying generative models as upstream planners to modify kinematic references for an independent tracker.
