title: CalibSwitch: Observation-Driven Camera-LiDAR Extrinsic Recovery and Selective Maintenance for Multimodal Perception
authors: Haifa Zhang,Yijing Wang,Zhiqiang Zuo
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
abstract: Camera–LiDAR perception on mobile robots and intelligent vehicles depends on reliable sensor geometry throughout deployment. Installation variations create uncertainty in the initial extrinsics, while changing observation quality makes frame-wise estimates fluctuate during operation. This paper presents CalibSwitch, an observation-driven framework that separates absolute extrinsic recovery from selective state maintenance. A cross-modal absolute extrinsic generator (CAEG) combines projection-free bidirectional feature interaction with geometry-regularized learning to recover complete SE(3) candidates from image–point observations and coarse view context, without a supplied numerical initial transform. A selective recurrent calibration policy (SRCP) combines observation quality and temporal history to determine when a candidate should replace the working geometry consumed by a frozen multimodal detector. On nuScenes, CAEG achieves mean translation and rotation errors of 0.248 m and 5.884∘. Under sustained geometric transitions, SRCP reaches a mean composite error of 1.46 with 9.70% candidate commitments, outperforming quality-based and temporal-consistency gating at comparable commitment rates. Relative to unconditional per-frame updating, it improves frozen-detector mAP and NDS by 1.43 and 0.92 points. Paired geometry–observation uncertainty tests, two real-vehicle platforms, and 13.5-FPS single-camera Jetson execution demonstrate the system value of selective geometric-state maintenance for continuous perception.
introduction:
Camera–LiDAR fusion combines image semantics with metric spatial information for perception on mobile robots, intelligent vehicles, and industrial sensing platforms [24, 3, 19]. Its operation relies on the geometric relationship between physically separated sensors. Practical systems undergo independent installation, assembly adjustment, sensor replacement, and platform transfer; the actual working configuration can consequently differ from the design or previously calibrated configuration [23]. Structural and operational changes add further uncertainty during deployment [17, 35]. These engineering conditions motivate a system that can establish usable geometry from current observations and maintain that geometry throughout continuous operation.

Geometric adaptation and reliable operation act on different aspects of this problem. A persistent configuration change calls for a new working extrinsic. Meanwhile, illumination, occlusion, scene structure, and LiDAR sparsity change the reliability of instantaneous estimates [37, 4]. A large difference between a new estimate and the maintained state may therefore reflect either a lasting geometric change or a transient observation disturbance. The system must use the available sensing evidence and its history to decide when to adapt. This motivates treating extrinsics as maintained perception states whose acceptance is governed by observation reliability.

Existing calibration recovers sensor geometry through engineered targets, natural-feature alignment, motion constraints, or learned cross-modal representations [21, 2, 17]. Residual learning efficiently corrects a supplied transform within a learned neighborhood [28, 12, 25, 36], while target-free alignment and consistency-aware estimation recover geometry through scene or multiview evidence [8, 9, 35]. Online estimation further exploits trajectories and finite histories [30, 16]; event-triggered fusion uses information-dependent update decisions to support continuous operation [6, 22]. Together, these developments motivate two coupled operations for deployment: generating a complete candidate from current multimodal evidence and deciding whether that candidate should become the geometry used by the perception system.

The key insight of CalibSwitch is that generating a geometric estimate and committing it to a working perception state are distinct operations. The candidate T^t\widehat{T}_{t} represents geometry supported by current observations, whereas the maintained extrinsic TtT_{t} determines the geometry consumed by subsequent perception. Each commitment therefore affects both the current frame and the reliability of the working state over time. Jointly considering instantaneous observation quality and historical geometric consistency enables adaptation to persistent configuration changes while suppressing transient estimation disturbances. This persistent effect motivates recurrent decisions and sequence-level learning.

We implement this idea through an observe–generate–select–detect chain. The cross-modal absolute extrinsic generator (CAEG) uses camera images, LiDAR points, and coarse view context to recover complete camera-to-LiDAR transforms without a numerical initial matrix. Projection-free bidirectional feature interaction establishes joint image–point evidence, and geometry-regularized supervision connects pose parameters to rigid-body action and spatial consistency. The selective recurrent calibration policy (SRCP) selects keep or update, and a frozen BEVFusion detector consumes the resulting working state. Evaluation follows the same progression: initial recovery, selective maintenance, downstream perception, and natural deployment on two real platforms. The contributions are as follows.

We develop an observation-driven absolute extrinsic generator that combines bidirectional image–point interaction and geometry-regularized supervision to recover complete camera–LiDAR transformations, conditioned on coarse view context and without a supplied numerical initial matrix.

We develop an observation-driven absolute extrinsic generator that combines bidirectional image–point interaction and geometry-regularized supervision to recover complete camera–LiDAR transformations, conditioned on coarse view context and without a supplied numerical initial matrix.

We formulate online calibration maintenance as a recurrent state-commitment problem. The proposed policy combines current observation quality and historical consistency to adapt to persistent geometric changes while retaining reliable geometry during transient observation disturbances.

We connect recovery and selective maintenance to a frozen multimodal detector and establish their system value through pose recovery, joint uncertainty tests and matched-commitment comparisons, mechanism analysis, two real-vehicle platforms, and embedded execution.

1. We develop an observation-driven absolute extrinsic generator that combines bidirectional image–point interaction and geometry-regularized supervision to recover complete camera–LiDAR transformations, conditioned on coarse view context and without a supplied numerical initial matrix.

2. We formulate online calibration maintenance as a recurrent state-commitment problem. The proposed policy combines current observation quality and historical consistency to adapt to persistent geometric changes while retaining reliable geometry during transient observation disturbances.

3. We connect recovery and selective maintenance to a frozen multimodal detector and establish their system value through pose recovery, joint uncertainty tests and matched-commitment comparisons, mechanism analysis, two real-vehicle platforms, and embedded execution.

title: Geometry-Aware Humanoid Retargeting via Manifold ODEs
authors: Pengyu Zhu,Heye Wang,Xi Wang,Xuyang Wu,He Kong,Guodong Shi
abstract: In this paper, we focus on interaction-preserving motion retargeting, which transfers human demonstrations to humanoids while maintaining spatial relationships with objects and terrain. Previous work, such as OmniRetarget, addresses this task through temporally coupled constrained optimization, requiring repeated sequential quadratic programming (SQP) iterations at each frame. We study this problem from an ordinary differential equation (ODE) perspective by modeling the continuous-time limit of its framewise Karush–Kuhn–Tucker (KKT) conditions as an ODE on the robot configuration manifold. This viewpoint offers two benefits: (i) it connects OmniRetarget’s SQP iterations to a backward discretization of the ODE, enabling us to establish their local convergence under suitable regularity assumptions; and (ii) it leads to TaSP-KKT (tangent-space parametrization for KKT flow), a new retargeting method based on a forward discretization of the KKT flow. The proposed method achieves the same first-order convergence to the ODE solution as the corresponding backward scheme while requiring only one weighted tangent-cone projection and a closed-form manifold update per step, thereby avoiding repeated inner SQP iterations. Numerical experiments show that TaSP-KKT achieves retargeting quality comparable to, though slightly lower than, that of OmniRetarget while running approximately twice as fast.
introduction:
Whole-body tasks such as carrying objects and stepping onto a platform require humanoid robots to coordinate their limbs while maintaining contact with objects and the environment [7, 6]. Human demonstrations provide examples of this coordination and can serve as references for learning robot behaviors. However, differences in body proportions, joint structure, and motion limits prevent human motions from being transferred directly to a robot. Generating usable robot motion references therefore requires adapting both the demonstrated movements and their interactions with the scene to the robot’s embodiment. Motion retargeting aims to enable a target character or robot to reproduce a source motion despite differences in body proportions or skeletal structure while preserving the motion’s essential characteristics.

Early approaches to motion retargeting include the spacetime optimization of Gleicher [5] and the inverse-rate formulation of Choi and Ko [3]. More recently, General Motion Retargeting (GMR) [1] combines local scaling with differential inverse kinematics to generate humanoid motion references. Interaction-preserving motion retargeting, which maintains spatial relationships and contacts during motion transfer, has also received much attention. For example, Contact-Aware Retargeting [24] combines a geometry-conditioned recurrent network with encoder-space optimization to reduce interpenetration and preserve self-contacts and ground contacts. M-R2ET [26] uses a learned model to predict residual motion corrections that account for skeletal relationships and body geometry, aiming to reduce interpenetration and missing contacts when transferring motion between characters with different skeletal structures.

Among the most recent work is OmniRetarget [25], which uses an interaction mesh to represent spatial relationships among the body, objects, and terrain. At each frame, it minimizes Laplacian mesh deformation subject to kinematic constraints using a sequential quadratic programming (SQP) solver. The resulting references reduced penetration and foot skating and supported object carrying and terrain traversal on a Unitree G1 humanoid.

In this paper, we study humanoid motion retargeting and OmniRetarget from the perspective of ordinary differential equations (ODEs). Our motivation is twofold. First, OmniRetarget solves a sequence of temporally coupled constrained optimization problems, but the original work does not establish convergence guarantees for its SQP iterations. The longstanding connections between optimization and ODEs provide tools for analyzing convergence [13, 20, 4]. These connections motivate us to establish theoretical guarantees for OmniRetarget through a dynamical formulation.

Second, an ODE formulation can guide the development of new algorithms. In deep learning, Haber et al. [8] use a continuous-time interpretation of residual networks to develop multiscale training methods, which attains higher classification accuracy and lower training cost. In diffusion generative modeling, Lu et al. [19] exploit the structure of diffusion ODEs to derive DPM-Solver, which use with high-order ODE schemes to accelerate sampling. These examples motivate using the structure of retargeting dynamics to design more efficient numerical methods.

ODE-based methods have also been explored in humanoid planning and retargeting. Klein et al. [15] generate robot arm motions as piecewise geodesics governed by second-order ODEs under an inertia-based Riemannian metric. Their subsequent work [16] modifies this metric using barrier functions to generate collision-avoiding trajectories. Li et al. [18] use a learned conditional ODE flow to adapt motions across characters with the same skeletal topology but different body proportions. MoReFlow [14] formulates human-to-robot motion mapping as an ODE flow in latent space and uses flow matching to train a neural network that parameterizes its velocity field.

In this paper, we model the evolution of the optimal robot configurations generated by OmniRetarget as an ODE on ℳ=𝕊3×ℝd\mathcal{M}=\mathbb{S}^{3}\times\mathbb{R}^{d}, where 𝕊3\mathbb{S}^{3} represents the floating-base orientation using a unit quaternion, and ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d} contains the base translation and joint coordinates. We then use this ODE formulation to analyze the convergence of OmniRetarget’s SQP solver and derive a computationally efficient retargeting algorithm. Our contributions are summarized as follows:

We develop a manifold ODE formulation of OmniRetarget. In particular, we characterize the evolution of OmniRetarget’s framewise KKT point as a projected flow on the robot configuration manifold ℳ=𝕊3×ℝd\mathcal{M}=\mathbb{S}^{3}\times\mathbb{R}^{d}. The formulation provides a common basis for analyzing the existing solver and designing new retargeting algorithms.

We connect OmniRetarget’s SQP iterations to a backward discretization of the KKT flow. Through this connection, we interpret the SQP iterations as Newton steps for the backward discretization and establish local convergence of the SQP solver.

We propose TaSP-KKT, a retargeting algorithm based on a forward discretization of the KKT flow. It achieves the same convergence order as the SQP-based backward scheme. Each step requires only one weighted tangent-cone projection and a closed-form manifold update, avoiding repeated inner SQP iterations and thus reducing the computational cost. Preliminary numerical experiments show that TaSP-KKT achieves retargeting quality comparable to that of OmniRetarget while running approximately twice as fast.

title: Joint-Health-Aware Reinforcement Learning for Robust Robot Control Under Actuator Degradation
authors: Haifa Zhang,Yijing Wang,Zhiqiang Zuo
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
abstract: Robots deployed in unstructured environments are susceptible to actuator-authority degradation, which reduces the effective control authority of individual actuators and can cause reinforcement learning policies trained under nominal dynamics to fail. Existing robustness approaches rely on discrete fault labels, broad domain randomization, or global latent variables, often without explicitly modeling continuous per-joint residual actuation capability. We propose a joint-health-aware reinforcement learning framework for robust robot control under simulated actuator degradation. Our framework encodes actuator condition in a continuous joint-health vector and models degradation as multiplicative attenuation of executed actions. A dedicated HealthNet estimator infers per-joint health from recent observations and actions, allowing the policy to redistribute control effort across healthy and degraded joints. We evaluate the method on Walker, Go2, Cassie, and Panda-based ManiSkill manipulation tasks under diverse degradation masks and severity levels. The method outperforms nominal and degradation-trained no-health baselines on the main evaluated metrics. Relative to the nominal baseline, task-level locomotion returns improve by up to 250.1% and manipulation success rates by up to 15.2 percentage points; in the high-degradation Cassie group, return increases from 3.94 to 40.50 (+928.0%). Ablations support the contribution of per-joint health estimation, action-degradation modeling, and health-conditioned control.
introduction:
Robots deployed in unstructured environments may experience actuator degradation or partial loss of control authority. Such failures are fundamentally different from ordinary sensing noise or mild dynamics perturbations. When a joint degrades, the command issued by the policy may no longer be faithfully realized by the corresponding actuator: a weakened hip, knee, calf, or wrist can still receive large control commands, but the resulting motion may be attenuated or nearly absent. This joint-level action–response mismatch is especially harmful for locomotion and manipulation, where successful behavior depends on coordinated multi-joint control. Fig. 1 illustrates how a nominal controller and a health-conditioned policy respond differently to the same degradation on each platform.

While existing approaches enhance robustness to dynamics shifts, few explicitly represent how much actuation capability remains at each individual joint. Fault detection and diagnosis techniques typically describe failures using discrete labels, binary indicators, or predefined fault categories [1, 2]. Domain randomization improves average robustness by training policies over diverse dynamics, but the controller is not directly informed about which actuator is degraded [3, 4, 5]. Online adaptation and latent-context schemes infer hidden dynamics from recent interaction history, yet the inferred variables are usually global or unstructured, lacking direct correspondence to individual joints [6, 7, 8]. As a result, these schemes provide limited explicit information for redistributing control effort under heterogeneous partial actuator degradation.

Achieving robust control under actuator-authority degradation motivates an explicit representation of residual per-joint actuation capability. A degraded robot cannot simply replay its original motion pattern, nor should it abandon partially impaired joints entirely. Rather, the controller needs to estimate which joints remain functional and how severely they are degraded, then use that information to redistribute control effort. This motivates coupling per-joint health estimation with policy conditioning, so that estimated residual capability directly informs action generation.

To this end, we propose a joint-health-aware reinforcement learning framework for robust robot control under actuator-authority degradation. The framework characterizes actuator condition via a continuous joint-health vector ht∈[0,1]Jh_{t}\in[0,1]^{J}, where each element captures the residual control authority of one actuator. During training, sampled health vectors modulate executed actions through a multiplicative degradation gate, producing structured action–response mismatch under simulated actuator degradation. A dedicated HealthNet estimator predicts current joint health from a short observation–action history, and the policy conditions on this prediction to adapt its actions. During deployment, true health is unavailable; the policy relies exclusively on estimated health to reduce dependence on degraded joints and exploit the remaining capability of healthier ones.

We evaluate the framework on Walker, Unitree Go2, Cassie, and Panda-based ManiSkill manipulation tasks under diverse degradation masks and severity levels. The method improves performance over nominal and degradation-trained no-health baselines. Relative to the nominal baseline, task-level locomotion returns improve by up to 250.1% and manipulation success rates by up to 15.2 percentage points.

The main contributions of this work are threefold:

Actuator-authority degradation is formulated as a continuous per-joint health representation, and its effect is modeled through an action degradation mechanism, enabling finer-grained characterization of residual control authority than binary or categorical fault indicators.

A joint-health-aware reinforcement learning framework with HealthNet is developed to estimate per-joint health from recent observation–action history and condition the control policy on the predicted health vector for degradation-aware control redistribution.

The proposed method is evaluated across locomotion and manipulation benchmarks, including Walker, Unitree Go2, Cassie, and Panda-based ManiSkill tasks, demonstrating consistent robustness improvements under diverse joint-degradation patterns and severity levels.

1. Actuator-authority degradation is formulated as a continuous per-joint health representation, and its effect is modeled through an action degradation mechanism, enabling finer-grained characterization of residual control authority than binary or categorical fault indicators.

2. A joint-health-aware reinforcement learning framework with HealthNet is developed to estimate per-joint health from recent observation–action history and condition the control policy on the predicted health vector for degradation-aware control redistribution.

3. The proposed method is evaluated across locomotion and manipulation benchmarks, including Walker, Unitree Go2, Cassie, and Panda-based ManiSkill tasks, demonstrating consistent robustness improvements under diverse joint-degradation patterns and severity levels.

title: HandMimicX: Learning Human-Like Dexterous Manipulation via an Object-Centric Policy from Egocentric Videos
authors: Zihan Gao,Yufei Liu,Yuhong Zhang,Zhen Yu,Xinhao Huang,Zhinan You,Kai W. Ho,Zipeng Ye,Peng Jiao,Haoqian Wang
abstract:
Learning dexterous manipulation from human videos remains an open challenge, particularly in the context of transferring a single demonstration into a spatially generalizable robotic skill and maintaining physically plausible human-like interactions. Unlike prior works that emphasize hand-motion imitation,
we introduce an object-centric framework for acquiring dexterous skills from egocentric human RGB-D videos. Within our framework, we formulate the reinforcement learning (RL) objective in terms of object motion to decouple the underlying skill from the specific hand trajectory and impose constraints on hand–object interaction states to promote more anatomically natural hand configurations. Extensive experiments in simulation and on real robots demonstrate that our method enables efficient learning from human videos and generalizable skill transfer across novel spatial configurations. Project page:
https://anonymous.4open.science/w/handmimicx/index.html.
introduction:
Recent advances in embodied intelligence have demonstrated the potential of learning robot manipulation policies from human videos [1, 2, 3, 4]. However, directly transferring
human demonstrations to robots remains challenging due to the gap between human motion and
robot embodiments, as well as the discrepancy between visual observations and physical execution [5, 6, 7].

Reinforcement learning (RL) provides a powerful mechanism to bridge this gap by optimizing interaction
behaviors under physical constraints in simulation. Under this paradigm,
human demonstrations can be transformed into physically feasible robot manipulation
policies. However, acquiring a robust and generalizable skill from a single human demonstration remains challenging. Existing RL approaches largely rely on hand motion as the primary supervision signal, learning residual actions to refine the reference motion [5, 8, 9, 10]. While this paradigm enables precise motion imitation, it relies heavily on accurately reconstructed hand–object trajectories, making performance sensitive to even minor misalignments and favoring kinematic reproduction over the acquisition of transferable skills. By contrast, object-centric policies [11, 12] prioritize desired object states, shifting the learning objective from replicating a demonstration to capturing what the task is meant to accomplish.
Nevertheless, their disproportionate emphasis on object-level task success often leads to unrealistic hand–object interactions, including physically implausible contacts and unnatural finger configurations.

In light of these challenges, we propose HandMimicX, a novel object-centric reinforcement learning framework for acquiring an underlying manipulation skill from a single egocentric human video. The “X” indicates moving beyond trajectory mimicry toward generalizable skill acquisition. To bridge egocentric human videos and dexterous control, we jointly reconstruct hand-object interactions (HOIs). However, camera motion degrades reconstruction accuracy, particularly in terms of hand–object alignment. We therefore refine the reconstructed hand translation using depth to improve spatial consistency. To transcend the trajectory constraints inherited from the human demonstration video, we condense the full-sequence reconstructions into object geometry and interaction priors to retain the most critical task-relevant elements. Using the reconstructed geometry, we train an RL policy to manipulate the object to arbitrary 6-DoF target poses, while the interaction prior regularizes the resulting hand–object interactions toward physically plausible configurations. For real-world deployment, we use DAgger [13] to distill the policy and reduce its reliance on privileged information. Ultimately, our framework transforms a single human demonstration video into a transferable dexterous skill that generalizes beyond the demonstrated spatial configuration. In summary, our contributions are as follows:

We propose HandMimicX, a novel object-centric RL framework that learns a generalizable dexterous manipulation skill from a single human video.

We build a joint 4D HOI reconstruction pipeline that recovers spatially consistent hand–object motion from dynamic egocentric views.

title: HIPC: Humanoid Iterative Planning and Control via Goal-Conditioned Motion Closure
authors: Yi Han,Xingyu Chen,Zixuan Lang,Qianyang Wu,Yuhang Lin,Ji Ma,Liang Li,Dongting Li,Xinpeng Liu,Ruoli Dai,Hesheng Wang,Renjing Xu,Lei Han
comment: Website:this https URL
abstract:
Recent generative models are widely used to provide whole-body motion for humanoid tracking. Current methods combine motion generators with controllers in an open-loop paradigm, which leads to critical issues: tracking errors can accumulate into spatial drift, and the planner cannot adapt to unexpected physical disturbances without feedback from physical execution.
However, directly feeding realized states back to the planner in a closed loop can cause discontinuities, resulting in physical jitter and even falls, since such states are out of distribution during training.
To bridge this gap, we propose HIPC, a real-time Humanoid Iterative Planning and Control framework that couples a generative model with motion tracking into a unified planning-and-control paradigm.
HIPC introduces a goal-conditioned motion planning trained with a canonical motion representation that avoids gimbal-lock singularities under extreme orientations and supports motion generation on diverse geometric and semantic conditions.
Then, HIPC adopts two strategies, deviation-decayed recovery and history re-anchoring, to mitigate the out-of-distribution shift caused by realized-state feedback.
Finally, HIPC operates a real-time asynchronous planning-and-control system, with latency compensation to reduce temporal mismatch for inference delay.
Extensive experiments confirm the effectiveness of HIPC under switching and composition of diverse conditions. Results show that HIPC achieves state-of-the-art goal-reaching accuracy among existing methods while simultaneously demonstrating robustness to physical perturbations and the ability to recover from falls.
introduction:
Recent general motion trackers (Luo et al., 2026; Zeng et al., 2026; RoboParty Lab Team, 2026) have made diverse whole-body behaviors executable through a single policy, providing a reusable control interface and shifting the challenge upstream from task-specific control to motion planning.
Early works like optimization-based planning (Kuindersma et al., 2016) is difficult to scale up due to high-dimensional whole-body coordination and complex contact constraints (Gu et al., 2026a), motivating generative planners that synthesize diverse references for general tracker (Xie et al., 2026).
Although the recent planner (Chen et al., 2026) provides explicit objectives that guide whole-body movements to goal, it still lacks diverse goal condition type and precise closed-loop execution.

Composing a generative planner with a whole-body tracker leaves the planning-to-control interface open-loop (Kaynov, 2008), Since physical execution inevitably deviates from kinematic references, creating a Tracking Gap.
Although the tracker locally corrects such deviations, the tracking errors remain invisible to the planner and can accumulate into spatial drift, motivating motion planning control paradigm to maintain spatial consistency.
Meanwhile, physical disturbances and imperfect state estimation may cause the robot state to deviate from the planned motion (Rotella et al., 2014), potentially exceeding the tracker’s recovery capability and requiring the planner to adapt motion generation through body-state feedback.
Both challenges call for incorporating realized physical states into generative motion planning.
Nevertheless, directly incorporating realized states causes an Execution Distribution Gap, as physical execution histories differ from the kinematic distribution during training.
Existing self-rollout strategies mitigate autoregressive distribution shift (Chen et al., 2026), but do not directly capture structured deviations induced by downstream dynamics.

Moreover, replanning from realized states that deviate from the current reference can create discontinuities between successive motion chunks. Non-negligible Inference Delay (Black et al., 2026; Black et al., 2025) further misaligns planning and execution as the robot continues to evolve during generation.
Together, these effects can produce abrupt reference transitions, physical jitter, and even loss of balance.
Closed-loop motion-data refinement can incorporate controller feedback during training (Chen et al., ), but couples motion synthesis to a specific downstream controller (Xu et al., 2026).
The key challenge is to close the planning-control loop while enabling smooth physical execution without sacrificing planner-controller modularity.

In this paper, we introduce HIPC, a real-time Humanoid Iterative Planning and Control framework that closes the loop between generative motion planning and whole-body tracking.
HIPC combines a more diverse goal-conditioned motion planner with execution-consistent state feedback and latency-aware asynchronous architecture.
It corrects accumulated spatial drift and supports recovery from physical disturbances while preserving planner-native motion histories.
It further anticipates the state reached during planner inference for smooth reference handoff.
This enables closed-loop whole-body planning without requiring controller-specific rollout data or sacrificing planner–controller modularity.

In summary, the primary contributions of this work are three-fold:

Goal-Conditioned Motion Planner with Canonical Representation.
We introduce a generative model in a goal reaching paradigm as motion planner, and train this generator with a canonical motion representation conditioned on diverse geometric goals and semantic text.

Goal-Conditioned Motion Planner with Canonical Representation.
We introduce a generative model in a goal reaching paradigm as motion planner, and train this generator with a canonical motion representation conditioned on diverse geometric goals and semantic text.

Execution-Consistent Motion Closure for Real State Feedback.
We propose a history re-anchoring strategy to incorporate realized robot states into the planning history while keeping it close to the planner’s training distribution.

Latency-Aware Asynchronous Planning and Control.
We decouple low-frequency generative planning from high-frequency whole-body tracking through a non-blocking asynchronous dual-system architecture, which maintains continuous real-time control and smooth reference handoff during close-loop replanning.

1. Goal-Conditioned Motion Planner with Canonical Representation.
We introduce a generative model in a goal reaching paradigm as motion planner, and train this generator with a canonical motion representation conditioned on diverse geometric goals and semantic text.

2. Execution-Consistent Motion Closure for Real State Feedback.
We propose a history re-anchoring strategy to incorporate realized robot states into the planning history while keeping it close to the planner’s training distribution.

3. Latency-Aware Asynchronous Planning and Control.
We decouple low-frequency generative planning from high-frequency whole-body tracking through a non-blocking asynchronous dual-system architecture, which maintains continuous real-time control and smooth reference handoff during close-loop replanning.

title: Cross-Embodiment Motion Planning by Coupling Body-Agnostic World Model with Differentiable Ego-Dynamics
authors: Zhidong Wang,Zirui Li,Haoran Xu,Yujie Yan,Zitong Shan,Jingsong Liang,Han Yu,Chen Lv
abstract:
Motion planning in clutter is embodiment-specific: the feasible
free space and reachable commands depend on each robot’s geometry and
dynamics. Existing cross-embodiment policies output
normalized commands that disregard these differences, or
compensate through per-robot training and distillation.
World models can in principle pool cross-embodiment data, yet
command-conditioned models bind their latent dynamics to a
single action space, while pose-conditioned models omit the
mapping from commands to body-specific motion.
On flat ground, however, embodiment affects the planner’s observations only through the camera ego-motion.
This letter proposes Hourglass, an hourglass-shaped architecture that
factorizes cross-embodiment motion planning at this interface: a
body-agnostic world model and each robot’s differentiable ego-dynamics,
which map commands to that ego-motion, are coupled only through it.
The world model is trained on data pooled across embodiments and
camera mounts; each robot’s ego-dynamics is a reduced-order template
with identified physical parameters.
A generalist parameter-conditioned policy is learned once at this junction:
each imagined step rolls out the template and then the world model,
and imagination training through each robot’s template makes the
policy body-aware.
On seven simulated robots of five locomotion types, the generalist policy
outperforms imitation-learning and diffusion-policy baselines on the
same world model by 3.8–10.6
percentage points in success rate and matches per-robot specialists
without dedicated training, while approaching its parameter-conditioned
MPPI teacher within 1.4–2.8 points without an online map.
After three minutes of teleoperated driving for identification,
the synthetic-data-trained model transfers zero-shot to a real
skid-steer robot unseen in training, navigating unseen indoor
scenes.
introduction:
Mobile robots vary widely in embodiment,
from wheeled bases and quadrupeds to humanoids and
wheeled-legged platforms, yet they share the core problem of
local motion planning: generating velocity commands that steer
the robot toward a nearby goal through cluttered environments
without collision. Training a separate learned planner for each
embodiment cannot scale, motivating recent cross-embodiment approaches
based on foundation
models [1, 2, 3],
embodiment-aware
policies [4, 5, 6], and world
models [7, 8]. Global planning produces a route that is largely
embodiment-agnostic, whereas local planning must respect each
robot’s geometry and dynamics: the geometry constrains which
gaps are passable, and the dynamics govern which commands can
be executed in time. A cross-embodiment local planner must
therefore account for these body-specific properties without
requiring a dedicated training stage or dataset for each robot.

Existing approaches handle these embodiment differences at
different levels, but each conflates the environment
representation with the embodiment in some form.
Shared-interface policies output normalized commands and
delegate execution to each robot’s low-level
controller [1, 9, 3], leaving
the planner blind to the robot’s dynamics.
Embodiment-aware policies restore dynamics awareness through
per-robot training, whether by distilling
specialists [4, 5] or by attaching residual
modules trained with reinforcement
learning [5, 6], so each new robot
needs its own training stage.
World models move the problem into the
representation: command-conditioned models need
command-labelled data and retraining for each
robot [7, 5], while pose-conditioned models
pool data but drop the mapping from commands to
motion [8, 10].
All three lines of work entangle the environment with the
embodiment, yet on flat ground the embodiment affects observations
only through the camera ego-motion.

Building on this observation, this letter proposes Hourglass,
an hourglass-shaped architecture (Fig. 1) that
factorizes cross-embodiment motion planning at the camera ego-motion: a
body-agnostic world model and the differentiable ego-dynamics of each
robot, which map commands to this ego-motion, are coupled only through
it. A parameter-conditioned policy is learned at this junction
(Fig. 2). The main contributions are:

Body-agnostic world model. Conditioned only on
ego-motion and camera parameters, the world model is body-agnostic,
pooling data across embodiments and camera mounts, and is nearly
unaffected when a robot’s own data are held out, provided its camera
mount is covered.

Cross-embodiment policy through differentiable
ego-dynamics. At each imagined step, coupled imagination rolls out each robot’s
template and then the world model, training a generalist policy
by analytic gradients and making it body-aware without per-robot
specialists or dedicated training.

Cross-embodiment evaluation and zero-shot transfer.
On seven simulated robots of five locomotion types, the generalist
policy outperforms imitation-learning and diffusion-policy baselines
on average and matches per-robot specialists; after three minutes of teleoperated
driving for identification, the synthetic-data-trained model transfers
zero-shot to an unseen real skid-steer robot.

1. Body-agnostic world model. Conditioned only on
ego-motion and camera parameters, the world model is body-agnostic,
pooling data across embodiments and camera mounts, and is nearly
unaffected when a robot’s own data are held out, provided its camera
mount is covered.

2. Cross-embodiment policy through differentiable
ego-dynamics. At each imagined step, coupled imagination rolls out each robot’s
template and then the world model, training a generalist policy
by analytic gradients and making it body-aware without per-robot
specialists or dedicated training.

3. Cross-embodiment evaluation and zero-shot transfer.
On seven simulated robots of five locomotion types, the generalist
policy outperforms imitation-learning and diffusion-policy baselines
on average and matches per-robot specialists; after three minutes of teleoperated
driving for identification, the synthetic-data-trained model transfers
zero-shot to an unseen real skid-steer robot.

title: Learning from Physical Experience:Context-Space Adaptation for Robotic Manipulation
authors: Yihan Zeng,Yisu Li,Kaixin Huang,Marc WuDunn,Amelia Kovacs,Mikael Harseno,Kimmy Lin,Porter Hunley,Fred Shentu,Philipp Wu,Zhongyu Li,Zike Yan
abstract: Recent multimodal foundation models exhibit strong perception, reasoning, and in-context learning capabilities, but translating these capabilities into physical action remains challenging. Through real-world experiments across diverse manipulation tasks, we find that ChatGPT-6-Astra, a state-of-the-art general-purpose reasoner, can serve as a physically actionable, context-responsive manipulation policy, demonstrating effective fine manipulation and spatial reasoning. Building on these findings, we introduce LEXP, a harness for learning from physical experience through context-space adaptation. LEXP combines task-level planning with an experience module that interprets execution evidence, extracts and retains lessons with applicability conditions, and reuses relevant lessons to generate contextual feedback for subsequent actions. Model weights and the action interface remain fixed throughout. Across 12 real-world manipulation tasks, LEXP achieves 23/3623/36 successful trials (63.9%), compared with 19/3619/36 (52.8%) with memory alone and 2/362/36 (5.6%) for vanilla Astra. On three tasks, bread transfer, sort trash and toiletries, and retrieve drawer, removing planning reduces success from 7/97/9 to 4/94/9, while removing retained experience reduces it to 3/93/9. Execution traces illustrate feedback-guided corrections and cross-episode reuse of an inspection strategy. Execution analyses illustrate how task structure and experience-derived feedback guide task progression, action correction, and experience reuse. These results support context-space adaptation as a practical mechanism for turning physical interaction into reusable guidance for robotic manipulation.
introduction:
A long-standing goal of robotic manipulation is to perform diverse tasks reliably in unfamiliar and changing physical environments. This requires robots to adapt when familiar strategies fail and
reuse what they learn from physical interaction. The challenge is to turn limited physical experience into reliable, transferable improvements in behavior. Existing approaches pursue this goal through different adaptation mechanisms. Vision–language–action (VLA) models learn from robot demonstrations through supervised fine-tuning [11, 22]. World action models [29]aim to reduce task-specific adaptation by jointly predicting video and actions, enabling zero-shot execution of unseen tasks and environments on pretrained embodiments, while related video-model policies [10] instead use demonstration-based fine-tuning and rollout-informed planning . Real-world reinforcement learning improves policy parameters through repeated physical interaction [21], but requires reward specification and infrastructure
for physical trials and resets [21, 17, 18]. These requirements make demonstrations, reward engineering and physical trial infrastructure central to the cost of adaptation. General-purpose multimodal reasoners offer a complementary interface: observations, instructions and execution feedback can condition executable tool calls without updating model weights. Their relevance to robotics depends on whether this contextual flexibility supports effective action revision and reusable improvements under a limited physical interaction budget.

We investigate this possibility through real-world experiments with GPT-6 Astra [20], across 12 robotic manipulation tasks covering fine manipulation, spatial reasoning, long-horizon execution, tool use, bimanual coordination, and force control. Across these tasks, we vary access to interaction history, and examine recovery demonstrations and online language guidance. Two complementary findings emerge. First, Astra shows promising fine-manipulation and spatial reasoning capabilities when given access to interaction history: interaction history inform subsequent corrections and help the robot reason about object relations and pose. Second, its behavior is steerable through context. Visual demonstrations and textual corrections support revisions to grasp checking, object repositioning, motion direction, arm selection, and action order. These benefits vary across tasks, but together highlight both Astra’s executable competence and its capacity for context steering—two prerequisites for improving manipulation through experience-derived context rather than additional parameter training.

Building on these observations,we introduce LEXP, a harness for learning from physical experience through context-space adaptation (Figure 1). A context compiler combines task instructions, current observations, interaction history, and agent-generated experience feedback to condition executable actions. A planner decomposes the task into subtasks, tracks progress, and proposes a method for the current subtask. The experience module evaluates this method against recent actions, measured execution outcomes, and current observations, drawing on retained lessons to generate feedback for the actor’s next decision. It also extracts and updates structured lessons from physical interaction, recording their applicability, supporting evidence, and limitations for subsequent reuse. This separates interaction history, which preserves past exchanges, from reusable experience, which retains findings beyond the history window and across attempts. The models remain frozen and the action interface stays fixed; adaptation occurs through changes to the context guiding execution. The design builds on reflective context optimization [1, 3] and prior physical adaptation systems [16, 28, 6, 34].

Across 12 real-world manipulation tasks, LEXP achieves 23/3623/36 successful trials, compared with 19/3619/36 with memory alone and 2/362/36 for vanilla Astra. Ablations and execution analyses further examine how task-level planning and retained experience
support task progression and subsequent action decisions.

Our contributions are threefold:

A real-world evaluation suite spanning 12 manipulation tasks to investigate executable capabilities, adaptation through interaction history, and context steering in a general-purpose multimodal reasoner. Across three fine-manipulation tasks, memory increases Astra’s success rate from 0/90/9 to 8/98/9.

LEXP, a harness that combines task-level planning with the extraction and reuse of physical experience to guide robotic manipulation through context-space adaptation. Across 12 tasks, LEXP achieves 23/3623/36 successful trials, compared with 19/3619/36 with memory alone and 2/362/36 for vanilla Astra.

Component ablations and execution analyses examining the roles of planning and retained experience. Across three tasks, bread transfer, sort trash and toiletries, and retrieve drawer, complete LEXP achieves 7/97/9 successful trials, compared with 4/94/9 without planning and 3/93/9 without retained experience.

title: TRACE: Target-State Risk-Aligned Conditional Execution for Embodied Tracking
authors: Mingyang Lyu,Gongce Cao,Yiyang Jia,Lu Jia,Erliang Lin,Yuhao Zhang,Yinqian Sun,Pin Lyu,Feifei Zhao,Bo Wang
comment: including appendices
abstract:
Embodied visual tracking requires a robot to follow a language-specified person under
occlusion, look-alike distractors, and ambiguous instructions. We show that improving
tracking persistence can simultaneously increase safety violations. Using a compact
0.60.6B vision-language-action (VLA) tracker with a frozen backbone, we update only the
planner head with proximal policy optimization (PPO). PPO improves success and following
rates across all three EVT-Bench settings, but increases the collision rate on
distracted tracking because episodes that previously ended in target loss can instead
end in contact. We introduce TRACE, an execution-time target-state risk gate that
preserves the learned policy and intervenes selectively. A lightweight risk head
processes 8484 cues, including candidate boxes, identity margins, a learned
range-and-bearing probe, and the policy’s commands. When the calibrated risk exceeds a
threshold, TRACE rescales the translational component of the next waypoint while
leaving yaw unchanged. The executed action is identical to PPO’s on more than 98%98\% of
steps. In paired evaluations on identical episodes, TRACE reduces the
distracted-tracking collision rate by 3.963.96 percentage points, while further improving
success and following rates. Matched slowdown controls without target-state timing do
not reproduce this improvement. Concurrent evaluation reproduces a collision reduction
of 3.773.77 points, compared with 0.290.29 points for identical-arm null pairs, indicating
that the effect exceeds evaluation variability. These results show that
target-state-aware execution can recover the safety cost of policy post-training with
minimal intervention.
introduction:
Embodied visual tracking (EVT) requires an agent to continuously follow a
language-specified person from egocentric observations over long
horizons (Luo et al., 2018; Zhong et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2025). The task requires the joint
solution of target identification, temporal association, and motion planning under
occlusion, look-alike distractors, and ambiguous instructions. Recent
vision-language-action (VLA) models integrate visual perception, language
understanding, and robot control (Brohan et al., 2023a; Brohan et al., 2023b; Kim et al., 2024; Black et al., 2024).
The strongest reported results on EVT-Bench come from a 77B-scale model trained on large-scale data (Wang et al., 2025), whereas deployment favors compact models with limited adaptation cost and low execution overhead.

We construct a compact three-stage tracking system based on a frozen Qwen3-0.6B
backbone. The supervised base model keeps the vision encoder, language backbone, and
recognition adapter fixed, while a planner head predicts eight future waypoints. We then apply PPO (Schulman et al., 2017; Schulman et al., 2015) only to the planner head, which improves success and following rates across all three EVT-Bench settings: the planner head is an effective control point for tracking persistence, and the representation backbone need not be updated. The improvement carries a safety cost in distracted tracking. Relative to the supervised model, PPO reduces early target loss but increases collisions, changing the terminal outcome of some episodes from target loss to physical contact (Figure 1A).

This observation exposes a limitation of optimizing persistence with a scalar task
reward. Existing safe-control and recovery
methods (Achiam et al., 2017; Ray et al., 2019; Johannink et al., 2019; Thananjeyan et al., 2021; Ames et al., 2019; Dalal et al., 2018)
typically impose geometric constraints or respond to local collision conditions. They
do not explicitly model the target-state uncertainty that precedes collisions during
distracted tracking. In our experiments, a distance-only execution filter does not
recover the safety degradation introduced by PPO (§4.4). These
results motivate an execution-time mechanism that uses the tracker’s target-state
estimate to intervene selectively while preserving the persistence learned by PPO.

We therefore introduce TRACE, a target-state risk gate applied after policy
prediction (Figure 1B). A lightweight head receives 8484 target-related cues, including candidate
bounding boxes, identity margins, a learned range-and-bearing probe, and the policy’s
commands and predicted waypoints. The head produces a collision-risk score. Once the
score exceeds a calibrated threshold, TRACE rescales the translational component of
the next waypoint while preserving its yaw component. At all other steps, the executed
action is identical to the PPO action. The gate reduces the distracted-tracking
collision rate (CR) from 13.7813.78 to 9.839.83, below the supervised baseline, while further improving success and following rates (SR, FR).

A compact VLA tracking stack with an empirical analysis of post-training
safety costs. We develop a 0.60.6B frozen-backbone VLA tracker and restrict PPO
post-training to its planner head. This design improves success and following rates
on all three EVT-Bench settings but raises the distracted-tracking collision rate from
11.0111.01 to 13.7813.78, establishing a measurable trade-off between persistence and
collision safety under planner-only post-training.

TRACE: selective target-state risk gating for safe execution. We
introduce an execution-time gate that predicts collision risk from target-state cues
and modifies only the translational component of the next waypoint when the risk
exceeds a calibrated threshold. On distracted tracking, TRACE reduces the collision
rate by 3.963.96 percentage points while increasing the success rate by 2.032.03 points and
the following rate by 2.142.14 points, at approximately 50​μ50\,\mus per step and fewer than
2%2\% of executed actions changed. Matched slowdown controls without target-state timing
remain at the PPO reference, and the effect persists across two scene corpora, three
collision geometries, held-out episodes, and a later code version.

Concurrent evaluation for separating intervention effects from benchmark
variability. Re-evaluating an unchanged policy shifts collision rate by up to 1.41.4
points and success rate by up to 2.72.7, so we evaluate the gated and ungated policies
concurrently together with identical-arm null pairs. Under this protocol, TRACE produces a collision-rate
change of −3.77-3.77 points, compared with −0.29-0.29 points for identical-arm pairs,
providing a paired estimate of the intervention effect relative to evaluator
variability.

title: CONSORT: Uncertainty-Constrained Multi-Robot Planning for Cooperative Localization in GPS-Denied Environments
authors: Tony Zhang,Ryan Bartholomew,Kalliyan Velasco,Joshua Mangelson,Brady Moon
abstract:
Centralized multi-agent path planning with cooperative localization in GPS-denied environments is generally computationally
intractable when formulated in full belief space due to tightly coupled uncertainty dynamics. Prior work typically approximates belief dynamics
or restricts inter-agent coupling. This work examines a multi-agent planning problem in which a primary agent must reach a goal in minimum time
subject to a chance-constrained collision-avoidance requirement and a terminal bound on localization uncertainty. We obtain a tractable surrogate
of the underlying belief-space problem by optimizing over the mean-state trajectories of all agents and propagating covariance for terminal constraint evaluation only.
We propose CONSORT (Cooperative Navigation with Support-Optimized Routing and Trajectories), a discrete-to-continuous pipeline combining hexagonal-grid joint search with spline-based trajectory refinement.
Across 50 randomized scenarios, the planners separate as the terminal uncertainty bound tightens, with CONSORT solving 80% of scenarios where the strongest baseline solves 54%, at comparable path length.
In marine simulations, with the plans executed under feedback control on an independently developed factor-graph estimate, the trajectories remain collision-free and their terminal uncertainty falls within 6% of the planner’s prediction.
introduction:
In environments where GPS signal is unreliable, such as underwater, or in regions subject to spoofing or jamming, agents must rely on other forms of information
for localization. In these environments, autonomous agents struggle with state uncertainty due to inertial measurement unit (IMU)
drift. As the estimation error accumulates, an agent’s pose uncertainty can grow to a point where waypoint tracking degrades and mission objectives are compromised.
Common planning strategies ameliorate this by biasing trajectories toward information-rich regions [1] and introducing agents to utilize inter-agent measurements for
cooperative localization [2, 3]. Consequently, trajectory planning must account for uncertainty propagation when estimation error impedes task performance.

As the joint belief of a team grows exponentially with its size and inter-agent measurements couple the agents’ beliefs, we optimize mean trajectories and propagate uncertainty only to evaluate constraints.

In this work, we consider a centralized multi-agent path planning with cooperative localization (MAPP-CL) problem, a variant of the CL-MRMP problem [4], in which a primary agent must reach a goal in minimum time while subject to a chance-constrained collision-avoidance
requirement and a terminal bound on localization uncertainty. We call this the escort problem: the support agents have no goal locations and are routed solely to hold the primary’s terminal uncertainty under the constraint (Fig. 1).

We propose CONSORT (Cooperative Navigation with Support-Optimized Routing and Trajectories), a centralized planner for this escort problem.11
1
            
            
            
          The Julia implementation, 50 benchmark scenarios, and simulation videos are available on the project page frostlab.byu.edu/consort-planner/.
We contribute the following:

A MAPP-CL formulation that jointly routes support and primary agents under a terminal uncertainty bound and chance-constrained obstacle avoidance.

CONSORT, a planner pairing joint heading-aware hexagonal lattice search with B-spline refinement, both enforcing curvature, collision, and uncertainty constraints.

A benchmark of 50 randomized scenarios on which CONSORT solves 80% at the 50% constraint level, against 54% for the strongest of four baselines.

Monte Carlo validation in HoloOcean [5] with an independent factor-graph estimator where plans stay collision-free and terminal uncertainty is within 6% of prediction.

title: TinyAstral: Transferring Self-Evolving Harnesses to Tiny Generalist Manipulation Agents
authors: Kehong Gong,Xiaoxu Zheng,Guanli Hou,Seunghun Lee,Mengqi Guo,Runjia Tan,Zhengyu Wen,Qi Wang,Xiaoyu He,Mingyuan Zhang,Michael Bi Mi
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
comment: . Project page:this https URL
abstract:
Robot agents built on vision–language models depend on both the planner and its harness: the tools, feedback, memory, and recovery logic around it. Can improvements to a large teacher’s harness be carried into a compact agent with lower inference compute cost?
We present TinyAstral, a two-stage approach. We first freeze an open-weight teacher and improve its harness through recursive self-improvement (RSI): frontier LLM agents read the teacher’s trajectories and propose harness edits, and each edit is accepted only if it passes a paired statistical test. We then freeze the final harness, collect teacher trajectories with reasoning and failure recovery, and distill a small student that replaces the teacher in the same harness.
On RoboTwin, harness evolution raises the teacher’s success from 33.4% to 63.6%; the final 4B student reaches 62.8%.
Across four harness versions, distilled 4B students score close to their corresponding teachers, and later versions yield stronger students, showing that harness evolution gains carry into compact models. The harness gains also transfer to other frozen planners without retraining.
On identical episodes, the final 4B student outperforms open 4B agents, the open 27B harness-RSI model SenseNova-RoboRSI, and our own teacher model placed in three competitors’ harnesses.
It stays close to its teacher on all three training benchmarks, and on three benchmarks never used for RSI or training it scores close to a 552B planner running the same harness. On the measured deployment episodes, it uses about one fifth of its teacher’s accelerator time.
introduction:
Vision–language models (VLMs) can operate robot arms by reading images and calling perception and motion tools [25, 18, 11, 12].
The model chooses the object, action sequence, and stopping point; the surrounding harness grounds these choices, executes them, and reports what happened. Tool interfaces, feedback, task memory, and failure recovery therefore contribute to the agent’s performance alongside the model itself [57, 40, 46, 10].

Two lines of work offer complementary ways to build these agents. Harness evolution improves the system around a frozen planner [40, 46, 10]; agent distillation trains compact models from a stronger agent’s trajectories [27, 24, 56].
We connect these approaches by asking: can we first improve a large teacher’s harness, then transfer the resulting decision-making capability to a small model?
This would allow the improved system to run with substantially less inference compute.

We present TinyAstral, a family of 0.8B–4B manipulation agents built in two stages (Fig. 2).
First, we freeze the weights of an open-weight teacher, Qwen3.8-Flash-Next [34], and improve its harness through a master-guided recursive self-improvement (RSI) loop. Humans specify the rules and budget in advance. Frontier LLM agents then inspect failures and propose harness edits, which the system automatically accepts or rejects according to pre-registered paired statistical tests.
Second, we freeze the final harness and collect teacher trajectories containing reasoning, tool calls, and recovery from injected failures. Together with auxiliary offline real-robot supervision, these trajectories train a compact student to interpret feedback, choose actions, recover from failure, and decide when to finish. At deployment, the student replaces the teacher in the same frozen harness.

We evaluate both stages and the connection between them. Harness evolution raises the frozen teacher’s RoboTwin success from 33.4% to 63.6%, and distillation produces a 4B student at 62.8%.
To test whether this connection holds beyond the final endpoint, we distill students at four harness versions. The four students score 36.2%, 49.8%, 60.0%, and 62.8%, each close to its corresponding teacher.
The same evolved harness also improves DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash and the untrained 4B initialization, showing that its gains are reusable across planners. On identical episodes the student outperforms every open competitor we ran, including our own teacher model inside three competitors’ harnesses (93.6% vs. 78.9% on Guava; 78.3% vs. 57.3% and 53.0% on LIBERO-PRO), and on unseen benchmarks the small 4B student scores close to a 552B planner in the same harness.

Our contributions are:

Harness evolution followed by distillation. A two-stage approach first improves a frozen teacher’s manipulation harness, then trains a compact planner from that teacher’s reasoning and recovery trajectories for deployment in the same harness.

Evidence that evolution gains transfer. The harness improves other frozen planners, and distilled students at four harness versions track the performance of their corresponding teachers, showing that system improvements carry into compact models.

Compact agents with lower inference compute cost. A single TinyAstral-4B model covers six benchmarks: on identical episodes it outperforms every open competitor we ran, including our own teacher model inside three competitors’ harnesses, scores close to its teacher on the three training benchmarks and close to a 552B planner on unseen ones, and uses about one fifth of the teacher’s accelerator time per episode in our deployment measurement.

2. Evidence that evolution gains transfer. The harness improves other frozen planners, and distilled students at four harness versions track the performance of their corresponding teachers, showing that system improvements carry into compact models.

3. Compact agents with lower inference compute cost. title: Capability-Conditioned Graph Control Barrier Functions for Zero-Shot Safe Navigation of Heterogeneous Mobile Robot Teams
authors: Joonkyung Kim,Janghyun Cho,Jeehyun Lee,Changjoo Nam,Yiwei Lyu
abstract:
Multi-robot systems are increasingly deployed as heterogeneous fleets
with diverse kinematic and actuation capabilities. While graph control
barrier function (GCBF) methods provide a scalable framework for
decentralized safe control, existing approaches typically assume
homogeneous robot dynamics. Methods that directly encode robot classes
can distinguish known types, but do not represent state-dependent motion
capabilities or naturally transfer to unseen robot models.
To address this challenge, we propose the
Capability-Conditioned Heterogeneous Graph Control Barrier
Function (CC-HGCBF), defined in a shared second-order reference-point
operational space. This formulation provides a common geometric
representation of safety across heterogeneous robots while retaining
their model-specific dynamics and admissible control constraints.
To enable zero-shot transfer, we introduce the Radial Capability Field
(RCF), a compact, fixed-dimensional representation of each robot’s
state-dependent finite-horizon reachable velocity set. Conditioning the
shared graph barrier and decentralized policy on the RCF enables them to
adapt to changes in robot state, kinematic constraints, and control
limits without relying on predefined robot identities.
We jointly train the barrier and policy using proactive safety labeling
and neural CBF-QP supervision, and evaluate them on mixed teams containing
both seen and unseen robot models. Experiments demonstrate scalable safe
coordination and zero-shot transfer to robot models and capability
variations withheld during training. Physical-robot experiments further
demonstrate zero-shot deployment to unseen kinematic models without
retraining.
introduction:
Multi-robot systems are increasingly expected to operate as evolving
fleets rather than fixed groups of identical platforms [1]. Robots may be replaced, new platforms introduced after deployment, and
a single mission may involve robots with different mobility and
actuation capabilities. This heterogeneity is particularly important
for safety-critical navigation. Robots with different kinematic
structures can respond very differently to the same interaction: an
omnidirectional robot may move laterally to avoid a collision, whereas
a car-like robot is constrained by its heading and steering
angle [2, 3].
Even at identical positions and velocities, their
avoidance capabilities may differ due to dynamics, control limits, and
current operating states. Safe coordination therefore requires
controllers that can operate across heterogeneous platforms and remain
effective when previously unseen robots join the team [4, 5].

Graph control barrier functions (GCBFs) [6, 7]
provide scalable decentralized safety by learning graph-structured barriers
and policies from local observations. However, existing GCBF formulations
typically assume common robot dynamics. Their graph representations capture
neighboring states and relative motion, but do not explicitly represent how
each neighbor’s dynamics constrain its future motion. Recent heterogeneous
GCBF methods address differences in state and action spaces through
zero-padding for feature alignment and robot-type embeddings for model
identification [8]. While such representations can
distinguish robot types observed during training, they do not describe the
motion capability available at the current state or naturally represent an
unseen model [4]. The central challenge
therefore remains: How can a single distributed graph barrier reason about
heterogeneous robot motion capabilities and transfer to unseen robot
models without retraining?

To answer this question, we propose a Capability-Conditioned
Heterogeneous GCBF (CC-HGCBF) framework for safe learning, where a
shared graph barrier and decentralized policy are conditioned on
robot-specific motion capabilities.
This enables a single learned controller to coordinate mixed teams and
transfer to previously unseen supported models without retraining. Specifically, (1) we propose CC-HGCBF,
a novel heterogeneous GCBF formulation in a shared
operational space, and establish its safety condition for mixed robot
teams. This formulation provides a common representation of relative motion and safety
while preserving model-specific responses and control constraints; (2) We introduce a state-dependent capability representation,
the Radial Capability Field (RCF), which encodes each robot’s
finite-horizon reachable velocity set in a fixed-dimensional form.
Conditioning the shared barrier and policy on the RCF enables zero-shot
transfer to unseen supported models without predefined model identities
or retraining; and (3) We evaluate the scalability and zero-shot generalization of
CC-HGCBF across increasing team sizes and obstacle densities, including
robot models and capability parameters withheld during training.
Comparisons with capability-agnostic, type-conditioned, and
static-capability baselines highlight the benefit of state-dependent
capability conditioning, while physical-robot experiments validate its
zero-shot deployment.

title: A Capability-Aware Backup-Recoverability Filter for Heterogeneous Multi-Robot Navigation
authors: Joonkyung Kim,Yanze Zhang,Wenhao Luo,Yiwei Lyu
abstract:
Safe navigation in heterogeneous multi-robot teams faces two coupled
challenges: differences in robots’ braking and turning capabilities
limit how each robot can respond to an approaching neighbor, while
simultaneous interactions require a single control action to satisfy
multiple collision-avoidance constraints.
Together, these challenges can make local safety constraints
incompatible with a robot’s admissible controls, leaving a
decentralized safety controller without a feasible action.
We propose a Capability-Aware Backup-Recoverability Filter (CA-BRF),
based on the insight that navigation actions should preserve access to
a certified recovery maneuver.
First, we construct a backup-recoverable set in a shared Cartesian
operational space by evaluating whether prescribed backup maneuvers
maintain pairwise safety until the robots come to rest.
Each maneuver respects the corresponding robot’s kinematic and actuation constraints, making the recovery certificate capability-dependent. Second, CA-BRF filters candidate controls by selecting admissible
interpolations between candidate and backup actions while coordinating
the selection across simultaneous interactions.
This preserves backup recoverability while retaining as much of the
candidate action as possible and ensures that all pairwise recovery
conditions are satisfied by a single executable control for each robot.
Together, we establish recursive feasibility and safety for the discrete-time closed-loop system even when the nominal safety-constrained optimization becomes infeasible. The validity and effectiveness of the proposed CA-BRF are validated in simulations with up to 30 heterogeneous robots and experiments of robots with five different kinematic classes.
introduction:
Heterogeneous robot teams combine complementary capabilities for
applications such as logistics [2],
exploration [3], and inspection [4].
Safe navigation in shared workspaces faces two coupled challenges:
kinematic and actuation constraints restrict each robot’s available
responses [5, 6], while simultaneous
encounters require compatible actions across several collision-avoidance
constraints. For example, braking may help a car-like robot avoid a
robot ahead, but its resulting loss of turning authority can limit its
response to another robot crossing its path [7];
a differential-drive robot has different options because it can rotate
in place. Safe coordination must therefore account for both each
robot’s state-dependent physical capability and the compatibility of
actions selected across its interactions.

Control barrier functions (CBFs) provide a principled approach to
safety enforcement by restricting desired controls to actions that
preserve a specified safe set [8].
Higher-order CBFs (HOCBFs) extend this approach to requirements whose
dependence on control appears through higher derivatives, as when
acceleration regulates the separation between robots [9].
Using robot-specific dynamics and admissible control sets, these
formulations can express safety requirements for systems with different
kinematic and actuation constraints [10].
However, enforcing several pairwise barrier conditions requires a
common admissible control satisfying all of them.
Higher-order barrier inequalities can conflict with actuator limits [11], and local constraints constructed for separate encounters can be individually feasible yet jointly incompatible
 [12, 13].
Consequently, the feasibility of each pairwise condition does not
establish the feasibility of their combined safety controller.

Existing methods address this issue by adapting barrier parameters or
decay rates [14, 15, 16],
relaxing or prioritizing selected constraints [17],
or allocating avoidance responsibility across agents
 [18, 19].
Such mechanisms can enlarge the feasible control region or reduce
unnecessary demands on a constrained robot, but they do not by
themselves ensure that the resulting requirements admit one compatible
control across simultaneous encounters.
Joint or distributed optimization can coordinate these requirements
explicitly [20], but a solution still requires a
feasible intersection of the imposed constraints and admissible
controls. In particular, a robot may receive individually achievable
obligations that require conflicting actions when combined [21].

An alternative is to certify a known safe continuation rather than
rely only on the instantaneous feasibility of barrier inequalities.
Backup-based methods identify states from which a prescribed controller
maintains safety and reaches an invariant terminal set
[22]; backup CBFs preserve this property through
control constraints [23]. This principle has been
extended to decentralized collision avoidance under limited actuation
[24].
For heterogeneous robots, however, the backup must remain admissible
under each robot’s kinematic and actuation constraints; a generic
maneuver may be incompatible with restricted steering or forward-only
motion [25]. Pairwise backup checks must also be
composed consistently across simultaneous encounters: certifying
different filtered actions for one robot does not certify the action it
executes. Predictive safety filters search more flexibly for safe
continuations [26], but their online
optimization scales with the prediction horizon and number of coupled
robots [27, 28].

This raises the central question of our work: how can robots continue navigating while ensuring that an admissible recovery maneuver remains available throughout their interactions?
A collision-free configuration may already be unsuitable for the prescribed backups if the robots are approaching too rapidly. The recovery condition must therefore account for motion along the backup trajectories rather than current separation alone.

To this end, we propose a Capability-Aware Backup-Recoverability Filter
(CA-BRF) that certifies model-specific backup maneuvers and consistently
filters desired controls to preserve their availability across
simultaneous interactions.
Our main contributions are:
1) Capability-dependent recovery certification.
We develop a recovery certificate that evaluates whether heterogeneous
robots can execute their prescribed backup maneuvers while maintaining
pairwise safety until reaching rest.
By incorporating model-specific braking and turning responses into a
shared operational-space formulation, the certificate identifies a
backup-recoverable set determined by the robots’ physical capabilities
and current motion;
2) Recoverability-preserving control selection.
We design a safety filter that checks admissible interpolations between
desired and backup controls and selects the largest verified candidate
fraction that retains the recovery certificate.
The full backup serves as an explicit fallback when the candidate HOCBF optimization does not return a feasible action;
3) Consistent multi-robot filtering with recursive feasibility
and safety guarantees.
We develop a component-wise selection mechanism that makes the
pairwise recovery certificates jointly valid under one executable
control per robot. Incorporating this consistency into the analysis, we establish
recursive feasibility of CA-BRF and safety for the discrete-time
multi-robot closed-loop system under the stated conditions.
