title: Mechanistic Interpretability for End-to-End Self-Driving
authors: Manav Gagvani,Benjamin Namikas,Sivamurugan Velmurugan,Nysa Kumar,Shrey Sharma,Thomas Peterson,Pratyush Mathur,Hyunseo Chang,Rohan Paleja
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Machine Learning (cs.LG)
comment: Accepted to the Conference on Robot Learning (CoRL) 2026. Project page:this https URL
abstract:
End-to-end (E2E) autonomous driving models achieve strong planning performance but remain largely opaque, limiting observability and trust. We apply mechanistic interpretability to E2E driving by training Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) on the internal activations of a simple, single-camera end-to-end path planning model. Unsupervised clustering of SAE latents reveals interpretable structure aligned with route intent, vehicle speed, and braking behavior, recovering route intent with 98.3% accuracy without supervision. Through paired counterfactual image edits, we further show that specific SAE features are visually grounded and systematically respond to scene changes such as traffic light state and stop sign presence. Steering individual SAE latents produces predictable, monotonic changes in planner outputs including lateral displacement, curvature, and braking. Finally, we demonstrate a practical application of these representations: we build a lightweight adapter trained on SAE latents that reduces trajectory selection error by 3.44%, outperforming an equivalent adapter that omits SAE latents, confirming that the sparse representation captures useful information for interpretability. Code and visualizations are available at
https://mgagvani.github.io/mechanistic-interpretability-for-e2e-driving/.
introduction:
Road safety remains one of the most urgent motivations for autonomous driving research. Each year, road traffic kills approximately 1.2 million people worldwide, making autonomous vehicles both a research and public health problem [40, 34]. Companies such as Wayve are deploying learned end-to-end (E2E) autonomy models on public streets [38, 25], but as E2E autonomous driving systems transition from simulation to deployment in the real world, post-deployment safety through observability and understanding of model behavior becomes increasingly important.

Over the past decade, the field of autonomous driving (AD) has shifted from modular pipelines with handcrafted perception, planning, and control modules, to end-to-end models that directly learn from data to map raw sensor data and ego state into driving decisions [5, 29]. Despite advancements in the application of Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models for autonomous driving [31, 33, 9], the black-box nature of E2E models diminishes trust and restricts practical applications due to limited safety bounds and understanding of model behavior in diverse or out-of-distribution scenarios. To address this shortcoming, some E2E methods produce intermediate outputs such as bird’s-eye-view occupancy or motion prediction [14, 39], providing clues as to a model’s understanding of a scene but little insight within the exact inner workings of the network.

To better understand E2E models, we leverage techniques from mechanistic interpretability [12, 19]. Specifically, we apply Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs), an unsupervised learning technique that disentangles polysemantic representations by projecting them into a sparse latent space. This technique has been used to find highly interpretable features in LLMs [8] and visuomotor VLA policies [35, 17]. To our knowledge, we are the first to apply these techniques to E2E driving policies.

Our contributions are as follows:

An elegant, high-performance end-to-end planning module using trajectory scoring, without any intermediate labeled representations or large language modeling backbones, that achieves competitive open-loop planning performance on the Waymo Open Dataset’s E2E driving benchmark [42].

An elegant, high-performance end-to-end planning module using trajectory scoring, without any intermediate labeled representations or large language modeling backbones, that achieves competitive open-loop planning performance on the Waymo Open Dataset’s E2E driving benchmark [42].

We show that trained SAE features organize into interpretable clusters aligned with route intent and kinematic behavior, and that these features respond systematically to counterfactual visual changes in driving scenes.

We show that SAE latents are useful representations for model steering and improvement. Latent steering produces structured changes in planner behavior consistent with clustering and image edit analyses, and using SAE latents as inputs to an adapter subnetwork improves model performance over the original dense query activation.

title: Veloxity: Towards Memory-Safe UAV Embedded Firmware using the Rust Programming Language
authors: Derek Ward,Brian Bascom,Tyler Larsen,James Usevitch,Phil Tokumaru,Tim McLain
abstract: Recent years have witnessed increased momentum towards memory-safe programming languages for safety-critical systems. Memory-safe languages can eliminate entire classes of common software errors that have historically required extensive analysis and expenditure to avoid. Nevertheless, memory-safe language adoption in aerospace remains fragmented and incomplete, particularly for unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs). Recent Rust UAV projects either run only in simulation, are closed source, or have not been integrated with an established autonomy ecosystem and tested against existing C/C++ firmware. To address this gap, we present Veloxity: an open-source embedded UAV autopilot written in the memory-safe Rust programming language. Veloxity lowers the barrier to using memory-safe languages within modern ecosystems by providing a minimal, modular foundation for autonomous UAVs. We compare Veloxity to equivalent autopilots written in C++ in simulation, with hardware testbenches, and via outdoor waypoint-following flight tests, demonstrating functional parity with improved performance. These results indicate that modern memory-safe languages are a viable option for reliable and performant firmware for autonomous aerospace systems.
introduction:
Advances in autonomy research have expanded the safety assurances of unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs), but the low-level software on which safe flight ultimately depends is still largely written in unsafe languages.
In small UAVs, timing-sensitive sensor processing, estimation, control, mixing, and actuator output remain on an embedded flight controller, making the robustness of the embedded firmware paramount. Defects in the firmware (particularly those related to program memory use) can result in loss of vehicle and damage to livelihood.
Most open-source flight-control firmware is implemented in C or C++ [9, 10], languages that provide limited compile-time protection against memory errors and unsynchronized shared-state access.
Memory-safety violations such as out-of-bounds accesses, use-after-free errors, and data races can corrupt program state or terminate execution.
Because their effects may emerge far from the original defect and depend on a particular execution timing, these faults can be difficult to reproduce (and thus difficult to diagnose).
In flight firmware, the resulting corruption or loss of execution can affect sensing, state estimation, control, or actuator output while the vehicle is airborne.
Preventing such faults largely relies on development practices including coding standards, review, static analysis, and testing.

High-assurance languages and toolsets such as Ada and SPARK offer stronger verification, but obtaining that assurance can impose substantial development tradeoffs.
It can require developers to define proof obligations, work within language restrictions, and maintain specialized verification expertise.
These costs have not prevented the use of Ada and SPARK in high-assurance aerospace software or targeted flight-control demonstrations.
For example, Adamant provides a model-based, platform-agnostic Ada framework for embedded spacecraft flight software, including multitasking and support for SPARK proofs [6]. The Crazyflie’s stock firmware is written in C [4], but a separate demonstration rewrote the vehicle’s stabilization subsystem in SPARK, proved it free of runtime errors, and flew it with the remaining C drivers and FreeRTOS infrastructure unchanged [11].
However, the proof effort, specialized expertise, and comparatively small development ecosystem associated with Ada and SPARK can impede widespread adoption in hobbyist and open-source UAV communities, where rapid iteration and integration with existing software are priorities.
This leaves room for approaches that balance compile-time protection with rapid development and compatibility with established research ecosystems.

Rust [12] is a modern programming language built to enforce memory access constraints through ownership rules and its type system, while retaining much of the familiar syntax of C/C++. In Rust, memory management can largely be checked and verified at compile time, but maintains execution speeds similar to C/C++ that are required for low-level control and resource-constrained embedded software.
These protections do not depend on a garbage collector, and Rust’s no_std environment supports systems without a conventional operating-system runtime.
Rust is also favorable for AI-assisted development due to the detailed compiler diagnostics capabilities that code-generation systems can use to perform iterative development and checking.
Perhaps the most compelling motivation Rust provides is the evidence from large companies that these safety benefits do not come with penalties in productivity or development.
For instance, in a survey of more than 1,000 Google developers who contributed Rust code (many of whom came from C++), Google found no evidence of lower productivity in Rust relative to the languages those developers had previously used; more than half reported becoming as productive in Rust within four months [13].
Despite the advantages, evidence remains limited for Rust in embedded flight firmware or for its evaluation within an established autonomy ecosystem.

Rust has only recently begun to appear in UAV software. Peng [5] is a Rust quadrotor framework for simulation, trajectory planning, and control, but does not run on flight hardware. Fusion Reflex [3] is a commercial flight controller whose Linux-hosted software is written in Rust, but it is not open source. Most recently, Cybflight [7] runs a modular Rust autopilot for calculating state estimation and nonlinear control directly on an STM32H743 flight controller. None of these, however, operate within an existing ROS 2 [14] autonomy ecosystem or present a comparison against an established C or C++ firmware. To our knowledge, no published literature has compared the use of Rust to more common alternatives in embedded UAV firmware. To overcome this shortcoming, we present the following contributions:

An open-source11

title: Contact Imitation Interface: Transferring Dexterous Skills by Showing How Contact Unfolds
authors: Zhixuan Xu,Yichen Li,Bingchen Wu,Rui Wang,Yiwen Hou,Zixuan Liu,Tianyu Qiu,Lin Shao
comment: (8-page main paper and 7-page supplementary material). Project website with code and hardware designs:this https URL
abstract:
Robot-free human demonstrations offer a promising route to scaling dexterous
manipulation data. The key challenge is to preserve the demonstrator’s natural
dexterity while producing contact-grounded observations and actions that
transfer to robot hands. We present Contact Imitation Interface (CIMI),
a framework with contact-grounded demonstration and learning interfaces.
The demonstration interface combines shared contact geometry and fingertip RGB
views with contact-alignment-first retargeting and reprojection of wider scene
views. The learning interface introduces a hierarchical policy in which a
contact-surface planner predicts relative contact-surface trajectories and a
controller coordinates wrist and finger commands to improve contact alignment.
CIMI combines contact-grounded observations, retargeting, and action
representations, improving mean final-stage success
by at least 50 percentage points over baseline policies across six hand–task
pairs on LEAP and Wuji.
Hardware designs and software are publicly available.
introduction:
Low-cost teleoperation and portable hand-held grippers have enabled scalable
demonstration collection for parallel-jaw manipulation
[1, 10]. A human can fully control a
gripper’s low-dimensional action space through its pose and opening, using
either the robot itself or a portable gripper to demonstrate manipulation.
Extending this approach to dexterous hands is especially challenging for
contact-sensitive tasks: differences in human and robot kinematics and
contact-surface geometry make it difficult to reproduce the demonstrated
sequence of contacts with the object.
This calls for a demonstration interface that preserves natural human dexterity
while capturing contact-grounded observations and motion that transfer to robot
hands.

Existing approaches anchor demonstrations in either the human or robot embodiment.
Human-centric interfaces prioritize natural manipulation with minimal
constraint. Video and motion capture recover human hand motion
[3, 4, 5, 6], while
instrumented gloves and wearable devices can additionally capture contact
geometry or tactile interaction
[7, 8, 9, 10].
The recorded hand motion and sensory observations remain tied to the human
embodiment: retargeting may not
preserve the demonstrated contact evolution, and recorded observations may
differ from those available during robot execution. Robot-centric interfaces
instead establish compatibility through the collection hardware. Teleoperation
records robot-native observations and actions
[1, 11, 12], while exoskeletons and
linkages mechanically map human motion to robot configurations
[11, 14, 15]. This compatibility often requires
robot-specific hardware or operator expertise and can restrict demonstration
motion. The resulting trade-off is between demonstrator freedom and robot-side
fidelity (Table I).

To address this trade-off, we introduce the Contact Imitation Interface (CIMI),
which combines contact-grounded demonstration and learning interfaces:

1) We design a contact-grounded demonstration interface.
Human and robot hands use fingertip modules with matching contact-surface
geometry and camera placement. Each module includes an RGB camera, termed a
contact camera, that captures local fingertip–object interactions.
Cameras mounted at the wrist and thumb–index web space (context cameras)
provide wider scene views for manipulation.
Transferring demonstrations requires aligning contact motion and
visual observations between human and robot hands. However, differences in
hand kinematics can prevent simultaneous alignment of contact surfaces and
context-camera poses. We therefore propose contact-alignment-first retargeting
and context-view reprojection. By jointly optimizing wrist and finger motion,
retargeting prioritizes reproducing the demonstrated contact; we retain the
contact-camera images and reproject context views to the robot
viewpoints.

2) We develop a contact-grounded learning interface.
Policies commonly predict relative wrist motion and finger-joint commands
[11]. In contact-sensitive tasks with high-degree-of-freedom hands,
we observe that this representation can lead to poor wrist–finger coordination
and contact misalignment. We propose a hierarchical policy where a
contact-surface planner predicts relative contact-surface trajectories from visual
and proprioceptive inputs. A contact-surface controller converts these trajectories
into coordinated wrist and finger commands.

By centering both demonstration and learning on contact surfaces, CIMI enables
contact-sensitive dexterous skills to be learned from natural human
demonstrations and reproduced across different robot hands. Experiments on LEAP
and Wuji cover contact-sensitive tasks including grasping a 1 cm cube, wedging
and lifting a flat coin, retrieving a letter, and screwing in a bulb. Across six
hand–task pairs, CIMI improves mean success by at least 50 percentage points
over baseline policies.
Videos are available at
https://nus-lins-lab.github.io/CIMIWeb/.

title: STAR: Steering Action Representations during Inference
authors: Guangyu Zhao,Yongchang Zhang,Haoxuan Ru,Kaichen He,Haoran Wen,Kun Zhan,Zeyu Zhang,Yin Li,Yiwu Zhong
abstract:
Vision-language-action models (VLAs) map language instructions and visual observations to robot actions, showing strong capabilities across robotic manipulation tasks.
However, in our probing experiment, we find that action representations near the action output do not fully preserve task-relevant visual grounding.
Motivated by this late-layer grounding gap, we introduce STAR, for STeering Action Representations, a training-free inference method for pre-trained VLAs.
STAR applies an exponential moving average over late-layer residual updates, allowing later action representations to inherit object-aware update directions from earlier layers without model updates or architectural changes.
It further uses recent proprioceptive states to adapt the mixing strength, using conservative mixing when execution dynamics change rapidly.
Experiments on robot manipulation benchmarks show that STAR improves late-layer object awareness and increases average task success rates by 4.0 percentage points.
Our code is available at https://github.com/PKU-VaLuE-Lab/STAR.
introduction:
Despite the tremendous success of vision-language models (VLMs) [27, 7, 16, 26, 2, 1],
previous work has shown that they may overly rely on language priors, producing responses that are not fully grounded in the visual input [25, 19, 15, 10, 51].
Meanwhile, recent studies also observe that vision-language-action models (VLAs) exhibit similar behavior patterns, such as insufficient use of task-relevant visual cues [45, 36, 48, 54, 21] or distraction from irrelevant visual tokens [20, 44, 58, 22].
Inspired by these works, we ask a key question: how strongly are action representations in VLAs grounded in task-relevant visual evidence?

To probe the dependence of action representations on visual evidence, we design a controlled experiment.
As illustrated in Figure 1 (a), we mask the target object pixels by replacing them with the mean RGB values of the image.
By masking the visual information important for action execution, we expect the action representations to differ from those produced without interference.
To measure the representation change induced by object masking, we define an object awareness score, computed as ‖hmk−hok‖/‖hok‖\|h^{k}_{\mathrm{m}}-h^{k}_{\mathrm{o}}\|\ /\ \|h^{k}_{\mathrm{o}}\|. Here, hkh^{k} is the hidden state of the kk-th layer in Figure 1(b), while o\mathrm{o} and m\mathrm{m} denote the original and masked observations, respectively.
This metric provides a heuristic estimate of how strongly task-relevant visual evidence affects the action representation.
A larger score indicates a larger difference in the representation after masking.
The resulting object-awareness score for π0.5\pi_{0.5} [39] is reported in Figure 1 (c).
We find that, during native inference, object awareness increases through early-to-middle layers and drops in late layers.
This suggests that visual evidence is gradually aggregated into action representations from early to middle layers, but fades away in late layers.
This probing experiment demonstrates a grounding gap in late layers during VLA inference.

To address the gap, we introduce STAR, for STeering Action Representations, a training-free method that regularizes the action representations in late layers without updating model weights.
Intuitively, STAR steers late-layer action representations by carrying residual updates from earlier layers to later layers.
Specifically, STAR applies an exponential moving average (EMA) [14] over late-layer updates.
When action semantics change rapidly, such as during end-effector rotation or fine-grained adjustment, the intervention should be conservative.
Conversely, when the robot does not rotate, such as when moving in a straight line, the intervention can be stronger.
These differences in execution dynamics are reflected in recent proprioceptive trajectories.
In short, STAR uses a proprioception-modulated EMA to smooth cross-layer residual updates, carrying object-aware directions from earlier layers.

This design is validated through our object awareness measurement and robotic manipulation benchmarks. In the test of object awareness, as shown in Figure 1 (c), STAR increases the object awareness of late-layer action representations.
In robotic manipulation benchmarks, STAR enhances the performance of π0.5\pi_{0.5} [39] and GR00T-N1.5 [33] in LIBERO-PRO, as shown in Figure 1 (d), and yields an average success-rate improvement of 4.0 percentage points in our main experiments.

Our contributions are summarized as follows:

•  We introduce STAR, a training-free VLA inference method that regularizes action representations toward better visual grounding.

•  Our technical innovation is an EMA that combines residual updates across late layers, together with a modulation strategy that adjusts its coefficient using proprioceptive states.

•  Extensive experiments validate that STAR can consistently improve pre-trained VLA models across benchmarks, with an average success-rate improvement of 4.0 percentage points.

title: Confidence-Modulated Safety Filtering for End-to-End Policies
authors: Javier Borquez,Jaime F. Fisac
abstract:
End-to-end policies, from task-specific controllers to robot foundation models, learn complex
behavior from raw observations but are not guaranteed to remain safe, so they are often wrapped
in a safety filter.
The resulting system operates under two domains: the filter’s operational design domain (ODD),
where its assumptions hold and safety is certified, and the policy’s competence domain, where it
is reliable.
Filters typically fix their conservativeness regardless of the policy’s competence, trading
performance inside the ODD against margin beyond it.
We ask whether the policy’s confidence should set that level, and propose a filter-agnostic
pipeline that modulates it at runtime: inside the ODD, where every setting is safe, confidence
buys performance; beyond it, low confidence adds margin, which helps when it flags where the
filter’s model fails.
Preliminary F1TENTH simulations, where this holds, show the modulated filter combining the
strengths of permissive and conservative filters.
introduction:
End-to-end policies that map observations directly to actions have become a practical route to
capable autonomous decision-making, from task-specific
controllers [1, 2, 3] to generalist robot
foundation models [4, 5, 6].
Trained on enough data, they often perform well and, much of the time, act safely.
But not always: their competence is tied to the domain of the inputs they were trained on, and away
from it their behavior is unspecified.
A racing policy that drives a familiar track flawlessly may steer into a wall once the lighting
changes or the tires lose grip [7, 8].
Worse, such failures arrive without warning: the policy issues an action exactly as it always does,
and nothing in its action signals that it has left the regime in which its behavior was
learned [9, 10].
A standard remedy for safety-critical deployment is to wrap the policy in a safety filter
that monitors its proposed actions and overrides them when they threaten to drive the system into
failure [11, 12, 13].

A safety filter, however, is only as good as the assumptions behind it.
Its certificate rests on a model of the world, such as the system dynamics, a map of free space, a
bound on disturbances, and holds only within the operational design domain (ODD) where those
assumptions are met.
Inside the ODD, the filter keeps the system safe regardless of the policy it guards; beyond it, the
filter keeps acting, but nothing is guaranteed [11, 14].
The learned policy has its own competence domain, the conditions under which its training
makes its behavior reliable.
The two domains do not need to coincide, yet standard safety-filtered pipelines treat the policy as an
arbitrary black box and ignore whether it is operating within its competence
domain [15, 16].

Blind to the policy’s competence, standard filters commit to a single level of conservativeness, set
by design parameters such as a barrier decay rate or a safety-value
threshold [17, 18].
Inside the ODD every setting is safe, but a conservative filter overrides a competent policy early
and often, eroding its performance, while a permissive one lets an unreliable policy reach the
boundary of the safe set, where abrupt fallback interventions are
costly [19, 20].
Beyond the ODD, losing the certificate does not make failure inevitable: the filter becomes an
imperfect one, and its conservativeness sets a margin that may or may not translate into safety.
On a race track, a wide margin may save a car whose filter assumes dry asphalt once the track turns
wet, yet it also brakes the car on straights the policy has driven thousands of times.
Whatever value is chosen is fixed and spent uniformly, whether or not the policy has proven reliable
there.

A fixed conservativeness has been questioned before, with adaptation driven by
performance [21, 22, 23], by the filter’s own prediction
errors [24], or by the policy’s own uncertainty, which can tighten a CBF
filter [25, 26] or trigger a switch to a fallback when inputs look
novel [27].
Building on this line of work, we ask whether the task policy’s confidence should set a safety filter’s
conservativeness: a confidence monitor βtask\beta^{\text{task}} estimates how much the task policy can
be trusted on the current input and sets the filter’s conservativeness (Fig. 1).
When confidence is high, the policy is likely reliable and the filter steps back; when it is low, the
policy’s behavior is unpredictable and conservativeness costs little, provided that low confidence
signals risk.
Inside the ODD, safety is untouched, since every setting is certified, and modulation only buys
performance; beyond it, modulation adds margin where the policy is less trustworthy.
We give a filter-agnostic formulation, for any confidence measure and any filter whose
conservativeness can be graded, and use the two domains to make explicit what modulation buys
inside and beyond the ODD, and under which conditions.

title: FlapSim: A Composable MuJoCo Simulation Platform and Reduced-Order Aerodynamic Model Hierarchy for Flapping-Wing Robotics
authors: Mingshan He
abstract: Flapping-wing simulation must reconcile high-frequency wingbeat aerodynamics with the slower dynamics relevant to flight control and reinforcement learning. We present FlapSim, a modular open-source MuJoCo simulation platform that combines robot descriptions, wing geometry, and composable aerodynamic models in a deterministic simulation pipeline. Across 4848 held-out scenarios spanning frequency, gimbal, wind, frequency-step, gust, and cross-robot flat-plate regimes, we compare five reduced-order configurations operating at 1​ms1\,\text{ms} with a 50​μ​s50\,\mu\text{s} quasi-steady blade-element reference. The built-in hover cycle-averaged baseline achieves a 67.51×67.51\times CPU speedup but only 0.65930.6593 mean wrench fidelity. Combining multirate 2121-substep clock synchronization, three-dimensional linear/quadratic inflow and gust coupling, analytical blade-element geometry scaling, and phase-locked 1​f​–​6​f1f\text{--}6f harmonics raises mean fidelity to 0.96460.9646 at a 65.19×65.19\times speedup in a five-block model. A streamlined four-block model without explicit step-transient lag states achieves 0.96620.9662 fidelity at a 67.98×67.98\times speedup. Controlled ablations show that stroke harmonics are particularly important during frequency transitions, improving held-out frequency-step fidelity by +0.3176+0.3176. Transfer-function analysis explains this effect: fixed-window cycle averaging retains harmonic contributions when the wingbeat frequency changes, so within-cycle reconstruction also improves the filtered wrench. Once phase alignment and harmonic synthesis are included, explicit transient lag states provide no additional benefit in this benchmark. These results characterize the accuracy–computation tradeoff of the aerodynamic hierarchy and identify timing, inflow, geometry, and harmonic representation as central considerations for reduced-order flapping-wing simulation.
introduction:
Flapping-wing micro air vehicles (FWMAVs) and bio-inspired aerial robots generate lift, thrust, and control moments through rapid, large-amplitude wing reciprocation coupled with passive or active feathering rotation [1, 2, 3, 4]. Unlike fixed-wing aircraft or rotary-wing quadrotors whose aerodynamic loads vary smoothly at the rigid-body attitude control rate, flapping wings operate in an unsteady low-to-moderate Reynolds number regime (R​e∈[102,104]Re\in[10^{2},10^{4}]) characterized by leading-edge vortex (LEV) attachment [5, 6], rotational circulation during stroke reversal [7, 8], wing–wake interaction [9, 10, 11], and aeroelastic pitch recoil [12, 13, 14]. While direct Navier–Stokes computational fluid dynamics (CFD) captures these three-dimensional vortex structures [15, 16], its computational cost of hours per wingbeat precludes closed-loop flight controller synthesis, system identification, or reinforcement learning.

Quasi-steady blade-element models—evaluating spanwise wing-section kinematics with empirical RoboFly translational and rotational force coefficient fits [9, 10, 7, 14]—provide a tractable middle ground whose accuracy depends on the kinematics and aerodynamic effects included [17, 16, 18]. However, because the wing’s instantaneous velocity, angle of attack, and pitching rate oscillate at 20​–​50​Hz20\text{--}50\,\text{Hz} (with higher harmonics up to 300​Hz300\,\text{Hz}), resolving blade-element loads alongside multibody dynamics motivates small integration steps; this study uses Δ​tref=50​μ​s\Delta t_{\text{ref}}=50\,\mu\text{s} (20​kHz20\,\text{kHz}) [19, 20]. At 50​μ​s50\,\mu\text{s}, simulating 1​s1\,\text{s} of flight requires 20,00020{,}000 multibody and aerodynamic evaluations, making simulation cost relevant to model-predictive control [21, 22] and large-scale policy optimization [23]. Conversely, rigid-body cycle-averaged models step at Δ​t=1​ms\Delta t=1\,\text{ms} (1​kHz1\,\text{kHz}) by replacing within-stroke blade-element integration with stroke-averaged thrust and moment maps, with model-dependent speed and accuracy tradeoffs; simple hover formulations can omit 3D ambient wind drag, unsteady gust transients, cross-robot planform scaling, and within-cycle harmonic forces [24, 25, 26, 27].

To investigate and bridge this fidelity-versus-compute gap systematically, we present FlapSim, a modular simulation platform for flapping-wing robotics built on MuJoCo 3.8 [28, 29]. FlapSim treats aerodynamic models, environmental wind/gust fields, wing kinematics, sensors, and controllers as composable plugins communicating over a deterministic signal bus. FlapSim provides a hierarchy of aerodynamic plugins ranging from a regression-tested 50​μ​s50\,\mu\text{s} per-step quasi-steady blade-element simulator down to a 1​ms1\,\text{ms} cycle-averaged rigid-body model equipped with automated virtual-wind-tunnel identification.

This paper makes two contributions:

Platform Architecture and Software Characterization: We document FlapSim’s software architecture, robot manifest and CAD/MJCF/URDF import pipeline, first-class wing planform integral engine, phase-ordered plugin execution loop, Gymnasium learning interfaces, and identification tooling, grounded in a deterministic codebase inventory (6969 Python modules, 9,1779{,}177 lines of code across 1313 subpackages, 1717 registered plugins, 117117 unit and regression tests).

Quantitative Characterization of the Reduced-Order Aerodynamic Hierarchy: Across 4848 held-out test scenarios spanning six operating regimes (frequency, gimbal, wind, frequency-step, gust, and parametric flat-plate robots), we benchmark five 1​ms1\,\text{ms} reduced-order aerodynamic configurations against the 50​μ​s50\,\mu\text{s} per-step blade-element reference. We demonstrate that combining multirate 2121-substep clock synchronization, 3D linear/quadratic wind and multi-rate gust coupling, analytical blade-element planform scaling, and 1​f​–​6​f1f\text{--}6f stroke-harmonic synthesis raises 4848-scenario mean wrench fidelity from 0.65930.6593 (built-in hover baseline) and 0.82800.8280 (first-principles wind-lag baseline) to 0.96460.9646 (65.19×65.19\times speedup) in a five-block surrogate and 0.96620.9662 (67.98×67.98\times speedup) in a streamlined four-block surrogate.
Through controlled ablations and transfer-function analysis, we explain why within-cycle 1​f​–​6​f1f\text{--}6f harmonics govern mid-flight frequency-step fidelity (+0.3176+0.3176 held-out step lift) and show no additional benefit from explicit step-transient lag states in this benchmark.

Figure  provides a visual overview of the platform. The central view connects the robot’s gimbaled mounting, stroke kinematics, passive feathering, and blade-element force application. The insets relate this physical model to the stroke trajectory, drivetrain, parametric robot construction, and illustrative free-flight and wind/gust configurations. These views place the aerodynamic hierarchy in its broader simulation context; the quantitative comparisons in this report use the fixed-base protocol described in the experimental section.

The source code is available at https://github.com/MingshanHe/FlapSim; the project website is https://mingshanhe.github.io/FlapSim/.

title: From Teleoperation to Long-Horizon Dexterity: Evaluating Visuomotor Skills and Offline Proxies for Dexterous Manipulation
authors: Ammar N. Abbas,Aayush Jain,Prashanth Viswanath,Nivesh Gadipudi,Giulia Vilone,Jim Gibbons
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Machine Learning (cs.LG); Systems and Control (eess.SY)
comment: Accepted at CoRL 2026 Workshop
abstract: Imitation learning policies are intended to make robotic manipulation robust to variations in object pose, appearance, and environment that challenge pre-programmed motion. However, real-world performance remains difficult to predict, as conventional optimization signals such as validation loss show no consistent relationship with robot success. To identify the design choices that govern real-world performance, 281 imitation-learning policies spanning seven policy families were evaluated in approximately 1,700 real-robot trials of RJ45 connector grasping and insertion using a five-fingered robotic hand. Controlled ablations showed that observation and action representations dominated conventional optimizer and sampling choices. For point-cloud policies, region-of-interest cropping, representation in the robot-base frame, and normalization within the point encoder each improved success by 70–100 percentage points. For the vision-language-action policy, absolute rather than relative action prediction improved insertion success by up to 70 percentage points. Skill decomposition, multi-view perception, and recovery demonstrations were associated with the strongest-performing systems, although their effects were not independently isolated. Of 67 offline metrics evaluated, only five measures of predicted-motion smoothness and directness reliably correlated with insertion success (r=−0.70r=-0.70 to −0.80-0.80), and only within a single policy family. These results identify representation choices as key determinants of real-world imitation-learning performance and show that offline metrics can shortlist policies, but cannot replace real-robot evaluation.
introduction:
Imitation learning offers a practical route to robotic manipulation that
generalises across the variations in object pose, appearance and environment
that defeat pre-programmed motion, learning a direct observation-to-action
mapping from demonstrations rather than hand-engineered
controllers [2, 20, 5]. Recent
visuomotor policies including diffusion and flow-based action generators, transformer
decoders, and large vision-language-action models, have driven rapid progress
on real single-arm tasks [5, 20, 4]. Yet
the paradigm inherits well-known liabilities: behavioral cloning accumulates
error under co-variate shift [13], and real-world success
remains hard to predict because conventional offline signals such as validation
loss correlate weakly, or not at all, with task
performance [11]. As a result, the design choices that
govern a policy, like observation and action representations, encoder pretraining,
sampling and optimization, are typically settled by expensive real-robot
trials, and systematic evidence to guide them is scarce, especially for the
dexterous, contact-rich skills demanded by multi-fingered
hands [6, 1].

We study these questions on a representative contact-rich task: inserting an
RJ45 cable connector, which demands millimetre precision on a deformable object
where small changes in cable pose or grasp break fixed trajectories and still
challenge end-to-end learned
policies [5, 19, 4]. We decompose the task
into four stages: two moves between known poses handled by classical motion,
and two learned contact-rich skills, grasp and insert
(Section 2). We ask how best to build those skills for a
five-fingered hand. We contribute (i) a real-robot ablation study that isolates
individual policy components (data augmentation, image-encoder pretraining,
action representation, point-cloud reference frame (camera or robot base),
cropping and normalization, prediction horizon, optimizer, denoising sampler and
policy family) and reports for every comparison all training settings that
changed between the two runs; and (ii) a leak-free test of whether offline
metrics can stand in for robot trials.

title: CaPtain: A Pipeline for Post-Training Code-as-Policy Robot Agents
authors: Yijia Fan,Xilin He,Yilei Jiang,Dongming Wu,Jiaxu Wang,Xiangyu Yue
abstract:
Across coding, web, and tool-use tasks, language-model agents are now routinely trained with the same recipe: supervised fine-tuning (SFT) to learn the interface, then multi-turn reinforcement learning (RL) to master it.
Code-as-policy (CaP) puts robot manipulation in the same form, as the policy writes code against robot APIs and reads back the results, so the same recipe should apply.
Yet, existing CaP agents sidestep training: they either prompt closed frontier models or delegate manipulation to pre-trained vision-language-action models (VLAs) and high-level skills, while small open vision-language models (VLMs) fail outright.
We present CaPtain, an open post-training pipeline that brings this recipe to CaP and turns a small open VLM into a capable CaP agent, with no VLA, frontier model, or privileged state at test time.
CaPtain trains and deploys the policy inside CaPtain-Harness, which exposes low-level perception, geometry, and guarded-motion primitives across simulation and real hardware.
Within this harness, we first align the base model via SFT on synthetic trajectories generated with GPT-6 Astra, and then apply multi-turn RL.
Multi-turn RL, however, must credit tens of requests from the agent, whose physical effects often surface several turns later, with a single outcome observed only at the end of the episode.
Since training runs in simulation, we introduce a physical critic that reads the privileged physical state in simulator, which the policy never sees, and credits each request by how much it changes the predicted chance of success.
Starting from Qwen3.5-4B (0% zero-shot), CaPtain-4B achieves 55.4% held-out LIBERO success after SFT and 73.8% after RL.
On LIBERO-PRO, it reaches 78.5%, surpassing several frontier-model agents, and its RL gains persist across three perturbation suites (+17.6 to +21.2 points).
Without target-domain training, it attains 83.3% on SimplerEnv WidowX, exceeds frontier models on CaP-Bench, and runs on a real robot after simulation-only adaptation.
We release all code, data, and model weights.
introduction:
Language-model agents have improved rapidly in coding, web navigation, and tool use, and much of this progress follows a common recipe: the agent acts inside a fixed execution harness, supervised fine-tuning (SFT) teaches it the interface, and multi-turn reinforcement learning (RL) refines its behavior from the outcomes of its own interactions [26, 72, 25, 19].
Code-as-policy (CaP) agents [43, 27, 58] give robot manipulation the same form: the policy observes camera images, writes programs against perception and motion APIs, and reads back what happened.
Since the program is composed at test time, a CaP agent inherits much of the generalization of the language model that writes it, and frontier models have made this approach strikingly capable. Used directly as a robot policy, GPT-6 Astra ranks above every public entry on the RoboDojo leaderboard [90], and with a coding harness it solves 94.0% of LIBERO-PRO episodes [67].
This raises a natural question: Can a small open model be trained into such a CaP agent with the same SFT-and-RL recipe, rather than relying on a frontier model at test time?

In practice, existing CaP agents sidestep training, and in doing so hand the manipulation itself to components the agent cannot learn to improve.
One line of work prompts closed frontier models without weight updates [13, 39, 93, 50, 40]. These systems come with high finical cost of calling frontier models in each episode [13, 39, 93], cannot be fine-tuned for new robots or tasks, and cannot run on onboard compute.
Another line delegates manipulation to pre-trained vision-language-action models (VLAs) or high-level skills. PyRUA trains a 4B coder over a frozen VLA and a motion planner [67], AgenticRoboRL trains a planner around a frozen LIBERO-trained VLA [48], SenseNova-RoboRSI builds a 27B agent around reusable skills and optional VLA calls [64], and Gemini 4 Argon exposes code-as-policies through skills such as grasp and place [22].
In these systems, the code decides which skill to call, but the skill decides how to grasp, approach, and place. Therefore, the agent stays bounded by the data on which the skill was trained, and RL can at best learn to sequence it.
Small open vision-language models (VLMs), meanwhile, fail outright when asked to control a robot directly. Qwen3.5-4B solves none of the LIBERO episodes in our harness, and the few efforts that train such models rely mainly on SFT [45] or single-turn text-only RL [20].
What is missing is a complete SFT-and-RL recipe that teaches a small open VLM to manipulate through low-level primitives, with every manipulation decision made by the policy itself.

Applying the recipe at this low level is harder than at the skill level, for a reason that does not arise for language agents.
Without semantic skills such as grasp and place, the policy must itself decide where to grasp, from which direction to approach, and when to close the gripper, and these decisions are spread over tens of requests per episode, most of which only perceive or verify.
Multi-turn RL must then credit these requests, whose physical effects often surface several turns later, with a single outcome observed only at the end of the episode.
Outcome-only RL assigns the same credit to every request, while a language-model critic would have to infer physical progress indirectly from text and images.
Robot learning, however, offers an asymmetry that language agents lack: training runs in simulation, where exact object poses, grasp states, and sub-goal progress are known, even though the deployed policy must act from its cameras alone.
A critic can thus read the physical state that the policy cannot see, and credit each request by how much it moves the task toward success, while the policy itself still acts from its cameras at test time.

We present CaPtain, an open post-training pipeline built on these two observations.
CaPtain trains and deploys the policy inside CaPtain-Harness, an execution environment that exposes 22 low-level perception, geometric measurement, and guarded-motion primitives and nothing higher. There are no grasp, place, or open-drawer skills and no VLA. Perception returns masks and points, and motion takes an explicit end-effector pose or gripper command.
Every call returns a structured text receipt reporting what physically happened, such as measured poses, contact forces, or why a motion stopped, and the policy-facing API is unchanged across LIBERO [44], RoboTwin 2.0 [11], RoboDojo [10], SimplerEnv [38], CaP-Bench [20], and a physical robot.
We first apply SFT on in-harness trajectories generated with GPT-6 Astra, rendered in exactly the multi-turn format the policy sees at deployment.
We then run multi-turn RL with a simulator critic that reads privileged physical state hidden from the policy and credits each request by how much it changes the predicted chance of success, combining the streaming RL formulation of SAO [25] with asymmetric actor-critic training [56].
Since this change is measured at a fixed time index, requests that only perceive or verify receive near-zero credit, and credit concentrates on grasps and placements.
The critic is used only during training. At test time, the policy relies on camera images and receipts alone.

Applying CaPtain to Qwen3.5-4B yields CaPtain-4B, which raises the held-out LIBERO success from 0% to 55.4% after SFT and to 73.8% after RL.
On LIBERO-PRO, CaPtain-4B reaches 78.5%, above frontier-model agents such as K1 [40] (77.2%), WAA [93] (75.6%), and ASPIRE [50] (71.7%).
RL also gains more when it acts on low-level primitives: across the four LIBERO-PRO suites it adds 19.4 points to our SFT model, whereas RL over a frozen VLA adds 5.9 points in AgenticRoboRL [48], although the two start from different baselines.
These gains persist under perturbation, ranging from +17.6 to +21.2 points across LIBERO-PRO [97], LIBERO-Plus [18], and LIBERO-MAX [95], with all seven LIBERO-Plus perturbation dimensions improving significantly; by contrast, reported results for end-to-end policies show π0.5\pi_{0.5} [55] falling from 97% on LIBERO to 12.8% on LIBERO-PRO [97] and the RL-tuned RIPT-VLA [68] scoring no higher than its base model on LIBERO-Plus [18].
Without target-domain training, CaPtain-4B reaches 83.3% on SimplerEnv WidowX, scores 75.0 on CaP-Bench, above frontier models and a 7B coder trained with RL on that benchmark, and completes tasks on a physical robot after adaptation in a coarse simulated twin alone.
Transfer remains limited on RoboTwin 2.0 and RoboDojo (22.6% and 0.8% success), which require dual-arm coordination and unfamiliar arm kinematics.
Together, these results suggest that robot manipulation over a low-level execution harness can be post-trained like any other language agent.

CaPtain, an open, end-to-end SFT-and-RL pipeline that turns a small open VLM into a standalone CaP agent. We release the SFT data, the training code and the CaPtain-4B weights.

CaPtain, an open, end-to-end SFT-and-RL pipeline that turns a small open VLM into a standalone CaP agent. We release the SFT data, the training code and the CaPtain-4B weights.

CaPtain-Harness, a portable execution harness with low-level primitives only, exposing 22 perception, measurement, and guarded-motion capabilities with grounded text receipts.

A simulator critic for multi-turn VLM agents that converts privileged physical state transitions into dense per-request credit, with analyses showing that credit concentrates on physical manipulation decisions.

A comprehensive evaluation showing that RL gains persist across three perturbation suites, that a 4B policy surpasses several frontier-model agents at a small fraction of their cost, and that it transfers zero-shot across benchmarks and embodiments and to a physical robot without real-world data.

title: WorldBridge: Bridging Video and Action for Task Generalization in World Action Models
authors: Jun Cen,Yubo Guo,Hao Li,Liangkai Li,Yaoxu Lyu,Meng Wei,Zeqi Xiao,Sizhe Yang,Yuqiang Yang,Yifan Ye,Shanghang Zhang,Duo Zheng
comment: Authors are listed in alphabetical order. Project page:this https URL
abstract:
Achieving the broad task generalization of embodied models in physical environments remains a central challenge in robot learning.
We study this challenge in World Action Models (WAMs) through two complementary capabilities: video generalization, which predicts the visual evolution of new tasks, and action generalization, which translates these predictions into executable behavior through a video-to-action bridge.
By varying video and action supervision for tasks outside an initial training set, we examine their respective contributions to task transfer.
On RoboTwin 2.0, using only in-distribution video-action supervision yields a 25.07% success rate on out-of-distribution tasks.
Introducing videos of these tasks without their action labels raises success to 55.90%, while adding just one action-labeled demonstration per task further improves it to 70.70%.
These findings suggest that broader video coverage enables task transfer by leveraging existing inverse-dynamics capabilities, while even sparse action supervision further strengthens those capabilities.
Guided by this perspective, we introduce WorldBridge, a WAM with separate video and action experts connected through structured attention and trained with joint flow matching.
WorldBridge incorporates visual memory at two temporal scales and action forcing, alongside a unified data processing pipeline that standardizes and filters heterogeneous robot trajectories and egocentric hand-derived supervision.
Across multiple manipulation benchmarks, WorldBridge achieves state-of-the-art performance among the compared methods, including 96.23% on RoboTwin 2.0 full data setting and 80.9% on clean to random setting, 82.8% on RoboCasa GR1 TableTop, and 57.6% on DOMINO Level-1.
Our study highlights the complementary roles of video prediction and action grounding in developing robots that generalize across tasks.

Project page: https://worldbridge-jd.github.io/
introduction:
Task generalization marks a fundamental shift from earlier pretrained NLP models, such as BERT [16], to modern large language models (LLMs) [6, 63, 15].
Whereas earlier models typically require task-specific fine-tuning, a single LLM can perform diverse tasks specified through natural-language instructions or a few in-context examples, without updating its parameters for each new task.
This capability has motivated the pursuit of generalist embodied agents that can translate human instructions into a broad repertoire of physical behaviors.
Vision-language-action (VLA) models represent an important step toward this goal, transferring knowledge from large-scale vision-language pretraining into robot control [5, 47].
However, understanding an instruction does not automatically provide the physical competence needed to execute it.
Bringing task generalization into robotics requires connecting semantic knowledge to the visual dynamics and motor behaviors of physical interaction.

Despite substantial progress, a prominent focus of embodied generalization research remains robustness to changes in the conditions under which a task is performed, including object arrangements, camera viewpoints, lighting, and visual appearance.
Benchmarks such as LIBERO-Plus systematically evaluate these variations, exposing the brittleness of otherwise successful policies [19].
Task generalization introduces an additional challenge: a robot must execute behaviors beyond those covered by its original training tasks.
Achieving this capability requires understanding how a newly requested task should unfold and producing the actions that realize it, even when corresponding robot demonstrations are scarce or unavailable.

World Action Models (WAMs) provide a promising foundation for addressing this challenge by coupling visual prediction with action generation.
Video offers dense supervision of physical interactions, allowing models to learn how scenes evolve beyond the coverage of action-labeled robot data.
DreamZero demonstrates that video priors can support unseen-task execution and transfer from video-only demonstrations [68], while Zero-WAM explores task generalization through in-context human video guidance [75].
Recent advances in native video-action pretraining [72], systematic WAM pretraining [58], and temporal context [24] further strengthen this paradigm.
These developments motivate a more specific question: how do broader video coverage and additional action supervision contribute to task generalization, and when does the connection between them become the limiting factor?

In this work, we investigate task generalization in WAMs through two complementary capabilities: video generalization and action generalization.
Video generalization enables a model to predict the visual evolution required by tasks beyond its initial training distribution.
Action generalization refers to the ability to translate those visual predictions into executable actions beyond the tasks that supplied action supervision.
This translation forms a video-to-action bridge, serving the role of an inverse dynamics model (IDM).
A model may predict an appropriate visual future yet lack the action grounding needed to realize it.
Conversely, a transferable bridge can allow knowledge acquired from additional videos to improve task execution without corresponding action labels, which motivates studying the availability of video and action supervision separately.

Figure 2 illustrates this progression, which we examine by varying supervision for tasks outside an initial in-distribution (ID) training set.
With only ID video-action pairs, the model achieves nontrivial but limited generalization, obtaining a 25.07% success rate on out-of-distribution (OOD) tasks.
Adding videos of those OOD tasks while keeping action supervision restricted to the ID set increases OOD success to 55.90%.
This improvement suggests that expanded video coverage can support new task execution through a bridge learned from ID action supervision.
Keeping the video set fixed, adding only one action-labeled demonstration per OOD task further raises success to 70.70%.
These rapid gains are consistent with sparse paired examples strengthening the bridge for visual transitions that are already covered by the video data.
Together, these observations support a complementary account of task generalization: video supervision expands the range of task evolutions a WAM can model, while action supervision improves its ability to turn that knowledge into reliable control.

Guided by this perspective, we introduce WorldBridge, a WAM that couples video prediction and action generation through a Mixture-of-Transformers (MoT) architecture [35].
WorldBridge maintains separate video and action experts trained with a joint flow-matching objective.
A structured attention mask establishes a directional information path from observed context to future video representations and then to action predictions, making predicted visual dynamics an explicit source of conditioning for control.
Short-term and long-term visual memories provide information about local motion and task progression.
We additionally employ action forcing, assigning independent noise levels to actions within a chunk during training so that the action expert learns to predict actions using temporal context at varying levels of corruption.

To support learning across heterogeneous sources, we develop a unified pretraining data pipeline for robot trajectories and egocentric human demonstrations.
The pipeline standardizes control semantics and maps available robot controls and human hand-derived targets into a shared 46-dimensional action representation.
Dimension-wise validity masks preserve partial supervision across embodiments with different control interfaces.
Robot trajectories undergo kinematic and temporal consistency checks, while egocentric hand trajectories are standardized in a common reference frame and filtered using geometric and motion constraints.
This processing supports broader visual coverage together with usable action supervision, providing a common interface for learning the video-to-action bridge across diverse data sources.

Our evaluations demonstrate strong performance across a range of manipulation tasks.
WorldBridge achieves state-of-the-art results among the compared methods on multiple benchmarks, with average success rates of 96.23% on RoboTwin 2.0, 80.9% in the RoboTwin 2.0 C2R setting, 82.8% on RoboCasa GR1 TableTop, and 57.6% on DOMINO Level-1.
On RMBench, it matches the best result in our comparison, with an 83.0% success rate.
We further conduct real-world evaluations on the Agibot-G2 and AC-1 platforms, covering long-horizon execution, memory-dependent tasks, spatial localization, and bimanual coordination.
Together with our task-generalization study, these results support the value of jointly developing video prediction and action grounding.

Our contributions are threefold:

We study task generalization in WAMs through the complementary roles of video generalization and action generalization, quantifying the gains from additional task videos and sparse action supervision.

We introduce WorldBridge and a unified data processing pipeline that connect visual dynamics to executable control across heterogeneous robot and egocentric demonstrations.

We evaluate WorldBridge across RoboTwin 2.0, RoboCasa GR1 TableTop, RMBench, DOMINO Level-1, SimplerEnv-WidowX, and RoboDojo, covering diverse manipulation demands and distribution shifts. We further deploy it on AgiBot G2 and ARX AC-1, fine-tuning the same jointly pretrained checkpoint for each platform and evaluating long-horizon execution, memory-dependent interaction, spatial alignment, and bimanual coordination.

1. We study task generalization in WAMs through the complementary roles of video generalization and action generalization, quantifying the gains from additional task videos and sparse action supervision.

2. We introduce WorldBridge and a unified data processing pipeline that connect visual dynamics to executable control across heterogeneous robot and egocentric demonstrations.

3. We evaluate WorldBridge across RoboTwin 2.0, RoboCasa GR1 TableTop, RMBench, DOMINO Level-1, SimplerEnv-WidowX, and RoboDojo, covering diverse manipulation demands and distribution shifts. We further deploy it on AgiBot G2 and ARX AC-1, fine-tuning the same jointly pretrained checkpoint for each platform and evaluating long-horizon execution, memory-dependent interaction, spatial alignment, and bimanual coordination.

title: CausalWAM: Learning the Causes of Actions in World Action Models
authors: Juntao Cheng,Jinzhou Tang,Fan Feng,Henrik I. Christensen,Yujia Zheng
abstract: World action models (WAMs) learn latent variables from observations and use these to both predict the evolution of the scene and to generate actions. The prediction has to be of the whole scene, whereas only a portion of the scene causes actions. WAMs fitted to demonstrations do not, in general, guarantee that they will generate actions solely from the latent causes of the demonstrated actions (the action-relevant latent variables), as the model could just as well learn to imitate in this way whilst entangling the action-relevant latent variables with the nuisance variables. We therefore separate out what causes action from what prediction depends on. We prove that under a sparsity constraint the latent variables used to generate actions are an invertible function of the action-relevant latent variables alone and the true structure is identified up to a permutation of the latent variables. This requires neither sufficient temporal dependence nor any assumptions on how the unobserved regimes evolve and holds even when the action-relevant latent variables are statistically dependent on the rest. We therefore propose CWAM (Causal WAM), which incorporates the constraint into a pretrained WAM by adding a sparse routing path to its action head, with the world modeling objective remaining unchanged. Experiments on both synthetic data and real-world robots validate the theory as well as showcase the improved efficiency in closed-loop success.
introduction:
The action a robot performs when stacking a single block atop another depends on the position of both blocks and the fact that the gripper is currently holding the uppermost block. The camera image’s pixels will change significantly if the robot removes the tablecloth or clears away the clutter located behind the table; however, this will have no effect upon the motion itself. WAMs (World Action Models) like Fast-WAM (Yuan et al., 2026), and Cosmos 3 (NVIDIA, 2026) are able to extract latent variables from images and can be used to generate actions from those latent variables, while also being capable of generating images of potential subsequent frames. Since prediction has to account for the whole scene, these latent variables also describe the tablecloth and the clutter. We refer to the latent variables that cause the demonstrated actions as action-relevant latent variables, and to the others as nuisance variables.

Fitting the demonstrations well does not in itself guarantee that the WAM is acting from the action-relevant latent variables. For each step of the demonstration we could write ot=f⁡(st)o_{t}=f(s_{t}) and at=π⁡(st,ηt)a_{t}=\pi(s_{t},\eta_{t}) where sts_{t} is the latent state, ff is some unknown invertible function, π\pi is some unknown action mechanism and ηt\eta_{t} is exogenous noise. Separating action from prediction is then about recovering (up to certain indeterminacies) the action-relevant latent variables and which of those variables cause each action dimension. Without further assumptions, the latent causal variables cannot be identified from their observations (Hyvärinen and Pajunen, 1999; Locatello et al., 2019). Observing the actions as well doesn’t help with this ambiguity, as two models can give rise to the same distribution of (ot,at)(o_{t},a_{t}) whilst their latent variables differ by an arbitrary invertible transformation. This transformation can mix the action-relevant latent variables with the nuisance ones, so a very flexible action head could generate actions from variables which also contain information about the tablecloth (which doesn’t in fact cause the motion) and still fit the demonstrations equally well.

To make latent variables identifiable, existing works in nonlinear independent component analysis (ICA) introduce auxiliary variables, such as domain or time indices, or exploit temporal dependence (Hyvärinen and Morioka, 2016; Hyvärinen and Morioka, 2017; Hyvärinen et al., 2019; Khemakhem et al., 2020). For latent causal processes, identifiability has been established under sufficient temporal dependence (Yao et al., 2022) and conditions on the latent dynamics (Song et al., 2023). Interventions with known targets have also been introduced to pin down the latents (Lippe et al., 2022). Many of these assumptions might be violated for demonstrations in complex real-world scenarios such as robotics, where some time steps might be independent, the latent dynamics might not be Markov, and controlled interventions are either prohibitively expensive or simply impossible.

Another line of research constrains the generative process by restricting the function class or enforcing sparsity in the dependency structure (Kivva et al., 2022; Zheng et al., 2022; Lachapelle et al., 2022). Most of these studies, similar to those previously discussed, aim to recover all latent variables, requiring their conditions to hold even for nuisance variables that a robot can disregard. In contrast, results on partial identifiability focus on a subset of latent variables, determined by side information accompanying the data, such as content shared across views (von Kügelgen et al., 2021; Yao et al., 2024), components invariant across domains (Kong et al., 2022), or elements relevant to specific tasks (Zheng et al., 2026). For robots learning from demonstrations, the relevant subset consists of the latent causes underlying the demonstrated actions. Since no view, domain, or task label directly specifies this subset, the actions themselves must indicate which latent variables are pertinent. This raises the following question:

Moreover, we prove that the estimated action-relevant variables under the proposed constraint are an invertible function of the ground-truth latent variables causing the true action (Thm. 2). The latent causes of the actions are thus identified as a block and are separated from the nuisance variables. The theoretical guarantee relies purely on observational demonstrations, without requiring any interventions, sufficient temporal dependence, or any assumptions about the latent dynamics. The framework also allows dependence between action-relevant latent variables and the nuisance variables (e.g., a tablecloth could be correlated with the positions of the cubes). According to the established theory, we propose CWAM (Causal WAM), which adds a sparse routing path from the visual and task tokens to the action head in Cosmos 3 and applies a token-level surrogate of the constraint to this path (Sec. 4). In synthetic scenarios, we validate the identifiability claims shown by our theory. On RoboCasa365, LIBERO, and a real Franka R3 robot, the routing path improves aggregate closed-loop success over Cosmos 3 without it, and in most visualized frames its routing mass falls on the object being moved and its target (Sec. 5).

title: Sensorium: An Open-Source Multimodal Data Collection and Curation Library for Embodied Surgical AI
authors: Lorenzo Mazza,Ariel Rodriguez,Stefanie Speidel
comment: GenAI for Health Workshop @ NeurIPS 2026, Sydney
abstract: Embodied surgical AI requires reliable multimodal data, yet surgical data collection remains costly, difficult to repeat, and strongly dependent on the hardware setup. We present Sensorium, an open-source Python library for recording, processing, annotating, and curating multimodal surgical data from configurable robot and sensor streams using the Robot Operating System (ROS) and ROS 2 middleware. The library combines operator-facing data acquisition, configurable processing, semantic annotation, and episodic dataset generation. We evaluate Sensorium across 1,516 recordings of phantom, ex vivo, and in vivo porcine experiments involving multiple surgical tasks and sensing configurations, and report preliminary usability feedback.
introduction:
Recent progress in embodied surgical AI has increasingly relied on multimodal recordings of surgical activity, including video, robot kinematics, and semantic annotations. This trend is reflected in the emergence of multimodal surgical datasets [5, 17], which facilitate a range of learning paradigms and applications, from behavioral cloning for surgical task automation [13, 12, 6, 16, 18, 2], to surgical vision-language models [20, 14, 9, 27, 8] and generative surgical world models [7, 23].

However, acquiring such multimodal data and annotations in surgical settings is particularly expensive [4]. Data collection protocols require clinical input, clinicians have limited availability, and in vivo experiments
require substantial preparation, coordination, and ethical approval.
Recording tools must therefore support reliable acquisition and
preserve data for reuse with different representations, sampling
rates, and annotation protocols. Scarcity and limited repeatability also make usability a central requirement of the recording process: operators need clear indications of sensor readiness and recording state, along with immediate episode review before the experimental setup changes. The infrastructure should also accommodate varying robot and sensor interfaces across laboratories. This diversity is evident when looking at platforms used for surgical robotics research, including da Vinci Research Kit (dVRK) [11], KUKA robotic platforms [22], Franka Emika Panda [10], and UR5/UR5e [21, 19], as well as in Open-H-Embodiment Dataset [17], which aggregates data from a large variety of commercial, research, and custom robotic platforms.

Recent open-source multimodal data acquisition systems address parts of these requirements. SurgSync [28] provides timestamp-aligned acquisition recording of robot kinematics, stereo endoscopic video, and additional sensing on the dVRK, together with tools for post-processing and annotation. Its acquisition stack and hardware integration are designed around the dVRK and its associated sensing setup. MiDAS [26] is a framework targeted for robotic platforms that do not expose robot telemetry: it employs external electromagnetic and RGB-D tracking, and foot-pedal sensing to approximate robot kinematics. This leaves a gap for a general-purpose framework that directly records heterogeneous robot and sensor data while supporting their processing and annotation for embodied surgical AI systems.

To address this gap, we present Sensorium, an open-source Python library for collecting, processing, annotating, and curating multimodal surgical data for embodied AI applications. Sensorium integrates custom sensor modalities through ROS and ROS 2, and provides both a command-line interface and a browser-based graphical interface (GUI) for local and remote operation. The library includes tools for timestamp-based temporal alignment and stereo rectification, together with annotation functionalities for surgical phases [24, 3] and language instructions for language-conditioned surgical robot learning [12, 6]. Additionally, Sensorium organizes recordings into reusable episodic datasets and supports both raw CSV-based representations and the widely adopted LeRobot format [1, 17], facilitating their use across different surgical AI pipelines, including policy learning, vision-based force estimation, and world model training. Sensorium has been deployed as the recording application of an open-source laparoscopic robotics testbed [19], where it was used to collect a dataset of surgical robot demonstrations for bowel grasping and retraction on phantom and ex vivo [16, 25]. It was also used to record two in vivo porcine datasets covering endoscope guidance, tissue grasping, and tissue retraction, which were subsequently included in [17].

In summary, our contributions are the following:

An open-source, flexible, configuration-driven library for collecting and curating multimodal recordings from heterogeneous ROS-integrated surgical sensors and robots.

An operator-oriented browser GUI that unifies recording supervision, episode review, surgical-phase and language annotation, and dataset generation.

A real-world validation of the library across phantom, ex vivo, and in vivo porcine data-collection settings, complemented by preliminary usability feedback.

1. An open-source, flexible, configuration-driven library for collecting and curating multimodal recordings from heterogeneous ROS-integrated surgical sensors and robots.

2. An operator-oriented browser GUI that unifies recording supervision, episode review, surgical-phase and language annotation, and dataset generation.

3. A real-world validation of the library across phantom, ex vivo, and in vivo porcine data-collection settings, complemented by preliminary usability feedback.

title: PGGT-Loc: Primitive-Grounded Geometry Transformer for Feed-Forward Camera Localization
authors: Hanqiao Ye,Yuzhou Liu,Mengqi Rong,Jian Liu,Yangdong Liu,Shuhan Shen
subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Robotics (cs.RO)
comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026. including appendices. Code and models:this https URL
abstract:
Camera localization methods are mostly multi-stage pipelines relying on dedicated and complex maps that are costly to construct, store, and maintain over time.
Alternatively, well-structured maps that organize scenes with compact yet expressive primitives are often readily available, providing rich structural and semantic cues that humans can interpret.
However, their potential for direct camera localization remains largely unexplored due to the significant modality gap between map primitives and visual observations.
This motivates a new concept for localization, which estimates camera poses by grounding query observations to map primitives.
In this paper, we instantiate the concept in the context of planar primitives with Pggt, the Primitive-Grounded Geometry Transformer network.
Given a single query image and a set of planar map primitives, the network is trained to predict multiple localization targets for feed-forward 6-DoF camera localization that generalizes to unseen environments.
With this straightforward and scalable architecture, our method pushes the state-of-the-art localization performance on both dense surface maps and minimal layout models.
The code and models are available at https://github.com/3dv-casia/PGGT-Loc.
introduction:
Camera localization, the task of estimating the orientation and position of a query image relative to a pre-existing map, stands as a fundamental problem in computer vision and robotics, with wide applications in augmented reality (AR) [95], robotic navigation [42], and multi-agent collaboration [29].

One popular family of approaches, known as structure-based localization,
typically establishes 2D-3D correspondences between the query image and the scene structure, either by matching local features [11, 62, 34, 48, 72, 66] or through direct scene coordinate regression [69, 9, 10, 77, 36].
With these explicitly established correspondences, the camera pose is then estimated by a robust geometric solver such as PnP-RANSAC [24, 23, 40].
Note that these approaches require a dedicated map triangulated or trained from a large database of mapping images before a new image can be localized.
While more general map representations have been explored for the task, e.g., meshes [57] and NeRF/3DGS [91, 54, 17, 33], these methods still depend heavily on photorealistic scene appearance and often require an initial pose estimate for keypoint matching or iterative pose refinement.

Well-structured maps are arrangements of high-level primitives and may further be enriched with relationships among them [3, 97, 4, 63, 88, 5, 49, 50].
Despite the significant modality gap between the map primitives and visual observations, which hinders the straightforward adaptation of the aforementioned localization paradigms, we argue that these map representations encode rich structural and even semantic information that remains underexploited for direct camera localization.

Among the many map primitives, planes are particularly essential in representing physical surfaces, owing to their notable compactness and prevalence in structured environments [83, 86, 2], which has motivated a recent work, named PlanaReLoc [90], to explore their use for camera localization.
As illustrated in Fig. 1a, the method introduces a plane-centric feature-matching pipeline that first establishes cross-modal correspondences between planes in the query and the map, and then estimates the pose via 2D–3D registration.
While the method demonstrates the potential of planar primitives for streamlined camera localization without map texture, pose priors, or per-scene training, it still relies on an off-the-shelf plane recovery module to generate reliable 2D plane proposals and geometric priors for primitive matching and pose estimation, which poses a major bottleneck in practice.

Meanwhile, the three-stage pipeline in PlanaReLoc cannot be directly applied to minimal layout models [19, 97], whose primitives are restricted to architectural entities that do not span all physical surfaces.
For localization on such minimalist maps, the render-and-compare  paradigm dominates existing methods.
As depicted in Fig. 1b, the state-of-the-art method SPVLoc [25] first renders the layout map into a set of semantic panoramas by exhaustively sampling viewpoints across the scene, and then regresses the relative pose between the best-retrieved panorama and the query image.
Although this paradigm neatly bridges the modality gap, reducing structure-based localization to matching 2D renderings inevitably discards structural information that could otherwise be exploited.

In this work, motivated by the goal of fully leveraging high-level map primitives for more straightforward camera localization,
we introduce primitive-grounded localization, a new concept that casts the task as the grounding of query observations in map primitives.
Driven by the concept and inspired by the DUSt3R [82] architecture, we propose Pggt, a feed-forward network whose name stands for Primitive-Grounded Geometry Transformer.
As shown in Fig. 1c, Pggt takes a single query image and a set of map primitives as inputs, and predicts the camera pose w.r.t. the map in a single forward pass, eliminating the need to solve for the pose from explicit primitive correspondences or match the query against exhaustive 2D renderings of the map.
We summarize our contributions as follows:

We introduce primitive-grounded localization, a new concept to localize cameras against well-structured maps through the grounding of query observations in map primitives.

The concept is concretized in the context of planar primitives by Pggt, a cross-modal transformer network designed to ingest the query image and map primitives as direct inputs, and predict a set of localization-specific targets for feed-forward camera localization.

Pggt provides a shared base architecture for localization tasks on both surface maps and layout models, surpassing prior works and demonstrating the potential of primitive-grounded localization as a promising paradigm for diverse primitive-based map representations.

1. We introduce primitive-grounded localization, a new concept to localize cameras against well-structured maps through the grounding of query observations in map primitives.

2. The concept is concretized in the context of planar primitives by Pggt, a cross-modal transformer network designed to ingest the query image and map primitives as direct inputs, and predict a set of localization-specific targets for feed-forward camera localization.

3. Pggt provides a shared base architecture for localization tasks on both surface maps and layout models, surpassing prior works and demonstrating the potential of primitive-grounded localization as a promising paradigm for diverse primitive-based map representations.
