title: DrawSplat: Atlanta World-Guided Implicit Gaussian SLAM for Indoor Reconstruction
authors: Fan Zhu,Zhisong Xu,Ziyu Chen,Zhenjun Zhao,Takayuki Okatani
subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Robotics (cs.RO)
abstract: RGB-D SLAM requires accurate online tracking, high-quality rendering, and geometrically consistent reconstruction. Existing Gaussian SLAM methods mainly optimize Gaussian primitives with photometric, depth, or local frame-to-model constraints, which are often insufficient in indoor scenes with weak textures, large planar structures, noisy depth, and long trajectories. The resulting maps may suffer from pose drift, surface thickness artifacts, noisy normals, and blurred structural boundaries. We propose DrawSplat, an Atlanta World-guided implicit Gaussian SLAM framework for indoor reconstruction. DrawSplat follows a drawing-like process: explicit point-line geometry first sketches the structural layout, and implicit neural Gaussians then fill in high-fidelity appearance and continuous geometric details. It estimates camera poses, sparse geometry, and gravity direction through point-line joint tracking, infers structural planes from tracked lines using the shared-gravity component of the Atlanta World prior, and converts them into differentiable regularization terms on Gaussian centers and normals. To improve compactness and efficiency, DrawSplat further combines an anchor-based implicit neural Gaussian representation with adaptive structural sampling, which allocates Gaussian capacity to structurally informative regions. Experiments on multiple datasets show that DrawSplat achieves robust tracking, high-fidelity rendering, and strong geometric reconstruction among Gaussian-based SLAM systems, while maintaining a practical balance among quality, efficiency, and model size.
introduction:
Visual simultaneous localization and mapping (SLAM) aims to estimate camera motion and reconstruct 3D scenes from online image streams [4, 5, 6]. Beyond accurate tracking, modern SLAM systems are expected to build photorealistic, geometrically accurate, and structurally consistent scene representations [7, 8, 9], supporting free-viewpoint rendering and reliable geometric reasoning for augmented reality, robotics, embodied scene understanding, and spatial intelligence [10, 11, 12, 13, 14].

Neural radiance field (NeRF) [15]-based SLAM improves dense reconstruction through continuous implicit representations [16, 17, 18, 19, 20], but its optimization and rendering costs remain high for online use [21]. In contrast, 3D Gaussian Splatting [22] and some variations [23, 24, 25] provide efficient differentiable rendering [26], motivating recent Gaussian SLAM systems for online mapping and novel-view synthesis [27, 28, 29, 30, 2, 31, 32].

Despite this progress, Gaussian SLAM still struggles to build geometrically reliable indoor maps under weak textures, large planar regions, occlusions, noisy depth, and long trajectories [31, 33]. In such cases, photometric, depth, or local frame-to-model constraints alone may be insufficient, while indoor scenes provide useful structural regularities such as vertical-horizontal consistency, wall-floor intersections, planar boundaries, and long-range layout coherence. Without such guidance, Gaussian maps may suffer from pose drift, surface thickness artifacts, noisy normals, blurred boundaries, or incomplete planar reconstruction in corridors, staircases, walls, and door frames [23, 1]. Existing structural or implicit-prior methods [31, 34] alleviate these issues, but often introduce additional overhead, structural redundancy, or difficulty in maintaining appearance-geometry consistency.

Our core idea is to make Gaussian SLAM follow a drawing-like process: explicit geometry first sketches the scene structure, and implicit Gaussians then recover appearance and local details. In indoor environments, point-line geometry provides a sparse but stable structural sketch, including geometric skeletons, gravity direction, and structural planes, to guide differentiable Gaussian optimization while keeping the map compact.

To realize this idea, we propose DrawSplat, an Atlanta World [35]-guided implicit Gaussian SLAM framework for indoor reconstruction. DrawSplat follows a hybrid Gaussian SLAM paradigm [36]: the point-line front-end estimates poses, refines sparse geometry, and infers gravity without relying on the evolving Gaussian appearance map, while the back-end incrementally builds and optimizes an Atlanta World-guided implicit Gaussian map. Tracked line structures and gravity further induce structural planes constrained by the shared-gravity Atlanta World prior to suppress depth noise and enhance structural regularity. Finally, adaptive structural sampling and a joint map optimization objective enable efficient, compact, and appearance-geometry-consistent map generation, as shown in Fig. 1.

We evaluate DrawSplat on multiple datasets. It achieves strong tracking accuracy and reconstruction quality among Gaussian-based SLAM systems while maintaining a practical quality-efficiency trade-off. Compared with the second-best baseline, DrawSplat reduces trajectory error by 60% on the multi-room Replica Apartment dataset and improves rendering quality by 2.54 dB on the real-world ScanNet dataset. The main contributions are:

We propose an Atlanta World-guided Gaussian SLAM framework that combines explicit geometric tracking with implicit neural Gaussian mapping for high-fidelity indoor reconstruction with appearance-geometry consistency.

We introduce an Atlanta World-guided structural regularization strategy that converts tracked lines, gravity cues, and inferred structural planes into differentiable constraints on Gaussian primitives.

We design an adaptive structural sampling strategy that reallocates Gaussian capacity to structurally informative regions, improving the balance between reconstruction quality and runtime efficiency.

1. We propose an Atlanta World-guided Gaussian SLAM framework that combines explicit geometric tracking with implicit neural Gaussian mapping for high-fidelity indoor reconstruction with appearance-geometry consistency.

2. We introduce an Atlanta World-guided structural regularization strategy that converts tracked lines, gravity cues, and inferred structural planes into differentiable constraints on Gaussian primitives.

3. We design an adaptive structural sampling strategy that reallocates Gaussian capacity to structurally informative regions, improving the balance between reconstruction quality and runtime efficiency.

title: FOCUS: First-Order Control Using Optimal Transport Supervision for Imitation from Observations
authors: João A. Cândido Ramos,Lionel Blondé,Hugues Vinzant,Jacopo Castellini,Alexandros Kalousis
comment: Accepted at the NeurIPS 2026 Workshop on Physical Understanding for Decision-Making
abstract:
Imitation learning from observations must recover behavior from state-only demonstrations without known temporal correspondence. Differentiable simulators provide pathwise policy gradients, but differentiating through long, contact-rich trajectories can make optimization unstable.
We introduce FOCUS, which combines local optimal-transport alignment with short-horizon differentiable actor–critic learning. FOCUS matches agent rollout windows to multiple sampled expert segments using a soft best-of-KK objective that emphasizes locally compatible matches. The resulting transport-based costs provide differentiable imitation rewards, while a learned critic bootstraps value beyond the rollout horizon. FOCUS requires neither temporally aligned trajectories nor expert-aligned initialization or teacher forcing.
Across contact-rich locomotion tasks in DFlex, including a musculoskeletal humanoid controlled by 152 muscle activations, FOCUS improves sample efficiency and training stability over adversarial imitation-from-observation methods and prior differentiable imitation baselines.
introduction:
Imitation learning from observations (ILfO) must recover control from state-only demonstrations, without access to expert actions or known temporal correspondence between learner and expert trajectories. This makes supervision fundamentally ambiguous: the learner must determine both what behavior to imitate and where its current behavior corresponds to the demonstration.

Optimal-transport (OT) methods are well suited to the alignment problem because they can compare trajectories or state distributions without requiring point-wise temporal correspondence [12, 39, 9, 15, 23, 7]. In practice, however, these methods typically convert transport costs into surrogate rewards and optimize the policy with zeroth-order RL, inheriting the sample inefficiency and high-variance updates of black-box policy optimization [36]. Adversarial ILfO methods similarly learn from state-only demonstrations through discriminator-derived rewards [52, 60, 6], but can be sensitive to reward modeling, discriminator stability, and tuning.

Differentiable physics simulators provide a complementary route by exposing path-wise policy gradients through the environment dynamics. Simulators such as Brax [16], Warp [35], and DFlex [56] have made this setting practical, while first-order control methods such as SHAC [56], AHAC [19], and SAPO [55] stabilize differentiable control through short-horizon rollouts and critic bootstrapping. These methods, however, assume access to an environment reward. Differentiable imitation already addresses some alignment challenges: GDTW-IL [10] matches observed trajectories through known dynamics, and ILD [8] combines unsynchronized state matching with truncated gradients, using behavior-cloning pretraining. DiffMimic [45] uses expert-aligned initialization and teacher forcing.

We focus on combining local alignment of state-only demonstrations with short differentiable rollouts and critic bootstrapping for contact-rich control. Directly differentiating a trajectory-level imitation loss through long contact-rich rollouts is particularly brittle, since contacts, numerical stiffness, and large early mismatches can produce unstable or uninformative gradients [59, 49, 25, 20].

We introduce FOCUS (First-Order Control Using Optimal Transport Supervision), which turns temporally unaligned state-only demonstrations into short-horizon differentiable supervision. Rather than matching complete trajectories, FOCUS compares each agent rollout window against multiple sampled expert segments using local OT. Softmin-weighted best-of-KK aggregation emphasizes locally compatible matches while retaining differentiability, reducing destructive updates from phase-shifted or unreachable segments. The resulting transport costs provide differentiable imitation rewards, and a learned critic bootstraps value beyond the local matching window. This formulation requires neither expert actions, temporally aligned trajectories, expert-aligned initialization, nor teacher forcing, and can operate even when only a single expert trajectory is available. Fig. 2 illustrates the resulting computational graph.

Across DFlex locomotion tasks [56], including the SNU Humanoid with 152 muscle actuators, FOCUS improves sample efficiency over adversarial ILfO and differentiable imitation baselines, with stable learning on the challenging humanoid tasks. These results support using simulator derivatives for high-dimensional state-only imitation.

title: SACQ: Structure-Aware Codebook Quantization for Ultra-Low-Bit Vision-Language-Action Models
authors: Haesung Lee,Insu Han
subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Machine Learning (cs.LG); Robotics (cs.RO)
abstract:
Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models enable capable robot behavior,
but their large memory footprint limits deployment on resource-constrained robotic platforms.
Weight quantization is a natural remedy, yet post-training quantization (PTQ)
recipes inherited from large language models degrade when applied to VLAs at ultra-low precision.
Existing low-bit PTQ methods often fail to explicitly account for the structure of downstream operations and allocate precision without considering its effect on the policy actions.
We introduce SACQ, an ultra-low-bit weight-only vector-codebook quantization framework for VLAs.
SACQ combines
(1) structure-aware codebook fitting with role-specific quadratic
metrics that reflect input statistics and downstream sensitivity;
(2) action-aware mixed-bit allocation based on the increase in
final-action error as individual layers are compressed; and
(3) two-stage post-quantization refinement that reassigns codeword
indices with second-order error compensation and calibrates codebooks and row-group scales against the decoded action.
Using GR00T N1.7, SACQ achieves 93.85% average success across four LIBERO suites at 1.5 bits per language/action weight while reducing model memory by 4.83×4.83\times.
With INT8 activation quantization and low-precision attention, it retains 93.55% success while running 1.51×1.51\times faster than BF16.
On SimplER, SACQ further achieves 63.76% and 52.27% success under Visual Matching and Variant Aggregation at 2 bits per language/action weight, compared to 58.90% and 53.45% for BF16, respectively.
introduction:
Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have made rapid progress in robotic
manipulation by combining visual perception, language understanding, and action
generation within a single policy (Kim et al., 2025b; Physical Intelligence et al., 2025; NVIDIA et al., 2025).
Recent models perform strongly across diverse manipulation tasks, establishing
VLAs as an important approach to generalist robot policies.
At the same time, VLA models have grown substantially in scale, creating
significant memory demands for resource-constrained robotic platforms.

Post-training quantization (PTQ) is attractive in this setting because it reduces model memory without requiring full retraining.
However, ultra-low-bit VLA quantization is especially challenging because the
effect of a weight error depends strongly on where it appears in the policy.
For example, errors in query and key projections perturb the attention logits
that determine token mixing, whereas errors in feed-forward projections alter
the hidden representations passed to subsequent operations.
As a result, similar layer-local reconstruction errors can have substantially
different consequences depending on where they occur.
A related challenge is precision allocation: a layer that appears insensitive
under a local reconstruction objective can still have a large effect on the
final action.

Representative PTQ methods such as GPTQ (Frantar et al., 2023) minimize layer-wise reconstruction errors using approximate second-order information.
GPTVQ (Van Baalen et al., 2024) extends this reconstruction-based formulation to vector quantization by incorporating the Hessian of the layer-output reconstruction objective into codeword assignment.
Other vector-quantization methods, including AQLM (Egiazarian et al., 2024) and QuIP# (Tseng et al., 2024), further demonstrate the effectiveness of codebook-based representations for extreme LLM compression.
However, these methods primarily optimize quantization with respect to
layer-local reconstruction and do not explicitly account for the operation
in which each projection output is subsequently used.
For VLAs, recent quantization methods increasingly incorporate properties of action generation into the quantization process.
QVLA (Xu et al., 2026) uses action-related sensitivity to guide mixed-precision allocation, while ActQuant (Akbari et al., 2026) combines action-sensitive inter-tensor bit allocation with intra-tensor scale optimization.
HBVLA (Yan et al., 2026) extends VLA weight quantization to the 1-bit regime, while QuantVLA (Zhang et al., 2026) explicitly considers the structure of the diffusion action transformer in its quantization design.
Despite these advances, jointly accounting for projection-specific downstream sensitivity, final-action error, and ultra-low-bit codebook refinement remains challenging.

To address these challenges, we introduce SACQ, a weight-only vector-codebook framework for ultra-low-bit VLA quantization.
First, structure-aware codebook fitting uses projection-specific metrics that reflect each projection’s functional role, rather than relying solely on layer-local reconstruction.
Second, action-aware mixed-bit allocation assigns precision according
to the increase in final-action error per bit saved when each layer is moved
to a lower-precision state.
Third, two-stage post-quantization refinement first reassigns
codeword indices using second-order error compensation and then, with the
updated indices fixed, calibrates codebooks and row-group scales against the
decoded action.
On GR00T N1.7 (NVIDIA et al., 2025), SACQ retains 93.85% average success across the four LIBERO
suites at 1.5 bits per language/action weight, only 0.25
percentage points below the 94.10% BF16 reference, while reducing resident
model memory from 5.677 GB to 1.175 GB, a 4.83×\times reduction.
With an 8-bit activation setting (A8), SACQ achieves a 1.51×1.51\times speedup over BF16 while retaining 93.55% average success.
Evaluating GR00T N1.7 on the SimplER Google Robot benchmark (Li et al., 2025), SACQ further achieves 63.76% and 52.27% success
under Visual Matching and Variant Aggregation, respectively, at 2 bits per language/action weight (bpw), outperforming BF16 on Visual Matching while maintaining comparable performance on Variant Aggregation.

title: MotorSense: A Video-EMG Dataset of Motoric Representations for Action Understanding
authors: Eadom Dessalene,Michael Maynord,Amir-Hossein Shahidzadeh,Botao He,Yasamin Tabatabaee,Ruoshi Liu,Ruohan Gao,Paul Pu Liang,Yiannis Aloimonos
subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Robotics (cs.RO)
comment: NeurIPS 2026. . Project page:this https URL
abstract: Computer vision models learn hand action only from its visual consequences, without access to the underlying embodied motor signals. We address this absence with MotorSense - the first large-scale paired egocentric video and surface electromyography (EMG) dataset. MotorSense pairs bimanual EMG bands with egocentric video and yields synchronized video, bimanual EMG and IMU, and audio across 100100 hours of unscripted manipulation. EMG offers a powerful scalable alternative to manual annotation: it captures finger movement, hand configuration, and the forces exerted between hand and environment as a dense signal free of occlusion and labeler bias, whereas manual annotation is costly, subjective, and unreliable under occlusion. We use MotorSense to learn sensorimotor alignment, producing an organization of action that is shared across the visual and motoric spaces, through cross-modal pre-training between video and EMG. The resultant vision models are then transferred to downstream tasks that benefit from sensorimotor alignment: in this case, action recognition, 3D hand reconstruction, and 3D contact reconstruction. We further demonstrate a generative application in which EMG motor signals are used to condition a video diffusion model, yielding videos of fine-grained hand manipulation. Across four action-centric computer vision tasks and eight popular video datasets, we demonstrate that sensorimotor alignment provides a stronger foundation for visual representation learning than conventional self-supervised learning methods over video, outperforming every baseline across all tasks and datasets evaluated.
introduction:
When humans develop motor and perceptual capabilities, they rely not only on perceiving their surroundings and the visual effects of their actions, but more crucially on the internal motor experiences that accompany these percepts. Yet computer vision models are trained almost exclusively on the visual modality, with no direct access to embodied modalities such as muscle activity. Closing this gap requires incorporating such signals: learning from video alone leaves the underlying action structure implicit in a high-dimensional stream of pixels, whereas incorporating embodied signals transforms this hidden structure into an intrinsically lower-dimensional learnable signal. Among embodied signals, those tied to the hands are especially important, as it is through the hands that humans effect change in the physical world.

To make hand-centric embodied signals available to computer vision we introduce MotorSense, a dataset pairing egocentric video with direct measurements of hand motor activity collected via surface electromyography (EMG) — a modality that records the electrical activity of muscles through the skin. See Figure 1 for example sequences. MotorSense captures a dense signal reflecting how the entirety of the hand engages with the environment: the forces applied, finger movement, and hand configuration throughout each interaction, fine-grained information difficult to observe directly from vision due in part to occlusion. MotorSense goes beyond force datasets such as FEEL [15], TouchScale [35], and OpenTouch [53] with a richer and denser embodied signal, gathered without the use of hand-mounted sensors which visually and physically obstruct interaction. The direct measurement in MotorSense stands in contrast to labels annotated over video datasets (e.g. EPIC-Kitchens, Ego4D), which 1) require manual annotation effort, 2) require pre-defined ontology design, and 3) suffer from annotation error and imprecision.

MotorSense captures hand motor activity using EMG devices consisting of 8 equally spaced electrodes around the lower forearm (see Figure 2). EMG directly senses the electrical activity produced by muscles through the skin, where different muscles produce distinct activation profiles across the electrode array. EMG signals encode both hand forces [17] and fine-grained, dynamic finger articulation [50]. In addition to EMG, we record IMU streams from the wrist device capturing translational and rotational acceleration of the hand in space, and synchronize these signals with egocentric video.

Our primary use of MotorSense is representation learning through sensorimotor alignment between video and EMG data. We induce this alignment with a CLIP-style contrastive objective that jointly trains a video encoder and an EMG encoder in a shared embedding space, pulling together each video clip and the muscle activity that produced it and pushing apart mismatched pairs; EMG thus acts as a privileged supervisory signal that shapes the video representation during pre-training but is discarded at inference, so the aligned video backbone can be transferred to purely visual downstream tasks. We transfer this backbone to three tasks that emphasize hand–object manipulation: 1) recognizing actions in video; 2) 3D hand reconstruction from images; 3) 3D contact reconstruction from images.

Beyond representation learning, MotorSense also supports a generative application: conditioning an image-to-video (I2V) diffusion model on EMG. This addresses a key limitation of existing control modalities, which cannot specify fine-grained, physically grounded hand actions — language captures high-level activity but is underspecified, keypoint trajectories require annotation and are force-agnostic, and neither captures the fine-grained forces of manipulation. EMG supplies exactly this signal, making generative models more useful for VR/AR, where EMG wearables are already emerging as natural control interfaces [73].

The primary contributions of this work are as follows:

Release of the MotorSense dataset: We release the first large-scale paired egocentric video and surface electromyography (EMG) dataset, capturing the muscle activations that cause physical action rather than only their visual effects. MotorSense consists of 100100 hours of natural, unscripted hand–object manipulation, recorded with non-obstructive wrist-worn EMG bands paired with egocentric glasses.

Sensorimotor alignment for action-centric computer vision: We demonstrate that aligning a video encoder with bimanual EMG data through a CLIP-style contrastive objective is a powerful self-supervised pre-training approach, yielding large and consistent gains over a variety of visual-only pre-training methods.

Motor-code conditioning for fine-grained control of video diffusion: We learn motor codes, a discrete VQ-VAE representation of EMG discovered without manual labels, and use them as conditioning inputs to an image-to-video diffusion model. This allows for video generation responsive to fine-grained hand activity, and improves generation fidelity for hand–object interaction.

title: Consensus Within, Competition Between: Decentralized LLM Teams for Perimeter Defense
authors: Khawaja Abaid Ullah,Ananya Acharya,Mohammad Javad Khojasteh
comment: (33 main text and references, 55 supplementary material), 7 main figures. Code:this https URL
abstract:
The use of large language models (LLMs) to coordinate multi-agent teams raises a fundamental architectural question: whether task allocation should be centralized in a single LLM controller or distributed across autonomous LLM agents, particularly when communication is unreliable. In a deliberately simplified perimeter-defense simulation against LLM-controlled intruders, we compared a central commander, an auction-based consensus team and independent agents under five network conditions. Breach rates were 15% for the consensus team, 32% for the commander and 29% for independent agents, and of the different network conditions, only limited radio range changed a team’s breach rate, raising the commander’s. In consensus team, giving a low-cost LLM more authority over the bid computation raised breaches by 38 percentage points. With birds and civilian drones in airspace, we added a photograph for each to the input text state. Only the near-frontier model treated them apart from intruders. Intruders disguised as existing taxidermy bird drones were mistook as birds by both low-cost and near-frontier LLMs, going unpursued in 59–61% of near-frontier decisions (1–16% before). However, a one-sentence forewarning in the prompt lowered it to 0–25%. We find that LLM team with a dedicated external conflict resolution protocol results in fewest breaches.
Code: https://github.com/the-kas-lab/consensus-within-competition-between.
introduction:
Large language models (LLMs) increasingly act as the decision-makers of multi-agent teams, from software agents that solve tasks together Guo et al. (2024); Shen et al. (2023); Zhan et al. (2026); Hong et al. (2024) to robot teams that divide work and plan joint actions Kannan et al. (2024); Mandi et al. (2024). In robotics, this division of work is studied as multi-robot task allocation, the question of which robot should execute which task Gerkey and Matarić (2004). Many LLM teams allocate tasks through a central component, such as an orchestrator that delegates work or a single LLM that assigns subtasks to the whole robot team Yang et al. (2025); Kannan et al. (2024). Central coordination brings scalability bottlenecks and a single point of failure, which leaves the team exposed when the coordinator fails or becomes overloaded Yang et al. (2025). Decentralized multi-agent LLM systems remove this component. Each agent decides from its own local information and communicates directly with its peers Tran et al. (2025). Without an orchestrator, the agents of AgentNet Yang et al. (2025) reached higher accuracy than centralized multi-agent baselines on mathematics, logical question-answering and function-calling benchmarks, and robot arms with one LLM agent each proposed sub-task plans and paths through dialogue Mandi et al. (2024). The evidence is not one-sided. In multi-robot planning tasks, Chen et al. Chen et al. (2024) compared four designs for coordinating the LLMs of a robot team. The robots in the study cooperated without opponents, and each LLM agent was assumed to know the full environment. In the decentralized architecture, agents relay messages through a peer-to-peer network and achieve consensus via sequential debate rounds—iterative challenge-response exchanges designed to verify reasoning steps and organically converge on consistent information. This setup had the lowest success rate, below a central planner, while hybrid designs did best and the central planner scaled worst as robots were added. In a separate study, Kim et al. Kim et al. (2025) evaluated 260 agent-system configurations and found that independent agents, which do not communicate, amplified errors more than centrally coordinated ones, and whether coordination helped depended on the task.
Network degradation and agent attrition are unavoidable in distributed multi-agent systems, so we directly compare centralized and decentralized LLM coordination under these conditions. We study this problem in an adversarial game that serves as a simple abstraction of a cyber-physical system, aiming toward applications where an LLM in a hierarchical control setting decides and allocates tasks as an intruder approaches.

In perimeter defense, a team of defenders must intercept intruders before they reach a protected region Shishika and Kumar (2020), and the intruders score for each one that gets through Shishika et al. (2020). We call an intruder’s entry into the protected region a breach.
Perimeter defense belongs to the broader family of pursuit-evasion and reach-avoid differential games Jaleel and Shamma (2020), in which a team of intruders attempts to reach a target region while defenders attempt to capture or neutralize them Chung et al. (2011); Weintraub et al. (2023); Weintraub et al. (2020); Zhou et al. (2025).
Game-theoretic analyses build team strategies by decomposing the game into local games between small groups and assigning defenders to intruders Shishika et al. (2020), and learned policies imitate a maximum-matching assignment from each defender’s local perception Lee et al. (2023).
In scenarios such as counter-drone defense, defenders must detect intruders with limited sensing Park et al. (2021), share observations over a communication network Maity and Pourghorban (2024), and cope with message loss over non-ideal channels Otte et al. (2020). Assigning defenders to intruders is therefore an allocation decision made under partial and evolving information, where the contextual reasoning of LLM planners can be beneficial. Acharya et al. Acharya et al. (2026) propose a hierarchical architecture in which a per-team LLM planner assigns tactical roles to robots under partial observability, with execution delegated to low-level model predictive controllers. Foundation models Bommasani et al. (2021), including large language models (LLMs) and vision-language-action models, have been applied across many aspects of robotics, from semantic perception to end-to-end control Firoozi et al. (2025); Hu et al. (2023). A common pattern is hierarchical: a language model plans at a high level while lower-level skills or controllers execute the plan Ichter et al. (2023); Jülg et al. (2025). One reason is speed as inference latency is a recognized obstacle to deploying foundation models on robots Firoozi et al. (2025). Our study follows a hierarchical control design (cf. Matni et al. (2024)): in our study a call to the LLM planner took a median of 2.0 s, while model predictive control (MPC) Morari et al. (2015); Mayne et al. (2000) converts each agent’s task into accelerations every 0.1 s, with a barrier constraint keeping agents collision-free except for when a defender is pursuing to neutralize an intruder.
A second design choice is how much of each decision the LLM makes itself rather than leaving it to fixed rules, which we call its authority. At low authority the LLM chooses among options written in advance, as when SayCan Ichter et al. (2023) selects a robot’s next skill from a fixed set, which makes each step of the plan interpretable. At high authority it sets numbers that a solver then uses, as when an LLM writes the weights of a reward that MPC optimizes Yu et al. (2023). That design solved more robot tasks than an LLM that composed predefined skills, and its authors note that constraining what the LLM may set makes the system more stable at some cost in flexibility Yu et al. (2023). Our aim is to study how LLM-driven teams compete against each other in an adversarial game, and how centralized, and decentralized planners, with different levels of authority, compare under different communication conditions.

How a team allocates tasks determines what it needs from its communication network. A central allocator can in principle find the best assignment by gathering all information and planning for the whole team, but it has high communication demands and is a single point of failure Dias et al. (2006). When radio range is limited, reports and orders must be relayed, and a partitioned network cuts agents off from both.
Fully distributed allocation avoids this round trip, but good local choices may not add up to a good team assignment Dias et al. (2006), and agents that each pick their best task can pick the same one Gerkey and Matarić (2004). Market-based methods combine the two by letting agents bid for tasks Dias et al. (2006). The consensus-based auction algorithm (CBAA) reaches a conflict-free assignment through local message exchange alone and tolerates inconsistent information across the team Choi et al. (2009). Auction methods with conventional bids have been tested under lossy and fading communication Otte et al. (2020); Lott and Honary (2026), and LLM teams have been compared under centralized, decentralized and hybrid communication on cooperative planning tasks Chen et al. (2024). By framing the problem as an adversarial game, we let teams of LLMs compete directly against one another, and we compare a central LLM commander with decentralized LLM agents that resolve allocation conflicts through a consensus auction, under progressively degraded communication networks. We also evaluate both architectures when some agents submit falsified estimates (Section 4.4).

In a typical airspace, defender agents share the sky with birds and civilian drones, and detecting drones, birds, and other distractors is the subject of a dedicated benchmark challenge Coluccia et al. (2021). A textual state-based only defender treats birds, civilian drones and intruders the same way, i.e. as contacts. We refer to birds and civilian drones as non-hostile contacts. Without a recognition and classification mechanism, the defender cannot tell the intruders apart from the non-hostile contacts. And, pursuing a non-hostile contact costs more than just time as a defender that touches any contact is lost, resulting in reduction of defensive capacity. Multimodal LLMs, which accept images in addition to text, can inspect a contact before deciding whether to engage it, but whether this ability helps the team depends on two factors: the model must correctly classify the object, and the coordination interface must allow it to act on that judgment. Using image-based contact classification, we consider four contact types (birds, civilian drones, intruder drones, and disguised intruder drones) and ask how centralized and decentralized LLM teams, each run with both a low-cost and a near-frontier model, handle these contacts under the communication conditions studied above. We deliberately keep the perception component simple: the aim is a reproducible benchmark for multimodal LLM decision-making in adversarial games, in which the effects of team architecture and communication degradation can be isolated from perception difficulty.

Here we compare three LLM-coordinated defender teams that differ in where LLM decision-making is placed within the defensive architecture (Fig. 1). The first, the commander team, places all authority in a central commander, whose LLM assigns tasks to every agent. The second, the consensus team, has decentralized agents that bid for tasks and agree on who takes which through a consensus-based auction. Each agent’s LLM adjusts its own bids according to its authority. At low authority it can only choose a weight profile, a priority for each intruder and up to three preferred tasks. At high authority it sets the weights of the bid formula and a multiplier from 0 to 2 for each intruder’s pursuit value. The third, the independent team, uses the same LLMs and bids, but each agent chooses its task independently based on its own highest bid, without an auction.

Each team defends a region for 40 seconds against LLM-controlled intruders from 30 random starting configurations (seeds), with two and four intruders, under five network conditions (an ideal network, independent message loss, burst message loss, a compromised defender that falsifies reports, and limited radio range with relaying). Four lessons emerged. First, conflict resolution mattered. Across the four network conditions without falsified reports, intruders breached the region in 15% of episodes against the consensus team, 32% against the commander team, and 29% against the independent team, with most of the difference arising in episodes with four intruders.
Second, the commander team was the most sensitive to network conditions.
Its breach rate rose by 18 percentage points (95% interval: +1 to +36) when radio range was limited, whereas message loss and falsified reports did not result in any significant differences between the architectures. Third, level of authority assigned to LLM for decision making should depend on the capability of LLM being used
as with a low-cost model, high authority raised the number of breaches by 38 percentage points,
however, a near-frontier model under high authority did not see an increase in breach rate.
Fourth, non-hostile contacts, which tested the models’ visual-language capabilities, showed the same divide. Across five seeds, the near-frontier model never lost a defender to a non-hostile contact in either the centralized or the decentralized role, whereas each low-cost model team, lost 3 to 5 defenders in total across the five episodes.

These lessons come from a testbed that is deliberately simplified, so that coordination can be studied under control. Agents move as point masses with bounded acceleration in a two-dimensional arena of abstract units, with no wind or other disturbance. They sense opponents without noise and without missed detections inside a fixed field of view. The photographs are reference pictures rather than views from an onboard camera. We make no claim that this setup represents a deployed counter-drone system. Its value is as a benchmark for LLM-driven coordination, a simplified abstraction of cyber-physical teams.
In summary, we make the following contributions.

We establish a benchmark for multi-agent LLM coordination in a perimeter-defense game, in which LLM-driven defenders face LLM-controlled intruders over a network that can be degraded. The LLMs are used as released, without fine-tuning, task-specific training or example answers, and every episode can be re-simulated from its recorded model answers.

We compare central and decentralized LLM coordination on matched episodes under message loss, limited radio range and falsified reports, which gives the first two lessons.

We test how much an LLM should be allowed to decide, by running the consensus team at high authority with a low-cost and a near-frontier model, which gives the third lesson.

We extend multi-agent LLM coordination to multimodal, image-based contact classification, with birds, civilian drones and intruders disguised as taxidermy bird drones.

1. We establish a benchmark for multi-agent LLM coordination in a perimeter-defense game, in which LLM-driven defenders face LLM-controlled intruders over a network that can be degraded. The LLMs are used as released, without fine-tuning, task-specific training or example answers, and every episode can be re-simulated from its recorded model answers.

2. We compare central and decentralized LLM coordination on matched episodes under message loss, limited radio range and falsified reports, which gives the first two lessons.

3. We test how much an LLM should be allowed to decide, by running the consensus team at high authority with a low-cost and a near-frontier model, which gives the third lesson.

4. We extend multi-agent LLM coordination to multimodal, image-based contact classification, with birds, civilian drones and intruders disguised as taxidermy bird drones.

title: CuPIQP: A Batched and Differentiable QP Solver on GPUs for Robot Learning and Control
authors: Fenglong Song,Roland Schwan,Yuwen Chen,Yuning Jiang,Colin N. Jones
abstract:
Quadratic programs (QPs) are fundamental building blocks of many robotic tasks such as inverse kinematics, whole-body control, and model predictive control. Extending these methods to large-scale robot learning and control requires solving many QPs concurrently and, for end-to-end learning, differentiating through their solutions. Efficient batched optimization is therefore essential to bringing established model-based methods into GPU-based robotics pipelines. We present cuPIQP, a batched and differentiable QP solver on GPUs based on a proximal interior-point method, with unified support for dense, sparse, and multistage problems. The solver exploits parallelism across independent QPs and their internal structure while preserving per-problem numerical updates and termination decisions. Benchmarks with up to 16384 QPs per batch demonstrate solve-time speedups of up to 18.8×18.8\times over Moreau and 4.26×4.26\times over eight-core PIQP. In an end-to-end learning task, cuPIQP accelerates training by 4.6×4.6\times over QPAX and 7.8×7.8\times over Moreau.
By reducing the computational cost, cuPIQP provides efficient, reusable infrastructure for integrating model-based optimization into large-scale robot learning and control.
introduction:
Quadratic programs lie on the critical path of many robot
control tasks.
QP solvers have traditionally been designed to minimize the online latency for solving one or a tiny batch of problems. Existing solvers such as qpOASES [1], OSQP [2],
HPIPM [3], ProxQP [4] and PIQP [5] are highly effective under this execution model.

Nonetheless, an increasingly important class of robot learning and control workloads follows a different execution model, where optimization is embedded in an offline training pipeline and evaluated concurrently over a large number of instances [6, 7, 8, 9].
In such workloads, the same optimization layer is applied across problem instances arising from parallel environments or sampled trajectories [10]. The resulting computational primitive is a batch of BB independent QPs {𝒫j}j=1B\{\mathcal{P}_{j}\}_{j=1}^{B}, where the jj-th problem
𝒫j\mathcal{P}_{j} is given by

A class of GPU-enabled solvers targets individual large-scale sparse optimization problems [11, 12, 13] where sparse linear algebra is sufficiently intensive to amortize GPU kernel-launch and synchronization overheads, and reducing such overheads is therefore not a primary design objective.
By contrast, these overheads can dominate when solving large batches of small-scale QPs.
Moreover, they do not explicitly support batched solving.
Although independent QPs can be assembled into a single block-diagonal problem, this formulation represents repeated structure as generic sparsity rather than exploiting it through batch-oriented operations, potentially resulting in suboptimal performance.

Another class of solvers treats the batch as an explicit computational dimension for general QPs.
QPTH [14] and QPAX [15] implement a differentiable interior-point method that solves batches of dense QPs concurrently on GPUs.
Moreau [16] is a differentiable solver for sparse conic optimization problems with shared sparsity pattern, providing both CPU and GPU backends.
However, each solver is specialized for a single problem structure and does not provide unified support for dense, sparse, and multistage QPs.

A complementary line of work exploits batching at the level of the complete nonlinear MPC pipeline.
Recent GPU-based frameworks provide batched and differentiable sequential quadratic programming (SQP) implementations for large-batch MPC [17, 18, 19, 20]. These frameworks generate a batch of structurally homogeneous QP subproblems at each SQP iteration, making an efficient batched QP solver a core primitive of the overall pipeline.
On CPUs, acados [21, 22] provides a batched and differentiable interface by parallelizing independent solves across multiple processor cores.

Its main technical contributions are summarized as follows:

Batch-native GPU execution.
We design the solver around batches of independent QPs, exploiting problem-level parallelism for high throughput while retaining independent iterates, convergence decisions, solutions, and termination statuses for all problems in the batch.

We design the solver around batches of independent QPs, exploiting problem-level parallelism for high throughput while retaining independent iterates, convergence decisions, solutions, and termination statuses for all problems in the batch.

Structure-specialized QP backends.
cuPIQP supports dense, sparse, and multistage QPs through specialized data layouts and linear algebra backends under a unified solver interface, allowing users to exploit the structure of a variety of problem classes.

GPU-resident integration and differentiation.
Problem data, solver iterates, per-problem statuses, and adjoint computations remain on the GPU. The solver interoperates directly with CUDA-resident arrays without host staging, provides implicit differentiation through a PyTorch interface, and supports CUDA Graph capture on compatible execution paths to reduce CPU orchestration and kernel-launch overhead.

title: Robot Navigation and Canine Welfare: A Pilot Study Surfacing Challenges for Cross-Species Legibility and Proxy Validity in Animal-Machine Interaction
authors: Haoxiang Zhang,Nancy Smith
comment: Accepted at ACI2026
abstract: Autonomous delivery robots increasingly share residential spaces with companion animals, yet navigation behavior is rarely designed with animal welfare in mind. This paper presents a pilot study evaluating a curve-out maneuver, a laterally arcing pass-by trajectory triggered at the dog’s alert distance, proposed as a candidate welfare-informed navigation intervention grounded in canine social communication research and legible motion theory. Following a research through design approach, we developed and evaluated a first design iteration of the artifact in a naturalistic home environment with a companion dog. Contrary to our hypothesis, the curve-out produced a more acute stress response than the straight-line baseline. We argue that discontinuous execution limitation, the robot stopping and reorienting multiple times to approximate the arc, undermined legibility, which in itself became a stressor. The pilot surfaces the legibility of robot behavior to non-humans’ eyes and proxy stimulus validity as structural challenges for AMI and repositions the design problem for future work.
introduction:
Autonomous delivery robots, designed to deliver food and groceries, are increasingly being deployed in residential neighborhoods (Lakshmi and Bahli, 2020). As these systems move beyond controlled industrial contexts into urban spaces of daily living, they encounter not only humans but also companion animals. Väätäjä et al. (Väätäjä et al., 2023) report that about 17% of the dog owners surveyed found their dog reacted negatively when first encountering autonomous delivery robots, some developing persistent adverse associations. Those unexpected encounters signal the situation where the technology was not designed for animals but affects them anyway (Mancini, 2024), positioning dogs as usees who are affected by those robots and have no agency to opt out, negotiate, or influence the robot’s behavior (Hirskyj-Douglas et al., 2021). Animals in general appear to be excluded from obstacle-detection design: commercial delivery robot operators describe their sensors as targeting people, cars, and obstacles (Uber Technologies, Inc., 2026), seemingly classing companion animals alongside inert obstacles rather than as agents the system is designed to perceive and respond to. As a result, the burden of adapting to unpredictable robot behavior falls entirely on the animals. This work takes an early step toward redistributing that burden to the machine through deliberate design, using a single navigation intervention as a probe to surface the challenges such redistribution entails.

Following a research through design approach (Zimmerman et al., 2007) (Sas et al., 2014), this paper proposes an animal-welfare-informed robot navigation behavior, a curve-out maneuver, as a candidate design intervention for autonomous robots operating in animal-inhabited urban environments. This design is informed by ethological research on canine social communication, which identifies curved and indirect approaches as stress and conflict-reducing signals in multi-species interaction (Siniscalchi et al., 2018) (Firnkes et al., 2017), and in the legible motion theory of human-robot interaction (Dragan et al., 2013), which shows that the behavior design could communicate the intention of the agent to an observer. We treat trajectory geometry as a spatial design parameter and the curve-out as an artifact intended to transform a current problematic state, which is identified as a stress-triggering direct passing-by robot navigation behavior, to a preferred one, where robot movement actively signals non-threat and supports coexistence in a compact urban environment. The artifact represents a first design iteration, intended to be refined through subsequent cycles informed by pilot observation. A pilot evaluation was conducted in a naturalistic home environment with a companion dog with documented adverse reactions to delivery robots.

By isolating trajectory geometry as a spatial design parameter and conducting a structured pilot evaluation, this work contributes to the emerging Animal Machine Interaction agenda, surfaces cross-species legibility design as a candidate mechanism for future investigation, and documents the methodological challenges of evaluating welfare-informed robot behaviors with companion animals.

title: AquaProbe: Efficient Adaptation of Frozen Vision Models for Underwater Images
authors: Md Shihabul Islam Shovo,Nishi Kanta Paul,Trung Dong,Xiaomin Lin
subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Machine Learning (cs.LG); Robotics (cs.RO)
abstract:
Reliable visual perception is essential for safe autonomous underwater
exploration. Yet vision models pretrained on terrestrial images become less
reliable underwater, where turbidity, backscatter, and wavelength-dependent
attenuation alter scene appearance. Existing adaptation methods either spread adapters equally across
the encoder depth or select layers using the divergence between two fixed
domains. In this paper, we introduce AquaProbe for measuring how the location of the
domain gap changes with water type and imaging range. AquaProbe separates
newly introduced divergence from that accumulated through a frozen vision
encoder using paired clean and physically rendered images and allocates a
fixed LoRA budget according to the measured profile. The segmentation mean Intersection-over-Union (mIoU) for the proportional LoRA
rank allocation, based on the measured profile, is 70.1; this is a better
result than uniform LoRA rank allocation by 1.9 mIoU points while having the
same parameter budget of 0.59 million adapter parameters. The three-way
router, conditioned on estimated condition clusters, achieves 70.6 mIoU on the
standard SUIM split and 63.4 AUDRC under held-out degradation.
introduction:
Safe autonomous underwater exploration requires reliable visual perception,
which is often built on vision backbones pretrained on data from terrestrial
environments. Underwater images are distributed differently from the
pretraining distribution due to physically caused degradation: light is
attenuated at wavelength-dependent rates, and part of the observed radiance is
backscattered ambient light rather than scene radiance
[1]. With increased turbidity and imaging
range, contrast and visibility decrease, particular colour channels collapse,
and high frequency details are lost, so the domain shift is condition dependent.

Fine-tuning such a pretrained encoder is difficult because underwater
annotations are scarce and computation and energy resources for onboard
inference are constrained; consequently, full fine-tuning is rarely attractive.
Parameter-efficient fine-tuning helps address these problems by freezing the
backbone and training only a small set of additional weights
[15, 16, 19]. This reduces adaptation
cost, but given a limited budget for allocation, it is essential to determine
how this budget should be divided between the layers of the encoder.

Adapter allocation is commonly uniform, based on the assumption that the
domain shift affects all depths equally. Adaptive algorithms, including
importance-driven budget allocation [45], use the
optimisation statistics collected during training as opposed to directly
measuring the shift. Layer-wise similarity analysis provides such
a measurement [22, 38] and has been used to set
rank before training [7]. However, this analysis is performed
between a fixed pair of domains and therefore yields a static adapter
allocation, whereas underwater conditions vary continuously with water
type and imaging range, so one static profile may be insufficient. To measure
the variation and allocate LoRA rank accordingly, we introduce AquaProbe.

With AquaProbe’s degradation-conditioned representational divergence
analysis, we address three problems with the measurements of the
representation gap. First, the representation gap between a pristine set and
a corrupted one is characteristic only of this pair of distributions
[3] and cannot indicate whether its location reflects
the encoder or imaging conditions. Since underwater degradation has a
closed-form model, we render clean images with a two-term physical model
parametrized by Jerlov water type and imaging range, so that the profile is a
function of these parameters and the stability of the gap is an empirical
question. Second, layer-wise divergence is reported cumulatively and compounds
with depth, so the curve rises regardless of where the damage starts.
Instead, the per-block increase in divergence within the frozen encoder
is recorded. Third, allocation based on representational
measurements assumes that a large gap warrants more capacity, but this
assumption is rarely validated against downstream behaviour. A single-block
sweep characterizes this relationship. Finally, we derive a
rank-based allocation method from these profiles and compare it with uniform,
random, reversed, and prior allocation methods, as well as an
exploratory router operating over nested prefixes of per-cluster allocations.

Our contributions are as follows:

We present a degradation-conditioned probe that measures the
per-block increase in divergence and show that it behaves
differently from the commonly reported cumulative divergence.

The profile drift index is compared to the average from a null distribution
obtained through resampling, with peak dispersion greater than one
block in two out of the three backbones and falling below that
threshold for the third.

We investigate the relationship between divergence and adaptation
utility through a single-block sweep, converting an assumption made by
allocation-by-analysis methods into a measured quantity.

A rank allocation policy is developed from the profile, and its performance is
compared to uniform, random, reversed, and two prior allocation
methods under a matched budget, along with an exploratory router using nested
per-cluster prefixes with a matching parameter count (0.03%0.03\%).

3. We investigate the relationship between divergence and adaptation

4. A rank allocation policy is developed from the profile, and its performance is

title: How a group that cannot communicate knows itself by its enemy
authors: Gregory Falco
subjects: Computer Science and Game Theory (cs.GT); Multiagent Systems (cs.MA); Robotics (cs.RO); Systems and Control (eess.SY)
comment: main text; 35-page SI Appendix included as an ancillary file. Code and data:this https URL
abstract: Teams that cannot communicate seem stuck with what each member sees. We show that their opponent can tell them the rest. Silent hunters, jammed robots and traders who never meet all face an adversary that reacts to the group as a whole; every member can read that reaction, a tell, and learn what no member knows alone. One tell can do the work of a message from every member. The adversary would rather hide, but hiding interferes with its own task, and a team that commits in advance to how it will respond decides how much hiding is worth. A committed team never loses when its opponent cares more about its own goals, and does as well as a fully informed team exactly when the opponent’s stake outweighs any gain from lying. Below that point the team learns more by trusting less: in a solved Gaussian model it obtains the truth by promising not to use all of it and keeps the cost the opponent would have paid to conceal; an exact test decides when this holds in finite games. How a team spreads its trust matters too. A lone uninformed member with a full-support prior needs a private coin, but with additive squared-error losses two interchangeable members who respond differently replace it, and a small discount on trust insures against misjudging the enemy. Information, on this view, is not only gathered or aggregated; it is produced by how a team commits to respond.
